gm: Engaging in the Conduct of the Bodhisattvas

dm: The Introductory Meaning
gm: Prologue

dm: In the language of India: *Bodhicaryāvatāra*.
gm: In the Indian language: Bodhisattvacaryāvatāra.

dm: In the language of Tibet: *Byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa la 'jug pa* (Engaging in the Bodhisattva Deeds).
gm: In the Tibetan language: Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva.

dm: Homage to all buddhas and bodhisattvas.
gm: Homage to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas.

dm: The Benefits of Bodhicitta
gm: Chapter One: Explaining the Benefits of Bodhicitta

dm: Respectfully bowing to the Sugatas who possess the Dharmakāya, along with their heirs, and to all who are worthy of veneration, I shall describe the engagement in the vows of the Sugatas' heirs, Having condensed them in accordance with the scriptures.
gm: To the Sugatas, endowed with the Dharmakāya, along with their heirs, And to all who are worthy of homage, I respectfully bow down; Then, entering into the vows of the heirs of the Sugatas, I shall explain it concisely in accordance with scripture.

dm: There is nothing here that has not been said before, Nor do I possess any skill in the art of composition. Therefore, I have no thought that this will benefit others; I have composed this in order to habituate my own mind.
gm: There is nothing said here that has not appeared before, Nor do I have any skill in composition; Therefore, I have no thought of benefiting others, I have composed this to cultivate my own mind.

dm: Through this, the power of my faith to cultivate virtue may increase for a while; Furthermore, if others of equal fortune to myself should see this, It may prove meaningful for them as well.
gm: In order to cultivate virtue, the force of my faith Will for a time increase because of this; And if others, equal in fortune to myself, Should see these words, they may be meaningful.

dm: This leisure and endowment is extremely difficult to find. Having attained that which can accomplish the purpose of a human being, If one does not accomplish what is beneficial in this life, How could such a perfect opportunity ever be found again?
gm: These freedoms and advantages are extremely hard to find; Since the attainment that fulfills human purpose has been found, If one does not accomplish what is beneficial in this life, How will such a perfect opportunity arise again later?

dm: Just as a flash of lightning in the darkness of a cloud-shrouded night Momentarily reveals everything in its brilliant light, So too, through the power of the Buddha, A virtuous mind occasionally and briefly arises in the world.
gm: Just as on a dark night in the womb of clouds A flash of lightning brilliantly illuminates for an instant, In the same way, by the power of the Buddha, occasionally Worldly intelligence for merit arises for a moment.

dm: Therefore, virtue is always extremely weak, While sin is of great strength and utterly unbearable. Except for the mind of perfect enlightenment, What other virtue could ever overcome it?
gm: Thus virtue is perpetually feeble, While evil is extremely powerful and unbearable; If it were not for the mind of perfect awakening, What other virtue could overcome it?

dm: The Lords of Sages, who have deeply contemplated for many eons, Have seen that this alone is beneficial. By this, the boundless multitudes of beings Will easily attain the supreme bliss.
gm: The Lords of Sages, who have contemplated for many eons, Have seen that this alone is beneficial; By this, immeasurable multitudes of beings Will easily attain the supreme bliss.

dm: Those who wish to overcome the hundreds of sufferings of existence, Those who wish to dispel the miseries of sentient beings, And those who wish to enjoy hundreds of manifold happinesses, Should never forsake the awakening mind.
gm: Those who wish to destroy the hundreds of sufferings of existence, Who wish to dispel the unhappiness of sentient beings, And who wish to experience hundreds of great joys, Should never give up the mind of awakening.

dm: Once the awakening mind has been generated, in that very instant, The wretched ones bound in the prison of cyclic existence Are called children of the Sugatas, And become objects of homage for the world, including its gods and humans.
gm: If the mind of awakening is generated, in an instant, The wretched ones bound in the prison of cyclic existence Will be called children of the Sugatas, And will become worthy of reverence by the world's gods and humans.

dm: Like the supreme form of an alchemical elixir, It takes this impure body and transforms it into the priceless Jewel of a Victor’s body; therefore, firmly grasp That which is called the awakening mind.
gm: Like the supreme form of the gold-making elixir, It takes this impure body and transforms it Into the priceless jewel of a Conqueror's body; Therefore, firmly hold to this so-called mind of awakening.

dm: Since the sole Guide of beings, through his immeasurable intellect, Has thoroughly examined it and seen its great value, Those who wish to escape the realms of cyclic existence Should firmly grasp this precious awakening mind.
gm: Since the sole captain of beings, with limitless intellect, Has thoroughly examined it and found it to be highly precious, Those who wish to be separated from the states of wandering Should perfectly and firmly hold the precious mind of awakening.

dm: All other virtues are like the plantain tree; Once they have produced their fruit, they are exhausted. But the tree of the awakening mind perpetually bears fruit, And rather than being exhausted, it increases ever more.
gm: All other virtues are just like the plantain tree: Having borne their fruit, they are exhausted; But the tree of the mind of awakening constantly Bears fruit, is not exhausted, and continually grows.

dm: Even if one has committed extremely unbearable sins, Just as one relies on a hero to escape great terror, Why would those who are conscientious not rely upon That which swiftly liberates them?
gm: Even if one has committed extremely unbearable evils, Just as one relies on a hero when in great fear, By relying on it, one is liberated in an instant; Why do conscientious beings not rely upon it?

dm: Like the fire at the end of an eon, it will surely Incinerate great sins in a single instant. Its immeasurable benefits were explained By the wise Protector Maitreya to Sudhana.
gm: Like the fire at the end of time, it Certainly burns up great evils in a single instant; Its immeasurable benefits Were explained to Sudhana by the wise Lord Maitreya.

dm: To summarize that awakening mind, It should be understood as being of two types: The mind that aspires for awakening, and The mind that engages in awakening.
gm: In brief, that mind of awakening Should be understood as being of two types: The mind aspiring to awakening, and The mind entering awakening itself.

dm: Just as one understands the distinction Between the desire to go and the act of going, In the same way, the wise should understand The distinction between these two in proper sequence.
gm: Just as one understands the difference Between wishing to go and actually going, Likewise, the wise should understand the difference Between these two in their respective order.

dm: Although great fruits arise from the aspiring mind While wandering in cyclic existence, It does not produce a continuous flow of merit In the way that the engaging mind does.
gm: From the mind aspiring to awakening, Great fruits arise while in cyclic existence, but Unlike the mind entering awakening, A continuous stream of merit does not arise.

dm: From the moment one has correctly adopted that mind With an irreversible resolve In order to thoroughly liberate The infinite realms of sentient beings,
gm: From the moment that, In order to completely free the infinite realms of beings, With a mind that does not turn back, One perfectly takes up that mind,

dm: From this moment onward, even while sleeping or Becoming heedless, a force of merit Continuous and manifold Will arise, as vast as space.
gm: From then on, even while asleep Or inattentive, a force of merit, Uninterrupted and manifold, Continually arises, equal to the sky.

dm: This is reasonable, and as it was Requested by Subāhu, For the sake of beings with lesser aspirations, The Tathāgata himself has spoken.
gm: Along with the reasoning for this, In the Questions of Subāhu, For the sake of beings of lesser inclination, It was taught by the Tathāgata himself.

dm: If even thinking, "I shall dispel The mere headaches of sentient beings," Is a beneficial intention Endowed with immeasurable merit,
gm: "I shall cure just the headaches Of sentient beings"—even if one just thinks this, Possessing that beneficial intention Endows one with immeasurable merit.

dm: Then what need is there to mention the desire To dispel the infinite suffering of every single sentient being, And the desire to bring each one To immeasurable excellence?
gm: The discomforts of each and every sentient being, Immeasurable as they are, one wishes to dispel; And for each, immeasurable good qualities One wishes to accomplish—what need is there to mention?

dm: Whether it be a father or even a mother, Who else possesses such a benevolent intention? Do even the gods or the sages possess it? Does even Brahmā have such a mind?
gm: Whether it be a father or even a mother, Who has such a beneficial mind? Do the gods or the sages, Or even Brahmā have this?

dm: If those very beings have never before, Even in their dreams, dreamed of such an intention For their own sake, How could it ever arise for the sake of others?
gm: If, for those very sentient beings in the past, Such a mind, even for their own sake, Was not dreamt of even in a dream, How could it arise for the sake of others?

dm: That intention to benefit sentient beings, Which does not arise in others even for their own sake— This extraordinary jewel of the mind Is born as an unprecedented wonder.
gm: Even for their own sake, in others This intention for the sake of sentient beings does not arise. This extraordinary jewel of a mind Is born as an unprecedented wonder.

dm: The cause of joy for all wandering beings, The medicine for the suffering of sentient beings— How could the merit of such a precious mind Ever be measured?
gm: The cause of joy for all transmigrating beings, The medicine for the suffering of sentient beings— The merit of that jewel-like mind, How could it ever be measured?

dm: If even the mere thought of being beneficial Excels the worship of the Buddhas, What need is there to mention striving For the welfare and happiness of every single being without exception?
gm: If merely intending to be beneficial Is more exalted than making offerings to the Buddhas, Of all sentient beings without exception, What need is there to mention striving for their happiness and welfare?

dm: Although they have the desire to cast off suffering, They rush headlong into suffering itself. Although they desire happiness, through delusion They destroy their own happiness as if it were an enemy.
gm: Although having the wish to abandon suffering, They run directly toward suffering itself. Although desiring happiness, out of ignorance, They destroy their own happiness as if it were an enemy.

dm: For those who are destitute of happiness And burdened by many sufferings, It satisfies them with every joy, Cuts through all their suffering,
gm: For those who are destitute of happiness And who have many sufferings, It satisfies them with all happiness And cuts through all sufferings,

dm: And even dispels their delusion. Where is there any virtue equal to that? Where could there be such a friend? How could there ever be such merit?
gm: And dispels even their ignorance. Where is there a virtue comparable to that? Where is there a friend like that? Where is there even merit like that?

dm: If even one who returns a favor is worthy of some praise, What need is there to mention a Bodhisattva Who performs good deeds without being asked?
gm: If whoever repays a benefit done to them Is worthy of some praise, The Bodhisattva who does good without being asked, What need is there to mention?

dm: The world honors as a "doer of virtue" someone who provides A mere meal of ordinary food to a few beings, Giving it contemptuously just to satisfy them for half a day, Even if it is only a momentary gift.
gm: One who provides regular food to a few beings, Giving merely a meal for a brief instant, Or satisfying them for half a day with contempt, Is honored by people as a doer of virtue.

dm: What need is there to mention one who constantly bestows Upon an infinite number of sentient beings for an endless duration The unsurpassed bliss of the Sugatas, Which fulfills every heartfelt aspiration?
gm: To limitless numbers of sentient beings for a long time, The unsurpassable bliss of the Sugatas, Which fulfills all the wishes in their minds, What need is there to mention constantly giving?

dm: The Sage has declared that whoever gives rise to a malicious thought Toward such a benefactor, a Son of the Conquerors, Will remain in hell for as many aeons As the number of malicious thoughts produced.
gm: If anyone toward such a benefactor, a Child of the Conquerors, Generates an evil thought, that one For eons equal to the number of evil thoughts generated Will abide in hell, so the Capable One has taught.

dm: However, if one develops a deeply devoted mind, Its fruit will increase even more than that; Even when great difficulties arise for the Bodhisattvas, No sin occurs, and their virtue naturally increases.
gm: But if anyone gives rise to a mind of deep faith, Its fruit increases even more than that. Even in great adversity for the Children of the Conquerors, Non-virtue does not arise, and virtue naturally increases.

dm: I prostrate to the bodies of those in whom That most precious and excellent mind has arisen; I take refuge in that source of happiness, Who brings about bliss even for those who cause them harm.
gm: In whomever that supreme, precious mind Has been born, I bow to their body, and To those whom even doing harm connects one to happiness, I go for refuge to those sources of happiness.

dm: This is the first chapter, titled "Explaining the Benefits of the Awakening Mind," from the *Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva*.
gm: From Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva, this is the first chapter, called Explaining the Benefits of the Awakening Mind.

dm: Chapter Two: Confession of Negativities
gm: Chapter Two: Confession of Sins

dm: In order to fully embrace that precious mind, I make excellent offerings to the Tathāgatas, To the stainless Jewel of the sublime Dharma, And to the Sons of the Buddha, those oceans of virtue.
gm: In order to take hold of that precious mind, To the Tathāgatas and the holy Dharma, The stainless Jewel, and the Children of the Buddhas, Who are oceans of qualities, I make excellent offerings.

dm: Whatever flowers and fruits there may be, And whatever kinds of medicinal plants exist, Whatever precious gems there are in the world, And whatever pure and pleasing waters there are;
gm: However many flowers and fruits there are, And whatever kinds of medicine there are, However many jewels there are in the world, And whatever pure and pleasing waters there are,

dm: Likewise, the mountains of precious gems, The forest regions, secluded and delightful, The trees adorned and beautified with flowers, And all the trees whose branches hang low with excellent fruit;
gm: Jewel mountains, and likewise Forest regions, secluded and joyful, Trees adorned and fully decked with flowers, And trees with branches bowing down with good fruit,

dm: In the worlds of the gods and others, there are fragrances, Incense, wish-fulfilling trees, and jewel trees, Various kinds of harvests that grow without being sown, And all other ornaments worthy of being offered;
gm: Fragrances in the worlds of gods and others, Incense, wish-fulfilling trees, and jewel trees, Various crops that grow without being plowed, And other ornaments worthy of being offered,

dm: Lakes and ponds adorned with lotuses, Graced by swans with voices most melodious and charming, Reaching to the furthest limits of the vast expanse of space, All these things, which are entirely unpossessed;
gm: Lakes and ponds adorned with lotuses, Endowed with the highly melodious and pleasing calls of wild geese, Extending to the limits of the infinite sphere of space, All those things that are unowned,

dm: I take up with my mind and offer them well to the Munis, the supreme beings, Together with their spiritual heirs; O sublime objects of offering, you who are filled with great compassion, Regard me with affection and accept these offerings of mine.
gm: Taking them with my mind, to the Capable Ones, the supreme of beings, And to their Children, I make excellent offerings; May those holy objects of offering, the ones of great compassion, Think of me with love and accept these things of mine.

dm: I am destitute and lack merit, And have no other wealth for making offerings. Therefore, O Protectors who care for the welfare of others, Please accept this through your own power for my sake.
gm: I am without merit and extremely destitute, And I have no other wealth for offering. Therefore, may the Protectors whose thoughts are for the welfare of others, By their own power, accept this for my sake.

dm: To the Victors and their spiritual heirs, I offer my entire body forever. O Supreme Beings, please accept me completely; With devotion, I shall become your servant.
gm: To the Conquerors and their Children, I Offer my entire body forever. Supreme Beings, please accept me completely; With devotion I will become your subject.

dm: Since I have been fully accepted by you, I shall be fearless in existence and act for the benefit of sentient beings. I shall perfectly transcend my previous misdeeds, And shall commit no further sins hereafter.
gm: Because I am completely accepted by you, I will not fear in cyclic existence and will benefit sentient beings. I will perfectly overcome my previous negative deeds, And I will not commit other negative deeds henceforth.

dm: In a bathing chamber of exquisite fragrance, With a floor of clear and sparkling crystal, Adorned with lovely pillars of blazing jewels, And draped with canopies of shimmering pearls,
gm: In a bathhouse that is exceedingly fragrant, Arranged with a crystal floor, clear and shining, Endowed with pleasing pillars of blazing jewels, And a canopy of radiant pearls spread above,

dm: To the Tathāgatas and their spiritual heirs, I offer a bath from many precious vases, Beautifully filled with delightful, scented water, Accompanied by manifold songs and music.
gm: To the Tathāgatas and their Children, With many jeweled vases of scented water, Beautifully and perfectly filled, alongside songs And various music, I offer a bath.

dm: With incomparable, clean, and highly perfumed cloths, I wipe their bodies dry. Then, I offer them supreme, beautifully colored, And exquisitely fragrant robes.
gm: With garments that are unequaled, Clean and infused with supreme fragrances, I dry their bodies. Then to them, excellently dyed Holy robes, exceedingly fragrant, I offer.

dm: With various fine garments, thin and soft, And hundreds of those most sublime ornaments, I shall adorn the noble Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, and the rest.
gm: With various fine garments, thin and soft, And with hundreds of those supreme ornaments, The noble Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, and others, I will adorn.

dm: With the finest perfumes, whose fragrance pervades The entire billion-fold world system, I shall anoint the bodies of all the Lords of Sages, Which blaze with a radiant luster like burnished, refined gold.
gm: With fragrances whose scent wafts throughout the three thousandfold world systems, By these supreme perfumes, the bodies of all the Lords of Capable Ones, Like purified and polished refined gold, Radiant and blazing, I will anoint.

dm: To the Lords of Sages, the supreme objects of veneration, I offer delightful Mandārava flowers, lotuses, Utpalas, and all other fragrant blossoms, As well as beautifully arranged and enchanting garlands.
gm: To the Lords of Capable Ones, the supreme objects of offering, with pleasing Mandāra flowers and lotuses, Utpalas, and all fragrant things, And beautifully strung, pleasing garlands, I make offerings.

dm: I also offer clouds of the finest incense, Captivating and pervasive in their scent. I shall also offer divine feasts Consisting of various kinds of foods and drinks.
gm: Supreme incense with a captivating, pervasive fragrance, Masses of clouds of its vapor I also offer to them; With meals comprising various foods and drinks, Divine feasts I will also offer to them.

dm: I shall also offer precious lamps Arranged in rows upon golden lotuses. Upon the ground, smoothed and anointed with perfume, I shall scatter beautiful loose flowers.
gm: Arranged in rows of golden lotuses, Jeweled lamps I will also offer. On the cleared ground anointed with incense, I shall scatter pleasing loose flowers.

dm: Immeasurable palaces resonant with delightful songs of praise, Beautifully ablaze with hanging ornaments of pearls and jewels— These, which have become the ornaments of infinite space, I offer to those whose very nature is compassion.
gm: Immeasurable palaces possessing pleasing songs of praise, Beautifully blazing with hanging ornaments of pearls and jewels, Which have become ornaments of boundless space, these too I will offer to those whose nature is compassion.

dm: Beautiful jeweled parasols with golden handles, Adorned with lovely arrangements of ornaments around their perimeter, Well-shaped and pleasing to behold, I raise these up And offer them forever to the Lords of Sages.
gm: Beautiful jeweled parasols with golden handles, Possessing pleasing forms of ornaments all around, Upright, well-shaped, and lovely to behold, I will always offer to the Lords of Capable Ones.

dm: Furthermore, may a multitude of other offerings, Possessed of music and sweet, captivating melodies, And clouds that soothe the suffering of sentient beings, Remain in their respective places.
gm: Besides those, masses of offerings, Accompanied by pleasing, sweet sounds of music, Which soothe the suffering of sentient beings, May clouds of these remain individually.

dm: Upon all the jewels of the sublime Dharma, And upon the reliquaries and the sacred images, May a rain of precious flowers and the like Fall in a continuous, uninterrupted stream.
gm: Upon all the rare and supreme holy Dharma, Stūpas, and images, May a rain of jewels, flowers, and the like, Fall without interruption.

dm: Just as Mañjughoṣa and the others Have made offerings to the Victors, So too do I make offerings to the Tathāgatas, The Protectors, and their spiritual heirs.
gm: Just as Mañjuśrī and others Made offerings to the Victorious Ones, Likewise, I make offerings to the Tathāgatas, The Protectors along with their Children.

dm: To those who are oceans of excellence, I offer praise with oceans of melodic branches. May those clouds of melodious songs of praise Certainly arise in every way.
gm: To those who are oceans of qualities, I Offer praise with oceans of limbs of melodious praise. May sweet clouds of songs of praise Certainly arise everywhere for them.

dm: To all the Buddhas of the three times, And to the Dharma and the Supreme Assembly, With as many bodies as there are atoms in the realms, I bow down and pay homage.
gm: To all the Buddhas who have gone in the three times, Along with the Dharma and the Supreme Assembly, With bodies as numerous as all the atoms in the fields, Bowing down, I pay homage.

dm: I prostrate to the foundations of the awakening mind and to the reliquaries; I prostrate to the preceptors, the masters, And to those who maintain the supreme ascetic discipline.
gm: To the bases of the awakening mind, And to the stūpas, I pay homage. To the preceptors and likewise the teachers, And to the supreme practitioners, I pay homage.

dm: Until I reach the heart of enlightenment, I take refuge in the Buddhas; Likewise, I take refuge in the Dharma And in the assembly of Bodhisattvas.
gm: Until reaching the essence of awakening, I go for refuge to the Buddhas; To the Dharma and the Bodhisattvas' Assembly, likewise, I go for refuge.

dm: To the fully enlightened Buddhas and Bodhisattvas Who dwell in all directions, And who possess great compassion, I join my palms and pray:
gm: To those who reside in all directions, The perfect Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, Who possess great compassion, Joining my palms, I make this request:

dm: From beginningless cyclic existence, In this life or in others, Whatever sins I have committed, Or caused others to commit,
gm: Since beginningless cyclic existence, In this life or in others, Whatever non-virtue I have unwittingly committed, Or caused to be committed,

dm: Overwhelmed by the confusion of ignorance, And whatever I have rejoiced in— Having seen those faults, I confess them to the Protectors from the depths of my heart.
gm: And, overcome by the confusion of ignorance, Whatever I have rejoiced in, Having seen these mistakes, I confess them to the Protectors from the depths of my heart.

dm: Whatever harm I have done to the Three Jewels, To my parents, or to my teachers and others, Through the gateway of the afflictions By means of my body, speech, and mind,
gm: To the Three Jewels, To parents, gurus, or others, Through afflictions, with body, speech, And mind, whatever harm I have done,

dm: Whatever sins I, a sinner stained by many faults, Have committed through my many transgressions, Those extremely unbearable deeds, I confess to all the Guides.
gm: Defiled by many faults, Whatever non-virtues I, a sinner, Have committed that are extremely unbearable, I confess them all to the Guides.

dm: I am terrified that I might die Before my sins have been purified. Please protect me with all haste, So that I may be certain to be liberated from this.
gm: Before my non-virtues are purified, I may meet my death. So that I may definitely be freed from them, I pray you, protect me swiftly!

dm: This Lord of Death is not to be trusted; He does not wait for what has or has not been done. Whether sick or healthy, No one can rely on this fleeting life.
gm: This Lord of Death cannot be trusted; He does not wait for what is done or not done. Whether we are sick or not sick, None can trust this fleeting life.

dm: Since I must depart, leaving everything behind, Not having understood this, I have committed various kinds of sins For the sake of friends and foes.
gm: I must leave everything behind and depart. Since I did not understand this, For the sake of friends and enemies, I have committed various kinds of non-virtue.

dm: Enemies will turn to nothing, And friends will turn to nothing; I too will turn to nothing, And likewise, everything will turn to nothing.
gm: My enemies will cease to be, My friends will cease to be, I too will cease to be, Likewise, all will cease to be.

dm: Just like the experiences of a dream, Whatever things I have enjoyed Will become objects of memory; All that has passed will not be seen again.
gm: Like experiencing a dream, Whatever things I have enjoyed Will become mere objects of memory; All that has passed will not be seen again.

dm: Even in this brief lifetime, Many friends and enemies have passed away; Yet the unbearable sins committed for their sake Remain before me.
gm: Even during this brief life, Many friends and enemies have passed away. But the unbearable non-virtues committed for their sake Remain right before me.

dm: Because I did not realize That I am merely a transient guest, Through ignorance, attachment, and hatred, I have committed many kinds of sins.
gm: That my existence is so fleeting, Since I did not realize this, Through ignorance, attachment, and hatred, I have committed many kinds of non-virtue.

dm: Without pausing for a moment, day or night, This life is constantly diminishing; Since no addition comes from elsewhere, Why should someone like me not die?
gm: Pausing neither day nor night, This life is constantly slipping away, And since no extra time is added from elsewhere, Why would someone like me not die?

dm: While I am lying upon my bed, Though surrounded by all my kinsmen and friends, The sensations of the severing of my life-force Must be experienced by me alone.
gm: While I am lying in my bed, Although surrounded by all my relatives and friends, The feelings of my life being severed Will be experienced by me alone.

dm: When seized by the messengers of the Lord of Death, What help are kinsmen, and what help are friends? At that time, merit alone provides protection, Yet that is what I have failed to cultivate.
gm: When seized by the messengers of Yama, What good are relatives, what good are friends? At that time, merit alone is a protection, But I have not relied upon it.

dm: O Protectors, because I was heedless And did not recognize such terrors as these, For the sake of this transient life, I have committed many sins.
gm: O Protectors, I, being careless, Unaware of such danger as this, For the sake of this impermanent life, Have committed many non-virtues.

dm: Even a person being led today to a place where their limbs will be severed becomes terrified; With parched mouth and sunken eyes, Their appearance is transformed from what it was before.
gm: Even a person being led today to the place Where their limbs will be amputated is terrified; With a dry mouth, dreadful eyes, and the like, Their appearance is transformed, different from before.

dm: Seized by the messengers of the Lord of Death, who have such terrifying forms, And stricken by the great illness of fear, What need is there to mention my extreme distress?
gm: Seized by the messengers of Yama With their terrifying physical appearances, And struck by the great terrifying disease, What need to mention my utter misery?

dm: Thinking, "Who can truly protect me from this great terror?" With eyes wide and bulging in panic, I will search in the four directions for a refuge.
gm: "Who from this great terror Will perfectly protect me?" Opening my terrified eyes wide, I will search the four directions for protection.

dm: Seeing that there is no refuge in the four directions, I then fall into utter despair. If there is no refuge to be found in that place, What shall I do then?
gm: Seeing no protection in the four directions, I will then become completely enveloped in despair. If there is no protection in that place, What shall I do at that time?

dm: Therefore, to the Victors, the protectors of beings, Who strive for the purpose of shielding all wanderers, And who, possessing great power, dispel every fear, From this very day, I go for refuge.
gm: Therefore, in the Victors, the protectors of beings, Who strive for the purpose of protecting beings, The mighty ones who clear away all fear, From today onward, I take refuge.

dm: To the Dharma realized within their hearts, Which dispels the terrors of cyclic existence, And likewise to the assembly of Bodhisattvas, I also go for refuge perfectly.
gm: In the Dharma that they have realized, Which clears away the fears of saṃsāra, And in the assembly of Bodhisattvas, Likewise, I perfectly take refuge.

dm: Terrified by fear, I offer myself to Samantabhadra; To Mañjuśrī, I also Offer my own body.
gm: Terrified by fear, I offer myself to Samantabhadra; To Mañjuśrī, I myself Shall offer my body.

dm: To the protector Avalokiteśvara, Whose compassionate conduct is never mistaken, I cry out with a piteous voice: "Please protect this sinful one!"
gm: Whose compassionate deeds are unerring, To the protector Avalokiteśvara as well, With an anguished cry, I call out: "Please protect me, a sinner!"

dm: To the noble Ākāśagarbha, And to Kṣitigarbha as well, And to all the great compassionate protectors, I cry out from my heart, seeking refuge.
gm: To the noble Ākāśagarbha, And to Kṣitigarbha, And to all the greatly compassionate protectors, Seeking refuge, I call out from my heart.

dm: At the sight of whom, the messengers of Yama And other hostile beings flee in terror To the four directions, I go for refuge to the Wielder of the Vajra.
gm: Seeing whom, the messengers of Yama And other malicious beings Flee in terror to the four directions, I take refuge in the Vajra-wielder.

dm: In the past, I have transgressed your commands; Now, seeing this great fear, I come to you for refuge; Please, swiftly dispel my fears!
gm: Previously I transgressed your commands, But now, seeing great fear, I take refuge in you, so Please swiftly clear away this fear.

dm: If, when frightened by an ordinary illness, One must act according to a physician's advice, Then what need is there to mention those Constantly afflicted by the diseases of a hundred faults, such as desire?
gm: Even if frightened by an ordinary illness, One must act according to the doctor's words; Of a hundred faults such as attachment and the like, When constantly stricken by their disease, what need to mention?

dm: If even one of these could destroy All the people living in Jambudvīpa, And no other medicine to cure them Can be found anywhere in any direction,
gm: Even by just one of them, in Jambudvīpa All the people dwelling there are destroyed; And if other medicines to cure them Are not found anywhere in all directions,

dm: Then the intention not to act according to the instructions Of the Omniscient Physician, who removes every pain, Is a state of extreme delusion And is truly contemptible.
gm: In that case, of the omniscient physician Who draws out all pain— The intention not to act according to his commands Is utterly foolish and an object of reproach.

dm: If one must remain cautious Even at a small, ordinary precipice, What need is there to mention the long-lasting abyss That falls for a thousand leagues?
gm: Even on a small, ordinary precipice, If one must remain careful, Of falling a thousand yojanas On a long-lasting precipice, what need to mention?

dm: It is not right to live at ease, Thinking, "I will not die this very day." The time when I shall cease to be Will undoubtedly arrive.
gm: Thinking, "Today alone I will not die," It is not right to remain at ease. The time when I will cease to be Will undoubtedly occur.

dm: Who has granted me fearlessness? How can I be certain of escaping this? Since I will surely come to nothing, How can my mind remain at ease?
gm: Who has given me fearlessness? How will I definitely escape from this? If I will undoubtedly cease to be, How can my mind remain at ease?

dm: Of all that I have experienced in the past and which has vanished, What remains for me? Yet, through my obsessive attachment to such things, I have acted in opposition to the Guru's commands.
gm: From what was previously experienced and perished, What remains for me? By being deeply attached to that, I have transgressed the gurus' commands.

dm: When I must leave this life and likewise Abandon my kinsmen and friends to go Somewhere all alone, What is the use of all those who are dear or those who are not?
gm: This lifetime, and likewise Relatives and friends having entirely abandoned, If I must go somewhere alone, What is the point of all friends and non-friends?

dm: From non-virtue, suffering arises. Thinking, "How can I be certain of escaping this?" It is right that I should constantly, Day and night, think only of this.
gm: From non-virtue suffering arises. "How will I definitely escape from that?" Constantly, day and night, by me Just this alone is right to be pondered.

dm: Because of my ignorance and delusion, Whatever natural misdeeds Or proscribed sins I have committed, Whatever they may be,
gm: Because I am ignorant and foolish, Natural misdeeds or Whatever proscribed negative deeds— Whichever ones I have done,

dm: In the presence of the Protectors, openly, With palms joined and a mind fearful of suffering, I prostrate again and again, And I confess all of these.
gm: Directly in the presence of the protectors, With palms joined and a mind terrified of suffering, Bowing down again and again, I will confess all of them.

dm: I pray that the Guides will regard my sins As the transgressions they are. Since this was not good, Henceforth, I shall never do it again.
gm: I beseech the guides to accept my negative deeds As being faults. Since this is not good, From now on I will not do them.

dm: This concludes the second chapter, the Chapter on the Confession of Sin, from the Engaging in the Bodhisattva's Conduct.
gm: From Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva, the second chapter, Confession of Negative Deeds.

dm: Adopting the Bodhichitta
gm: Chapter Three: Completely Taking Hold of Bodhicitta

dm: I joyfully rejoice in the virtue that relieves The suffering of all sentient beings in the lower realms, And in the abiding in happiness of those who suffer, With a heart full of delight.
gm: Of the lower realms of all sentient beings, In the virtue that relieves suffering, and In suffering beings abiding in happiness, With joy I rejoice.

bo: བྱང་ཆུབ་རྒྱུར་གྱུར་དགེ་བསགས་པ། ། དེ་ལ་རྗེས་སུ་ཡི་རང་ངོ་། ། ལུས་ཅན་འཁོར་བའི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལས། ། ངེས་པར་ཐར་ལ་ཡི་རང་ངོ་། ། སྐྱོབ་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་དང་། ། རྒྱལ་སྲས་ས་ལའང་ཡི་རང་ངོ་། །
dm: I rejoice in the accumulation of virtue That has become the cause for enlightenment. I rejoice in the definite liberation Of embodied beings from the suffering of cyclic existence. I rejoice in the enlightenment of the Protectors, And also in the levels of the Bodhisattvas.
gm: In the accumulated virtue that becomes the cause of awakening, In that I rejoice. From the suffering of samsara for embodied beings, In the definite liberation I rejoice. In the awakening of the protectors and In the stages of the Conquerors' sons too, I rejoice.

dm: I joyfully rejoice in the ocean of virtue That is the generation of the mind of awakening, which brings happiness to all sentient beings, And in the deeds that benefit all sentient beings, With a heart full of delight.
gm: Bringing happiness to all sentient beings, In the ocean of virtue of generating the awakening mind, and In the deeds that benefit sentient beings, With joy I rejoice.

dm: To the Buddhas of all directions, I join my palms and pray: For those wandering in the darkness of suffering, Please kindle the lamp of the Dharma.
gm: To the Buddhas of all directions, With joined palms I pray: For sentient beings confused in the darkness of suffering, I beseech you to light the lamp of Dharma.

dm: To the Victors who intend to pass into nirvana, I join my palms and pray: Do not leave these beings in blindness, But please remain for countless eons.
gm: To the Conquerors wishing to pass into nirvana, With joined palms I pray: So as not to leave these wanderers in blindness, I beseech you to remain for countless eons.

dm: Having performed all these acts in this way, Whatever virtue I have accumulated, By that, may all the suffering Of every sentient being be dispelled.
gm: Having done all these things in this way, Whatever virtue has been accumulated by me, By that, of all sentient beings, May all suffering be dispelled.

dm: For as long as there are beings who are ill, Until their diseases are cured, May I become their medicine, their physician, And their nurse.
gm: As long as wanderers are sick, Until they are cured of illness, The medicine and the doctor themselves, and Their nurse, may I become.

dm: By raining down showers of food and drink, May I dispel the suffering of hunger and thirst; During the intermediate eon of famine, May I myself become food and drink.
gm: Bringing down a rain of food and drink, May I dispel the suffering of hunger and thirst. During the intermediate eon of famine, May I myself become food and drink.

dm: For sentient beings who are destitute and poor, May I become an inexhaustible treasure, And remain present before them As every variety of necessary provision.
gm: For sentient beings who are destitute and poor, May I become an inexhaustible treasure, and As all the various kinds of needed requisites, May I remain closely present before them.

dm: My body, and likewise my possessions, And all my virtues of the three times, I shall give away without a sense of loss, To accomplish the welfare of all sentient beings.
gm: My body and likewise my wealth, and All virtues of the three times, In order to accomplish the welfare of all sentient beings, I shall give away without regret.

dm: By renouncing everything, one transcends suffering, And my mind seeks to achieve that transcendence; Since I must give everything away at once, It is best to give it to all sentient beings.
gm: By giving up everything, nirvana is attained, And my mind seeks to accomplish nirvana. Since I must part with everything at once, It is best given to sentient beings.

dm: I have already given this body To all embodied beings to do with as they please; Whether they constantly kill it, revile it, Or beat it, it is up to them to do as they wish.
gm: By me, to all embodied beings, Since this body has been given for their pleasure, Continually killing, abusing, or Striking and so forth, let them do as they please.

dm: Whether they make sport of my body, Or make it an object of ridicule and jest, Since I have already given this body away, What is the use of my guarding it?
gm: Whether they play with my body, or Use it as a source of ridicule and jest, Since I have already given this body away, What is the use of cherishing it?

dm: Let them do whatever actions they wish, Provided it does not cause them harm; May no one who encounters me Ever find it to be without meaning.
gm: That which does not bring harm to them, Let them do whatever action it may be. Whenever anyone focuses on me, May it never be meaningless for anyone.

dm: For those who, focusing on me, Develop a mind of anger or of faith, May that very state always become The cause for the fulfillment of all their goals.
gm: Focusing upon me, for those whose Minds of anger or faith arise, May that very thing always become for them The cause for accomplishing all their goals.

dm: Whether they speak ill of me, Or others do me harm, Or even if they mock me, May all be fortunate enough to attain enlightenment.
gm: Those who speak ill of me, or Others who cause me harm, or Likewise those who mock me, May they all have the fortune of awakening.

dm: May I be a protector for those without a protector, A guide for those traveling on the path, And for those who wish to cross over, May I be a boat, a ship, and a bridge.
gm: May I be a protector for those without a protector, A guide for those who travel on the path, And a boat for those who wish to cross over, May I become a ship and a bridge.

dm: May I be an island for those seeking an island, And a place of rest for those desiring rest; For all embodied beings who desire a servant, May I become their servant.
gm: An island for those seeking an island, A bed for those desiring a bed, And for embodied beings who desire a servant, May I become a servant for them all.

dm: May I be a wish-fulfilling jewel, a vase of excellence, A perfected mantra, and a great medicine, And may I be a wish-granting tree, And a cow of plenty for all embodied beings.
gm: A wish-fulfilling jewel and a fine vase, An accomplished knowledge-mantra and great medicine, And wish-granting trees, May I become a cow of plenty for embodied beings.

dm: Just as the great elements, such as earth, And like space itself, may I always be The basis for the various means of subsistence For immeasurable sentient beings.
gm: Just like earth and the other great elements, And like space, permanently, For limitless sentient beings, May I also be the ground of manifold sustenance.

dm: Likewise, for the realms of sentient beings Extending to the very ends of space, May I be the cause of their sustenance in every way, Until all have passed beyond sorrow.
gm: Likewise, extending to the limits of space, For the realm of sentient beings in all ways, Until they all attain nirvana, May I also be the cause of their sustenance.

dm: Just as the Sugatas of former times Generated the mind of enlightenment, And in the Bodhisattva trainings Abided and trained in successive order,
gm: Just as the previous Sugatas Generated the awakening mind, And in the trainings of the bodhisattvas, Just as they progressively abided,

dm: So too, for the benefit of all beings, Shall I generate the mind of enlightenment, And likewise, in those trainings, I shall train in successive order.
gm: Likewise, for the benefit of wandering beings, I shall generate the awakening mind, And likewise, in the trainings too, I shall progressively train.

dm: In this way, those endowed with wisdom, Having firmly adopted the supreme mind of enlightenment, In order to bring the conclusion to full completion, Should uplift their minds as follows:
gm: The intelligent ones who in this way Have excellently taken hold of the awakening mind, In order to make it flourish further, Should extol the mind like this:

dm: Today my life has become fruitful; I have well obtained this human existence. Today I am born into the family of the Buddhas; I have now become a child of the Buddhas.
gm: Today my life is fruitful; I have well obtained a human existence. Today I am born into the family of the Buddhas; Today I have become a child of the Buddhas.

dm: From now on, by any means necessary, I shall undertake actions befitting this lineage, And act in such a way that I do not defile This faultless and noble lineage.
gm: Now I must, whatever happens, Undertake actions in accord with the family, And upon this flawless, noble family, Bring no stain—thus shall I act.

dm: Just as a blind person might find A precious jewel within a heap of refuse, So, by some stroke of fortune, This spirit of awakening has been born within me.
gm: Like a blind man from a heap of refuse Finding a precious jewel, Just so, by some coincidence, This awakening mind has been born in me.

dm: It is the supreme nectar that overcomes The Lord of Death for all beings; It is the inexhaustible treasure that dispels The poverty of all beings.
gm: Destroying the Lord of Death for wandering beings, It is the supreme nectar. Dispelling the poverty of wandering beings, It is the inexhaustible treasure.

dm: It is the supreme medicine that completely Pacifies the illnesses of all beings; It is the shade tree of rest for beings Weary from wandering the paths of cyclic existence.
gm: Completely pacifying the illnesses of wandering beings, It is the supreme medicine. For wandering beings wandering and weary on the path of existence, It is the tree of rest.

dm: It is the universal bridge that delivers All beings from the lower realms; It is the rising moon of the mind that dispels The heat of the afflictions of all beings.
gm: For all wandering beings, from the lower realms It is the universal bridge that liberates. Dispelling the torment of the afflictions of wandering beings, It is the rising moon of the mind.

dm: It is the great sun that completely dispels The dimness of ignorance of wandering beings; It is the essence of butter extracted From churning the milk of the sublime Dharma.
gm: The dimness of ignorance of wandering beings, It is the great sun that uproots it. From churning the milk of the true Dharma, It is the essence of butter that has emerged.

dm: For the guests among beings who travel the path of existence And desire to enjoy the riches of happiness, This stands as the supreme bliss close at hand, Which brings total satisfaction to the great guests, the sentient beings.
gm: For wandering beings, the guests traveling the path of existence, Who wish to experience the enjoyment of happiness, This is stationed nearby as the supreme happiness, Satisfying the great guests, sentient beings.

dm: Today, in the presence of all the Protectors, I invite the world to the state of the Sugatas and to temporal happiness; Since I have invited you as my guests to this bliss, May the gods, asuras, and all others rejoice!
gm: Today, by me, in the presence of all the protectors, Wandering beings to Sugatahood itself, and Until then, to happiness, have been invited as guests; Let gods, asuras, and others rejoice!

dm: From "Engaging in the Bodhisattva Deeds," this is the third chapter, entitled "Fully Adopting the Awakening Mind."
gm: From Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva, the third chapter, called "Fully Taking Hold of the Awakening Mind."

dm: Chapter Four: Demonstrating Conscientiousness
gm: Chapter Four: Teaching Conscientiousness

dm: Having thus firmly grasped the Awakening Mind, The children of the Conquerors Must always, without distraction, Strive never to transgress the trainings.
gm: The son of the Conquerors, in that way, Having very firmly taken hold of the awakening mind, Unwaveringly and always, Should strive not to transgress the trainings.

dm: Whatever is undertaken impulsively, Or whatever has not been well examined— Even if a promise has been made regarding it, It is right to reconsider whether to proceed or to let it go.
gm: Whatever is undertaken recklessly, Or whatever is not well examined, Even if a promise is made regarding it, It is appropriate to examine whether to do it or abandon it.

dm: But that which has been examined by the Buddhas and their heirs With great wisdom, And which I myself have also examined again and again— What reason is there to delay in that?
gm: By the Buddhas and their sons, Whatever has been examined with great wisdom, And which I myself have examined again and again, What is there to postpone regarding it?

dm: If, after having made such a vow, I do not accomplish it through action, Then by deceiving all those sentient beings, What will my future destiny be?
gm: If, having promised in that way, I do not accomplish it in action, Having deceived all those sentient beings, What will my destiny become?

dm: If it is said that even regarding a minor, ordinary object, A person who intends in their mind to give it, But then does not give it, Will become a hungry ghost,
gm: Even regarding a slight, ordinary thing, Having intended in one's mind to give it, Whatever person does not give it, If it is said that they will become a hungry ghost,

dm: Then, having sincerely invited all beings To the unsurpassed bliss, If I were to deceive all those beings, How could I ever go to a happy realm?
gm: To unsurpassable happiness, Having invited them from the depths of my heart, If I deceive all wandering beings, How will I go to the higher realms?

dm: Even if one abandons the bodhicitta, The way in which those are liberated Is an inconceivable karmic process, Known only to the Omniscient One.
gm: Even though some people give up the awakening mind, As for their being liberated, The way of karma is inconceivable; Only the Omniscient One knows.

dm: For a bodhisattva, this is The gravest of all downfalls; For should it occur, The welfare of all sentient beings is diminished.
gm: For a bodhisattva, this Is the heaviest among the downfalls; Thus, if this happens, The benefit of all sentient beings is diminished.

dm: Anyone who, even for a single moment, Creates obstacles or hinders this merit, Diminishes the welfare of sentient beings, And for them, rebirth in lower realms is endless.
gm: Whoever else, even for a mere moment, Creates an obstacle to this merit, Because the benefit of sentient beings is diminished, Their lower rebirths will be limitless.

dm: If one’s own well-being is impaired by destroying the happiness of even a single sentient being, What need is there to mention destroying the happiness of all embodied beings as vast as the limits of space?
gm: Even the happiness of a single sentient being, If I destroy it, I will be ruined; Limitless as the entirety of space, Destroying the happiness of embodied beings, what need is there to mention it?

dm: Thus, if powerful downfalls and the power of bodhicitta alternate and contend within cyclic existence, It will take a very long time to attain the bodhisattva grounds.
gm: Thus, with powerful downfalls, And the powerful awakening mind, If they alternate in saṃsāra, It will take a long time to attain the grounds.

dm: Therefore, just as I have vowed, I must respectfully fulfill it. If I do not make an effort from this moment on, I shall sink lower and lower.
gm: Therefore, just as I have promised, I shall respectfully accomplish it. If from today I do not make effort, I will go lower and lower.

dm: Although countless Buddhas who act for the benefit of all sentient beings have passed by, I, due to my own faults, have not become an object of their healing care.
gm: Benefiting all sentient beings, Even though countless Buddhas have passed away, Due to my own faults, I Have not become an object of their healing.

dm: If I continue to act in this same way, The same will happen again and again; I will experience sickness, bondage, Mutilation, and being cut asunder in the lower realms.
gm: If I still act in this way, Again and again it will be the same: In the lower realms, illness and bondage, Cutting and cleaving, and so forth, I will experience.

dm: The appearance of a Tathāgata, the attainment of faith and a human body, And the fitness to cultivate virtue— Since such things are so rare, when will they ever be found again?
gm: The appearance of the Tathāgatas, Faith, obtaining a human body, And the fitness to practice virtue, like this, Since they are rare, when will they be obtained?

dm: Although today I am free from illness, have food, and am not in harm's way, Life is a momentary deception, And the body is like a temporary loan.
gm: A day without illness like this, With food and without harm, nevertheless, Life is deceptive in a moment, And the body is like something borrowed for a brief moment.

dm: With conduct such as mine, I shall not even attain a human body again. If a human body is not attained, There will be only sin and no virtue.
gm: With behavior like mine, Even a human body will not be obtained. If a human body is not obtained, There is only sin and no virtue.

dm: If, while I have the fortune to practice virtue, I do not perform virtuous deeds, Then what shall I be able to do when I am completely bewildered By the sufferings of the lower realms?
gm: Even when having the fortune to practice virtue, If I do not practice virtue, Completely bewildered by the suffering of the lower realms, At that time, what will I be able to do?

dm: If I have not performed virtuous deeds, And have instead thoroughly accumulated sins, Then for even a hundred million eons, I shall not even hear the sound of a happy rebirth.
gm: Having not practiced virtues, And having accumulated sins, For even a hundred million eons, Even the sound of the happy realms will not be heard.

dm: For that very reason, the Blessed One said That human status is extremely difficult to attain, Like a turtle’s neck entering the hole Of a yoke tossing upon a vast ocean.
gm: For that very reason, the Bhagavan Of a yoke drifting on the great ocean, Like a turtle's neck entering the hole, Declared that the human state is extremely difficult to obtain.

dm: If even a sin committed in a single instant Leads to remaining in the Avīci hell for an eon, Then what need is there to mention that, due to sins Accumulated in beginningless saṃsāra, I shall not go to a happy rebirth?
gm: Even by the sin committed in a single moment, If one dwells in Avīci for an eon, Due to the sins accumulated in beginningless saṃsāra, What need is there to mention not going to the happy realms?

dm: Having experienced only that much, One will not be liberated; For while experiencing it in that way, Other sins are produced in great abundance.
gm: Having experienced just that much, One will not be liberated from it, Because while experiencing it like this, Other sins are fully generated.

dm: Having found such leisure as this, If I do not habituate myself to virtue, There is no deception greater than this, And there is no folly greater than this.
gm: Having found such leisure, If I do not habituate myself to virtue, There is no deception other than this, And there is no bewilderment other than this.

dm: If, having realized this, I still succumb to laziness through delusion, Then at the time when death arrives, A great anguish will arise.
gm: If, having understood this, I am still lazy later out of bewilderment, At the time of my death, Great sorrow will arise.

dm: If my body were to be burned for a long time By the unbearable fires of hell, There is no doubt that my mind would be tormented By the blazing fire of unbearable remorse.
gm: If the unbearable fire of hell for a long time Burns my body, Due to the blazing fire of unbearable regret, My mind will doubtless be tormented.

dm: Having somehow, by good fortune, found this state of benefit That is so extremely difficult to obtain, If I am led back to those same hells Even while possessing conscious awareness,
gm: The state of benefit that is extremely difficult to find, Having found it by some chance, While I myself am possessed of understanding, If I am led back again into that hell,

dm: It is as if I have been rendered senseless by a magic spell; I am here utterly without my mind. I do not even know what has deluded me, Or what it is that dwells within me.
gm: As if bewildered by a mantra, I am reduced to having no mind here. Even I do not know what bewilders me; What is there inside me?

dm: These enemies, such as hatred and craving, Possess neither hands, feet, nor other limbs; They are neither brave nor wise, yet somehow, They have made me their slave.
gm: The enemies of hatred, craving, and so forth, Do not have arms, legs, and so forth, And though neither brave nor wise, how is it That they have made me like a slave?

dm: While dwelling within my own mind, They harm me at their pleasure; To not be angry at this and to remain patient Is misplaced patience, a state worthy of reproach.
gm: While dwelling in my mind, Doing harm to me at their pleasure, Patiently not being angry even at that, Is inappropriate patience and an object of reproach.

dm: Even if all the gods and demigods Were to rise up against me as enemies, They would be unable to lead me into Or cast me into the fires of the Avīci hell.
gm: Even if the gods and demigods All rose up against me as enemies, Even they would not be able To lead and place me in the fire of Avīci.

dm: This powerful enemy, the mental afflictions, Can in a single instant cast me Into that fire which, upon meeting even Mount Meru, Would not leave even its ashes behind.
gm: This powerful enemy of the afflictions, Upon meeting which, even Mount Meru Does not remain even as ashes, Casts me there in a single moment.

dm: These enemies of mine, the mental afflictions, Are as if without beginning or end; No other enemies are capable Of lasting for such a long time.
gm: My enemies, the afflictions, Are long-lasting, without beginning or end; All other enemies Are not capable of lasting for a long time like that.

dm: If one serves and honors others in a friendly way, They will all bring benefit and happiness; But if one serves the mental afflictions, They respond only with further suffering and harm.
gm: If amiably served and honored, All others bring benefit and happiness, But if the afflictions are served, They instead bring suffering and harm.

dm: If such a long-standing, constant enemy, The sole cause for the increase of a mass of harms, Truly takes up residence within my heart, How could I ever be fearless and joyful in cyclic existence?
gm: Thus, these long-lasting continuous enemies, The sole cause of the great increase of the multitude of harms, If they definitely take up residence in my heart, How could I be fearless and joyful in saṃsāra?

dm: If these guards of the prison of cyclic existence, Who become executioners in the hells and elsewhere, Dwell within the net of attachment in my mind, How could I ever find happiness?
gm: The guards of the prison of saṃsāra, These which become the executioners that kill in hell and so forth— If, in the net of attachment residing in the mind, They remain, how can there be happiness for me?

dm: Therefore, as long as I have not decisively destroyed this enemy before my very eyes, I shall not abandon my efforts in this regard; For those full of pride, who become enraged even at a minor, temporary harm, Will not sleep until they have defeated that enemy.
gm: Thus, as long as I do not manifestly And certainly destroy this enemy, I will not forsake my effort here. When angered by even a slight temporary harm, Those full of pride do not sleep until they have destroyed it.

dm: If those who wish to forcefully defeat in battle their enemies, Who are already miserable by nature and destined for death, Can disregard the pain of being struck by arrows and spears, And refuse to turn back until their goal is achieved,
gm: Those afflicted ones who suffer and naturally die, When arrayed in battle, even those intensely desiring to forcefully destroy them, Having ignored the suffering of being struck by arrows, spears, and weapons, If they do not turn back and flee without accomplishing the goal,

dm: Then what need is there to mention that I, Who am striving to defeat my natural and certain enemies— The constant cause of all suffering— Should not be discouraged or lazy, no matter what hundreds of sufferings arise?
gm: The constant cause of all suffering, Today, as I strive to destroy these definite natural enemies, Whatever becomes the cause of hundreds of sufferings, Needless to say, will not make me despair and lose heart.

dm: If even the scars inflicted by a meaningless enemy Are cherished like ornaments upon the body, Then why should suffering harm me, Who am perfectly striving to accomplish the great purpose?
gm: Even the scars inflicted by meaningless enemies Are worn like ornaments on the body; so For me, striving perfectly to accomplish the great purpose, Why should suffering be a harm?

dm: If fishermen, outcasts, farmers, and the like, Who think only of their own mere livelihood, Can endure the hardships of cold, heat, and so forth, Why should I not endure them for the sake of the world's happiness?
gm: Fishermen, outcastes, farmers, and so forth, Thinking only of their own livelihood, Endure the harms of cold, heat, and so forth; Why should someone like me not endure them for the happiness of wandering beings?

dm: When I vowed to liberate all beings, As far as the limits of space in the ten directions, From their afflictions, I myself was not yet freed from those very afflictions.
gm: Reaching the ends of space in the ten directions, To liberate wandering beings from afflictions, When I promised this, I myself Was not liberated from afflictions.

dm: Was it not like the speech of a madman To speak thus, without even knowing my own capacity? Therefore, in order to destroy the afflictions, I shall never turn back.
gm: Without knowing my own measure, How is speaking thus not crazy? Thus, in destroying afflictions, I will never turn back.

dm: I must be tenacious regarding this, And harboring a grudge, I shall engage in battle; Such forms of mental affliction are acceptable, Except for those that destroy the afflictions themselves.
gm: I will be attached to this, And, holding a grudge, I will engage in battle; Except for the afflictions of such a kind, That destroy afflictions.

dm: Even if I were to be burned or killed, Or even if my head were to be cut off, I shall never, in any way, Bow down to my enemies, the mental afflictions.
gm: Whether I am burned and killed, Or even if my head is cut off, it is better; In any case, to the afflictive Enemies I will not bow down.

dm: When an ordinary enemy is driven from a country, He settles in another land and takes possession of it; Then, once his strength has increased, he returns. But the nature of the enemy, the mental afflictions, is not like that.
gm: Even when ordinary enemies are expelled from the country, They reside in other countries and take possession, And, having regained their strength, they return from there; But the way of the afflictive enemies is not like that.

dm: The afflictions are abandoned by the eye of wisdom; Once dispelled from my mind, where will they go? Where will they dwell to return and harm me again? It is only that I, being weak-minded, lack persistence.
gm: Afflictions, afflictions, abandoned by the eye of wisdom, Cleared from my mind, where will they go? Where will they stay to return and harm me? It is just that I, of weak mind, lack effort.

dm: The afflictions do not reside in sense objects, nor in the collection of faculties, nor in between them; If they do not exist elsewhere either, then where do they dwell to harm the entire world? They are like an illusion; therefore, to abandon fear in your heart, apply yourself to understanding them. Why do you pointlessly inflict harm upon yourself in the hells and other such realms?
gm: Afflictions do not reside in the objects, nor in the sense faculties, nor in between. Nor elsewhere; if so, where do they reside and harm all wandering beings? They are like an illusion; therefore, banish fear in the heart and rely on effort for the sake of knowledge. Why should I be harmed meaninglessly in hells and so forth?

dm: Having reflected in this way, one should strive To accomplish the trainings as they have been explained. If one does not follow the physician's instructions, How can a patient who needs treatment be cured by medicine?
gm: Having pondered thus, for the sake of accomplishing The trainings just as explained, I will make effort. If one does not listen to the doctor's words, how can A patient who needs to be cured by medicines be healed?

dm: This concludes the fourth chapter, "Showing Heedfulness," from the *Entering the Bodhisattva's Conduct*.
gm: From Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva, the fourth chapter, called the Teaching on Conscientiousness.

dm: Chapter Five: Guarding Introspection
gm: Chapter Five: Guarding Introspection

dm: Those who wish to guard their training Must guard the mind with great effort; If one does not guard this mind, One will be unable to guard the training.
gm: Those who wish to guard the training Must strictly guard the mind; If this mind is not guarded, One will not be able to guard the training.

dm: By letting the elephant of the mind run wild, It inflicts the torments of the Incessant Hell; An untamed, mad elephant in this world Cannot cause such harm.
gm: Letting the elephant of the mind wander loose Causes harm in the Avīci hell; An untamed, maddened elephant Does not cause such harm here.

dm: If the elephant of the mind is firmly bound With the rope of total mindfulness, All fears will vanish, And every virtue will fall into one's hands.
gm: With the rope of mindfulness on all sides, If the elephant of the mind is tightly bound, All fears will cease to exist, And all virtues will come into one's hands.

dm: Tigers, lions, elephants, bears, Snakes, and all enemies, The guardians of the hell realms, And likewise sorcerers and demons—
gm: Tigers, lions, elephants, bears, Snakes, and all enemies, The guardians of the hells for sentient beings, Evil sorcerers, and likewise rākṣasas—

dm: By binding this mind alone, All of them are bound; By subduing this mind alone, All of them are subdued.
gm: By binding this mind alone, All of them will be bound; By taming this mind alone, All of them will be tamed.

dm: In this way, all fears And immeasurable sufferings as well Arise from the mind; Thus it was taught by the Speaker of Truth.
gm: Thus, all fears and Immeasurable sufferings too, That they arise from the mind Was taught by the Speaker of Truth Himself.

dm: Who intentionally created The weapons of the hell beings? Who created the floor of burning iron, And from what did those masses of fire arise?
gm: The weapons of the hells for sentient beings, Who intentionally created them? Who created the burning iron ground? From what did those masses of fire arise?

dm: The Sage has taught that all such things Are the result of a sinful mind. Thus, within the three worlds, There is no other fear besides the mind.
gm: All such things Were taught by the Sage to be the sinful mind. Thus, in the three worlds, There is no fear other than the mind.

dm: If the perfection of generosity Consisted in the removal of the world's poverty, Then since beings are still destitute today, How could the Protectors of the past have reached that perfection?
gm: If by eliminating the poverty of wandering beings, The perfection of generosity is achieved, Since there are still destitute beings, how did the past Saviors achieve the perfection?

dm: The perfection of generosity is said to be the mind Of relinquishing all possessions, together with their results, To all beings; Therefore, it is the mind itself.
gm: All possessions together with their fruits, By the mind giving them to all people, The perfection of generosity is taught; Therefore, it is simply the mind itself.

dm: To what place could fish and other creatures be moved So that they would not be killed? The perfection of ethical discipline is explained As the attainment of the mind of renunciation.
gm: Where could fish and so forth Be driven away so that they are not killed? From attaining the mind of renunciation, The perfection of moral discipline is explained.

dm: Unruly sentient beings are like space; It is impossible to overcome them all. But if this single mind of anger is overcome, It is the same as overcoming all those enemies.
gm: Unruly sentient beings are like space; They can never be entirely overcome. If this single mind of anger is overcome, It is equivalent to overcoming all those enemies.

dm: Where could there be enough leather To cover the entire surface of the earth? But with just the leather of one's shoe soles, It is as if the whole earth were covered.
gm: To cover this surface of the earth with leather, Where could that much leather be found? With just the leather for the soles of one's shoes, It is equivalent to covering the entire surface of the earth.

dm: Likewise, I am unable to turn back All external phenomena; But I shall turn back this mind of mine; What need is there to turn back anything else?
gm: Likewise, external phenomena too, Cannot be turned back by me, But I will turn back this mind of mine; What need is there to turn back others?

dm: Just as the result of generating a single clear mind Is birth as a Brahmā or the like, The results of body and speech are not such, Because their conduct is weak.
gm: Whatever result is generated by a single clear mind, Such as Brahmā and so forth, The results of body and speech, Because of weak conduct, are not like that.

dm: Even if one practices recitations and all kinds of austerities For a very long period of time, The Knower of Reality has said that if they are performed With a mind distracted elsewhere, they are useless.
gm: All recitations and ascetic practices, Even if practiced for a long time, If done with a mind distracted elsewhere, Are taught by the Knower of Reality to be meaningless.

dm: Those who do not understand this secret of the mind, The supreme essence of the Dharma, Will wander aimlessly and in vain, Even though they wish to attain happiness and destroy suffering.
gm: If someone, regarding the supreme principal of Dharma, Does not know this secret of the mind, Even though they wish to attain happiness and overcome suffering, They will wander meaninglessly and in vain.

dm: Therefore, I shall firmly grasp And properly guard this mind of mine. Apart from the ascetic discipline of guarding the mind, What is the use of many other disciplines?
gm: Therefore, this mind of mine, I shall hold it well and guard it well. Except for the discipline of guarding the mind, What is the use of many disciplines?

dm: If one dwells in the midst of a boisterous crowd, One should be attentive, just as one protects a wound. Even when dwelling among wicked people, One should always guard this wound of the mind.
gm: When dwelling in the midst of a wild crowd, Just as one carefully protects a wound, So too, when dwelling in the midst of bad people, One should always guard this wound of the mind.

dm: If one protects a wound out of fear of even its slight pain, Then why, fearing the crushing of the Samghāta and Raurava hells, Does one not guard the wound of the mind?
gm: Because of the minor suffering of a wound, If one who is afraid carefully protects the wound, Those who fear the Crushing and Destroying Hells, Why do they not guard the wound of the mind?

dm: If one conducts oneself in this manner, Whether dwelling among wicked people Or even in the midst of women, The steady practitioner of discipline will not degenerate.
gm: If one acts with such conduct, Whether dwelling in the midst of bad people, Or even dwelling in the midst of women, The steadfast observer of vows will not decline.

dm: Better that my gains, honor, and body, And even my very life should perish, And better that my other virtues should decline, Than that I should ever let my mind degenerate.
gm: My gain and honor, And body and livelihood had better perish, And other virtues had better decline, But the mind must never decline.

dm: To those who wish to guard their minds, I join my palms in prayer and say: "With all your effort, guard both mindfulness and introspective awareness!"
gm: To those who wish to guard their minds, Mindfulness and introspection, Guard them both with all your effort! Thus I join my palms in prayer.

dm: Just as people who are disturbed by illness Have no strength for any activity, So too, a mind disturbed by confusion Has no strength for any activity.
gm: People who are disturbed by illness, Are powerless in all activities; Likewise, when the mind is disturbed by ignorance, One is powerless in all activities.

dm: For those whose minds lack introspective awareness, Even what has been heard, reflected upon, and meditated on, Will not remain in their memory, Like water in a leaking jar.
gm: Of one who has a mind without introspection, Even hearing, thinking, and meditating, Like water in a leaky vase, Will not remain in memory.

dm: Even many who possess learning and faith, And who apply themselves with great diligence, Become defiled by the stain of downfalls, Due to the fault of lacking introspective awareness.
gm: Those who are learned and have faith, And many who dedicate themselves to effort, Because they incur the fault of lacking introspection, Will become tainted by downfalls.

dm: The thieves of non-introspective awareness, Following upon the decline of mindfulness, Steal even the merits one has carefully accumulated, Leading one to the lower realms as if plundered by robbers.
gm: The thieves of lacking introspection, Following upon the decline of mindfulness, Even when merits are accumulated, Robbed by thieves, one goes to the lower realms.

dm: This band of thieves, the mental afflictions, Is constantly searching for an opportunity; Having found an opportunity, they steal one's virtue, And destroy even the life of a happy rebirth.
gm: This host of affliction-thieves, Seeks for an opportunity; And having found an opportunity, steals virtue, And destroys even the life of the happy realms.

dm: Therefore, mindfulness should never be allowed To stray from the gateway of the mind. If it should stray, one should bring it back By recollecting the sufferings of the lower realms.
gm: Therefore, mindfulness from the door of the mind, Should never be let go. Even if it departs, recalling the harms of the lower realms, It should be closely maintained.

dm: Through associating with a spiritual master, Following the instructions of a preceptor, And through fear, the fortunate who act with respect Will easily develop mindfulness.
gm: From associating with gurus, And the instructions of preceptors, In the fortunate who act with respect out of fear, Mindfulness is easily generated.

dm: The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas Possess vision that is completely unhindered; Thinking, "I always stand In the presence of them all,"
gm: The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, Are endowed with unobstructed vision everywhere. "In the presence of them all, I am always dwelling."

dm: By reflecting in this way, one should maintain A sense of shame, respect, and likewise fear. Consequently, the recollection of the Buddha Will also arise in one again and again.
gm: Thinking like this, with shame, Respect, and fear, one should dwell. Thus, the recollection of the Buddhas, Will also arise in one again and again.

dm: When mindfulness stands at the gateway of the mind For the purpose of guarding it, At that time alertness will arrive, And even that which had slipped away will return.
gm: When mindfulness from the door of the mind, Remains for the sake of guarding, At that time introspection will come, And even what has gone will return.

dm: First, having recognized that a mind such as this Is possessed of faults, At that time I should remain As steady as a log.
gm: At first, a mind like this, Having known it to be faulty, At that time, I, like a piece of wood, Should remain steadfast.

dm: I should never look around With a distracted or aimless gaze; With a resolute mind, I should always Keep my eyes cast downward.
gm: Looking around distractedly without purpose, I should never do; Always with a resolute mind, I should look with eyes cast down.

dm: To rest the gaze, one may Occasionally look toward the horizon; If someone appears in the field of vision, One should look at them and say, "Welcome."
gm: For the sake of resting the sight, Occasionally I should look to the directions. If someone appears in the path of sight, Having looked, I should say "Welcome."

dm: To check for dangers on the path and so forth, One should repeatedly look in the four directions. After pausing to rest, one should turn around And look toward the area behind.
gm: In order to examine dangers on the path and so forth, I should look again and again to the four directions. Having rested, turning the head around, I should look to the direction behind.

dm: Having examined what is in front and behind, One should then proceed to go or come; Thus, in all circumstances, One should act with an understanding of what is necessary.
gm: Having examined in front and behind, I should go or otherwise come; Likewise, in all situations, Having known what is needed, I should act.

dm: Having prepared for an action with the thought, "My body shall remain in this way," One should then periodically observe How this body is positioned.
gm: "The body should remain like this," Having prepared the action, then, Occasionally, "How is this body Remaining?" I should look.

dm: The intoxicated elephant of the mind Must be bound to the great pillar of reflecting on the Dharma; One should examine with all diligence So that it does not escape from how it is tied.
gm: The mad elephant of the mind, To the great pillar of thinking on the Dharma, So that it does not escape from how it is tied, Thus, it should be examined with all effort.

dm: In such a way, one should strive So that meditative concentration does not slip away for even a single moment; One should individually examine the mind, Thinking, "Where is this mind of mine wandering?"
gm: So that one striving in concentration Does not stray even for a single moment, "Where is this mind of mine engaged?" Thus, one should individually examine the mind.

dm: If one is unable to do so due to involvement in dangers, festivities, and the like, one should act as is appropriate; For it is taught that at times such as when practicing generosity, the rules of discipline may be set aside in equanimity.
