gm: When involved with dangers and festivities and so forth, If one is unable, one should act at ease. Thus, at times of giving, It is taught to treat ethical discipline with equanimity.

dm: Whatever task one has reflected upon and begun, One should not think of anything other than that; With the mind directed toward that goal, One should first accomplish that very task.
gm: Whatever is intended and begun to be done, One should not think of anything other than that; With the thought directed to that, That very thing should be accomplished for the time being.

dm: If one acts in this way, all is well performed; Otherwise, neither task will be achieved. If there is no introspection, the secondary afflictions Will not fail to increase.
gm: In that way, everything is well done; Otherwise, neither will happen. The secondary affliction of lacking introspection, In that way, will not increase.

dm: When one encounters various kinds of idle chatter And many sorts of wondrous spectacles, One should abandon attachment To all of them.
gm: Various kinds of idle gossip, And many kinds of wondrous spectacles— When engaging in all of them, One should abandon attachment to them.

dm: If one begins to aimlessly dig the earth, cut the grass, Or draw patterns in the dirt, One should remember the training of the Sugatas And, out of fear, cease immediately.
gm: Digging the earth, cutting grass without purpose, And drawing lines in the earth and so forth—if one does these, Having remembered the training of the Sugatas, Out of fear, one should abandon it instantly.

dm: Whenever one desires to move, Or even when one desires to speak, One should first examine one's own mind And, remaining steadfast, act with propriety.
gm: Whenever one desires to move, Or even when one desires to speak, Having first examined one's own mind, With steadfastness, one should act with understanding.

dm: Whenever one's mind is affected by attachment Or the desire to be angry, One should not act and should not speak; One should remain like a log of wood.
gm: Whenever one's own mind has attachment, Or the desire to be angry—at that time, One should not act and should not speak; One should remain like a piece of wood.

dm: If there is agitation or mockery, Or if there is pride and arrogance, Or the intention to expose others' faults, Or if there is divisiveness and deceit,
gm: With wildness and mockery, Or if one possesses pride and arrogance, And the intention to expose faults, Or if there is an evasive or deceptive mind,

dm: Whenever one is intent on self-praise, Or on disparaging others, Or if one becomes abusive or filled with remorse, At those times, one should remain like a log of wood.
gm: Whenever one is devoted to self-praise, Or the very disparaging of others, Or becoming abusive and resentful, At that time, one should remain like a piece of wood.

dm: If one desires gain, honor, or fame, Or if one seeks a circle of attendants, Or if one's mind desires to be served, At those times, one should remain like a log of wood.
gm: Desiring gain, honor, and fame, Or desiring to seek attendants and retinues, If one's mind desires to be served, At that time, one should remain like a piece of wood.

dm: When the intention to neglect the welfare of others, Or the desire to pursue one's own interests, Or the urge to speak arises, At those times, one should remain like a log of wood.
gm: Forsaking the benefit of others, And desiring to pursue one's own benefit, If a mind desiring to speak arises, Because of that, one should remain like a piece of wood.

dm: When impatience, laziness, or fear arise, And likewise when impudence or idle chatter, Or attachment to one's own side arises, At those times, one should remain like a log of wood.
gm: Intolerance, laziness, and fear, Likewise shamelessness and senseless talk, If a mind attached to one's own side arises, At that time, one should remain like a piece of wood.

dm: Having thus examined the mind for afflictions And for strivings toward meaningless things, At that time, the heroic one should firmly Restrain it by means of the antidote.
gm: Thus, completely afflicted, Having examined the mind striving for meaningless things, At that time, the hero, by means of an antidote, Should hold it firmly.

dm: With deep certainty and supreme faith, With steadfastness, respect, and courtesy, With a sense of shame and dread of blame, Be peaceful and strive to bring joy to others.
gm: With utmost certainty and excellent faith, Steadfast, respectful, and courteous, With a sense of shame and with apprehension, Peaceful, and striving to make others happy.

dm: Do not be weary of the conflicting Desires of the childish, But be compassionate, thinking, "These arise from their afflictions."
gm: Of the childish who are mutually discordant, Not being disheartened by their desires, 'From these arisen afflictions, This mind has arisen,' thinking thus, being endowed with compassion, and

dm: In matters that are naturally blameless, For the sake of myself and other beings, I should always maintain this mind Without a sense of self, like an emanation.
gm: Regarding faultless things, Having mastered myself and sentient beings, Without "I", like an apparition, This mind should always be held.

dm: Reflecting again and again that after a long time I have obtained this supreme leisure, I should hold my mind as utterly unshakable as Mount Meru.
gm: After a long time, the supreme leisure, Reflecting again and again on having attained it, Such a mind, like Mount Meru, Should be held completely unshakable.

dm: If you, O mind, are not displeased when vultures, Craving flesh, drag this body all around, Why do you cherish it so much now?
gm: By vultures desiring flesh, Even when dragged back and forth everywhere, Mind, if you do not become displeased, Why do you care for it now?

dm: Having grasped this body as "mine," O mind, why do you guard it? Since you and this body are separate, What can it ever do for you?
gm: Having grasped this body as "mine", Mind, why do you guard it? If you and this are separate, What use is it to you?

dm: O deluded mind, why do you not grasp instead a clean wooden image? Why is it appropriate to guard this foul machine, This collection of impurities?
gm: Deluded mind, for what reason Do you not grasp a clean wooden form? This machine of a collection of impurities, Guarding this rotten thing, what is the use?

dm: First, with your own intellect, peel away this layer of skin; Then, with the blade of wisdom, Separate the flesh from the lattice of bones.
gm: First, this layer of skin, Separate it with your own intellect. And the flesh from the network of bones, Separate it aside with the weapon of wisdom.

dm: Having also dismantled the bones, Look right into the marrow and examine for yourself: "What essence is there in this?"
gm: Having also divided the bones, One should look down to the marrow, and "What essence is there in this?" You yourself should examine.

dm: If, despite searching with such effort, you find no essence there, Then why do you still guard this body With such an attitude of attachment?
gm: Even having searched with effort in that way, there, If you do not see any essence, Why still, with attachment, Do you protect this body?

dm: Since you cannot eat its impurities, Nor drink its blood, Nor suck its intestines, what use is this body to you?
gm: Impurities are not fit for you to eat, Blood also is not fit to drink, And intestines cannot be sucked, so What will the body do for you?

dm: At best, it is only fit to be guarded as food for foxes and vultures; This human body is meant only to be put to use.
gm: At best, by foxes and vultures, This is fit to be guarded for the sake of food. This human body Is fit only to be employed.

dm: Even if you guard it in this way, When the pitiless Lord of Death Snatches it away and gives it to the birds and dogs, What will you be able to do then?
gm: Even though you guard it like this, By the merciless Lord of Death If it is snatched and given to birds and dogs, At that time what can you do?

dm: If you do not provide clothing and such Even to a servant who cannot be put to work, Then why do you exhaust yourself nourishing this body Which, though cared for, will depart elsewhere?
gm: If one does not give clothes and so forth Even to a servant who cannot be employed, If this body goes elsewhere even when nurtured, Why do you exhaust yourself nurturing it?

dm: Having given this its wages, Now make it perform your own purpose; Do not give everything to this body If it brings no benefit.
gm: Having given wages to this, Now make it serve your own purpose. Without any benefit, to this You should not give everything.

dm: Regarding the body as a boat, a mere support for coming and going, Think of it as a vessel, And in order to accomplish the welfare of sentient beings, Transform it into a wish-fulfilling body.
gm: Merely as a support for going and coming, Conceive of the body as a boat, and In order to accomplish the welfare of sentient beings, Transform it into a wish-fulfilling body.

dm: Having thus gained self-mastery, Always maintain a smiling countenance; Completely abandon frowning and scowling, And be a friend to all beings and speak sincerely.
gm: Thus, since you are in control, Always bear a smiling face. Completely abandon frowns and grimaces, Be an honest friend to wandering beings.

dm: Do not move chairs and such things Carelessly or with loud noise; Do not open doors forcefully, But always delight in modesty and restraint.
gm: Chairs and so forth, recklessly You should not throw down with noise. Also, do not open doors violently; Always delight in acting quietly.

dm: The heron, the cat, and the thief, By moving stealthily and silently, Accomplish their desired aims; A sage should always behave in such a manner.
gm: Waterfowl, cats, and thieves, By going silently and stealthily, Accomplish their desired goals; The sage should always act like that.

dm: One should respectfully accept upon one's head The words of those skilled in advising others And who provide unsolicited benefit; Always remain a student to everyone.
gm: Skilled in exhorting others, and Words that act beneficially unasked, Accept them with respect upon your crown, and Always become the disciple of everyone.

dm: To all that is well-spoken, One should say, "It is excellently said." When seeing someone performing a meritorious deed, Generate joy by praising them well.
gm: To all words that are well spoken, You should say, "Excellently spoken." If you see someone creating merit, Generate joy well by praising them.

dm: Speak of virtues in private, And when virtues are spoken of, join in. When one's own virtues are spoken of, Recognize it as an appreciation of qualities.
gm: Speak of good qualities in secret, And if good qualities are spoken of, join in. If your own good qualities are spoken of, Understand that as them knowing good qualities.

dm: All such endeavors are for the sake of joy, Which is rare even if one were to buy it with wealth. Therefore, through the virtues performed by others, One should enjoy the happiness of being joyful.
gm: All undertakings are for the sake of joy, Yet that is rare even if bought with a price. Therefore, through the good qualities achieved by others, I should enjoy the happiness of joy.

dm: In this, there is no loss for oneself, And in the next life, there will be great happiness; Through wrongdoing, one is unhappy and suffers, And in the next life, the suffering will be even greater.
gm: In this, there is no loss for me here, And in the next life there is great happiness. Through faults there is unhappiness and suffering, And in the next life there is great suffering.

dm: When speaking, one should speak in a way that is agreeable, coherent, And clear in meaning, and pleasant; Free from attachment and aversion, One should speak gently and in moderation.
gm: When speaking, comforting and coherent, Clear in meaning and pleasing to the mind, Having abandoned attachment and hatred, One should speak gently and in moderation.

dm: Even when looking at sentient beings with one's eyes, One should think, "It is by relying on these very beings That I shall attain Buddhahood," And look upon them with a straightforward and loving manner.
gm: Even when looking at sentient beings with your eyes, Thinking, "Relying precisely upon them, I will become a Buddha," You should look with a direct and loving manner.

dm: Whether motivated by constant devotion Or by the application of an antidote, Great virtue arises toward those who possess qualities, Those who have been helpful, and those who are suffering.
gm: Motivated by constant strong aspiration, Or motivated by the antidote, Towards the fields of qualities and benefactors, And the suffering, virtue becomes great.

dm: Having become skillful and endowed with initiative, I shall always perform my tasks. In all activities, one should not Depend upon anyone else.
gm: Being skilled and endowed with faith, I should always perform actions myself. In all actions, upon anyone at all, I should not rely.

dm: One should practice the perfections, such as generosity, In an ever-ascending degree of excellence. One should not sacrifice a great benefit for a small one; The primary consideration should be the welfare of others.
gm: The perfection of generosity and the rest, Should be practiced, progressing higher and higher. One should not abandon the greater for the lesser. Principally, one should consider the benefit of others.

dm: Having understood this, one should always Remain diligent in working for the welfare of others. Because the Compassionate One sees far ahead, He permits even those things that were prohibited.
gm: Having understood thus, for the benefit of others, One should always remain striving. By the Compassionate One who sees far, Even prohibited actions have been permitted for that.

dm: One should share with those who have fallen into wrong paths, the protectorless, And those established in ascetic vows; One should eat only in moderation, And give away everything except for the three religious robes.
gm: To those fallen into ruin, the unprotected, And those abiding in ascetic practice, one should share; One should eat only a moderate amount, And give away everything except the three Dharma robes.

dm: This body, which practices the sublime Dharma, Should not be harmed for the sake of something minor. By acting in this way, the aspirations Of sentient beings will be swiftly fulfilled.
gm: The body that practices the sublime Dharma Should not be harmed for trivial reasons. If one acts thus, the wishes of sentient beings Will quickly be fulfilled.

dm: As long as the compassionate intention is not pure, One should not give away this body; Rather, in this and other lives as well, It should be given as a cause for accomplishing the great purpose.
gm: As long as the thought of compassion is impure, This body should not be given away; Rather, in this and other lives as well, It should be given as a cause to accomplish a great purpose.

dm: Do not teach the Dharma to those who are disrespectful. Do not teach those who, unless they are ill, wear turbans, Carry parasols, staffs, or weapons, Or have their heads covered.
gm: One should not explain the Dharma to the disrespectful, Nor to those who wear head-wraps while not sick, Nor to those holding umbrellas, staffs, or weapons, Nor to those whose heads are covered.

dm: Do not teach the profound and vast to those of lesser inclination, Nor to a woman without a man present. Toward both the lesser and the supreme teachings, One should always act with equal respect.
gm: Nor the profound and vast to the inferior, Nor to a woman without a man present. To the inferior and supreme Dharmas, One should apply equal respect in all cases.

dm: One who has become a vessel for the vast Dharma Should not be applied to the lesser Dharma. One must not completely forsake proper conduct, Nor deceive others with Sutra or Mantra.
gm: One who is a vessel for the vast Dharma Should not be engaged in the inferior Dharma; Conduct should not be completely cast aside, Nor should they be deceived with sutras and mantras.

dm: When discarding tooth-sticks or spitting, One should cover them. It is also criticized to discharge urine and so forth Into water or onto land intended for use.
gm: Tooth-sticks and saliva, When discarded, should be covered; Also, urine and the like, into usable Water or on land, it is deprecated to discard.

dm: Do not eat with a full mouth, with noise, Or with the mouth wide open. Do not sit with legs stretched out, And do not rub your hands together.
gm: With a full mouth, making noise, And with an open mouth, one should not eat; One should not sit with legs outstretched, And one should not rub the hands together.

dm: In vehicles, on beds, or in dwellings, Do not remain alone with another's wife. Having observed and inquired, Avoid everything that causes the world to lose faith.
gm: In vehicles, beds, and seats, One should not be alone with another's woman. Everything that causes the world to lose faith, Having observed and inquired, one should abandon.

dm: One should not make gestures with the fingers; Rather, with a gesture of respect, One should use the entire right hand To indicate the way in that manner.
gm: One should not indicate with a finger, But respectfully, with the right Hand used entirely, Even the path should be shown in this way.

dm: Do not wave your arms excessively; Move them only slightly and make a sound, Such as snapping your fingers, to give a signal; Otherwise, you will be acting without restraint.
gm: One should not wave the arms wildly, But move them slightly, making a sound By snapping the fingers and so forth as a sign; Otherwise, one will be uncontrolled.

dm: Just as the Protector lay when passing into nirvana, One should lie down in the desired direction; From the very beginning, firmly apply the intention To wake up quickly with alertness.
gm: Just as the Lord lay when passing into nirvana, One should lie down in the desired direction; With clear comprehension and the thought of rising quickly, One should definitely set the mind from the very beginning.

dm: Although the conduct of Bodhisattvas Is said to be immeasurable, One should certainly practice those activities That serve to train the mind.
gm: The practices of the Bodhisattvas Are taught to be limitless; The practice of purifying the mind, One should definitely practice at least that much.

dm: Three times during the day and three times at night, One should recite the Three Heaps Sūtra; By relying on the Victors and the spirit of awakening, One should pacify the remaining downfalls.
gm: Three times during the day and night, One should recite the Triskandha; By relying on the Conquerors and the awakening mind, One should pacify the remainder of downfalls thereby.

dm: Whether by one's own power or the influence of others, In whatever situation or whatever one is doing, One should diligently train in whatever Has been taught as the training for that occasion.
gm: Whether under one's own or another's power, In whatever situation, whatever one is doing, Whatever has been taught as a training, In that situation, one should exert oneself and train.

dm: There is nothing whatsoever That the Sons of the Victors should not learn; For the wise who abide in this way, There is no merit that does not accrue.
gm: That which is not to be trained in by the Sons of the Conqueror, Does not exist at all; For the wise one who abides in this way, There is nothing that does not become merit.

dm: Whether directly or indirectly, Do nothing other than act for the benefit of sentient beings; Solely for the sake of sentient beings, Dedicate everything toward enlightenment.
gm: Whether directly or else indirectly, One should do nothing other than the benefit of sentient beings; For the sake of sentient beings alone, One should dedicate everything for awakening.

dm: One should never forsake a spiritual friend Who is learned in the meaning of the Mahāyāna And possesses the supreme conduct of a Bodhisattva, Even at the cost of one's own life.
gm: Always, the virtuous spiritual friend, Who is skilled in the meaning of the Mahāyāna, And the supreme discipline of the bodhisattvas, Should not be given up even for the sake of one's life.

dm: Learn the manner of relying on a guru As described in the life story of Śrīsambhava; This and other teachings of the Buddha Are to be understood by reading the sūtras.
gm: From the liberation story of Śrīsaṃbhava, One should train in the manner of relying on the guru; This and other words spoken by the Buddha, Should be known after reading the sūtras.

dm: The trainings are revealed within the sūtras, Therefore, one should read the sūtras; The Ākāśagarbha Sūtra, in particular, Should be looked at first of all.
gm: The trainings appear in the sūtras, Therefore, one should read the sūtras; The Ākāśagarbha Sūtra, Should be looked at from the very beginning.

dm: Because it extensively demonstrates What must be practiced at all times, The Śikṣāsamuccaya as well Should certainly be looked at again and again.
gm: Because what is to be practiced constantly Is extensively taught in that, The Śikṣāsamuccaya, too, Should definitely be looked at again and again.

dm: Alternatively, for the time being, one should look at the concise Compendium of Sūtras; Both works composed by the noble Nāgārjuna should also be studied with diligence.
gm: Or else, for the time being, the brief Sūtrasamuccaya should be looked at; And the two composed by the Noble Nāgārjuna Should also be looked at with effort.

dm: Whatever is not prohibited therein Is exactly what should be practiced; In order to guard the minds of worldly beings, Having seen the trainings, one should practice them correctly.
gm: Whatever is not forbidden by whichever, That itself should be practiced; In order to guard the minds of worldly beings, Having seen the trainings, one should practice perfectly.

dm: Regarding the state of one's body and mind, One should examine them again and again; This alone, in brief, Is the definition of guarding introspection.
gm: The states of the body and mind, Should be examined again and again; That alone, in brief, Is the defining characteristic of guarding introspection.

dm: These must be practiced with the body; What can be accomplished by merely speaking words? Will a sick person be benefited By merely reading a medical treatise?
gm: These should be practiced with the body; What will be accomplished by merely uttering words? By merely reading a medical treatise, Will patients be benefited?

dm: This concludes the fifth chapter, "Guarding Introspection," from the *Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva*.
gm: From Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva, the fifth chapter: Guarding Introspection.

dm: The Perfection of Patience
gm: Chapter Six: Teaching Patience

dm: Whatever virtuous deeds have been accumulated, Such as generosity and offerings to the Sugatas, Over a thousand eons, A single moment of anger destroys them all.
gm: Accumulated over a thousand eons, Generosity, offerings to the Sugatas, and so forth— Whatever good conduct there is, all of that, A single moment of anger destroys.

dm: There is no evil like hatred, And no austerity like patience. Therefore, one should diligently practice patience In various ways.
gm: There is no misdeed like hatred; There is no ascetic practice like patience. Therefore, earnestly upon patience, One should meditate in various ways.

dm: If one harbors a mind of stinging hatred, The mind will not experience the taste of peace; One will find neither joy nor happiness, Will not sleep, and will become unstable.
gm: If one holds a mind with the dart of hatred, The mind does not experience peace, Neither joy nor happiness is obtained, Sleep does not come, and one becomes unsteady.

dm: Even those who depend on a master's kindness, Having been provided for with wealth and honors, Will seek to kill that master If he is possessed by anger.
gm: Those who, through wealth and honors, Have been favored and depend upon him, Even they, against the hate-filled Master, will rebel to kill him.

dm: Because of that, his friends will become weary of him; Even if gathered through generosity, they will not remain. In short, there is no one at all Who dwells in happiness while possessed by anger.
gm: Because of it, friends become disheartened; Though gathered by generosity, they do not stay. In brief, an angry person who dwells in happiness— There is no such thing at all.

dm: The enemy of anger produces these And many other such sufferings. Those who strive to conquer anger Will find happiness in this life and the next.
gm: The enemy of anger will create These and other such sufferings. Whoever applies effort and destroys anger, That one is happy in this life and the next.

dm: Finding its fuel in the mental unease Caused by the occurrence of the unwanted And the obstruction of what is desired, Hatred flourishes and then destroys me.
gm: From doing what is undesired and Hindering what is desired, there arises Mental unhappiness; having found this food, Hatred grows strong and destroys me.

dm: Therefore, I shall utterly destroy The sustenance of that enemy; For this enemy has no function Other than to cause me harm.
gm: Therefore, of that enemy, I Shall completely destroy the food; For, other than harming me, This enemy has no other task.

dm: No matter what befalls me, I shall not allow my joyful mind to be disturbed; For even if I become unhappy, my desires will not be fulfilled, And my virtues will decline.
gm: Whatever happens, I Shall not disturb my joyful mind. Even if unhappy, what is desired is not accomplished, And virtues will decline.

dm: If there is a remedy for it, Why be unhappy about it? If there is no remedy for it, What is the use of being unhappy?
gm: If it can be remedied, What is the point of being unhappy about it? If it cannot be remedied, What use is there in being unhappy about it?

dm: For myself or for my friends, I do not desire suffering, contempt, harsh words, Or unpleasantness; But for an enemy, it is the opposite.
gm: For myself or my friends, Suffering, contempt, harsh words, And unpleasantness are not desired; For enemies, it is the opposite of that.

dm: The causes of happiness occur only occasionally, While the causes of suffering are extremely numerous. Without suffering, there is no renunciation; Therefore, O mind, remain steadfast.
gm: The causes of happiness occur sometimes; The causes of suffering are very many. Without suffering, there is no renunciation. Therefore, mind, resolve to be steadfast!

dm: The followers of Durgā and the people of Karṇapa Endure the sensations of being burned, cut, and so forth; Why then am I so cowardly, When my goal is liberation?
gm: Devotees of asceticism and the Karṇapas Endure the sensations of burning, cutting, and so forth Pointlessly; for the sake of liberation, Why am I cowardly?

dm: There is nothing whatsoever That does not become easy through habituation. Therefore, by habituating yourself to minor harms, Learn to endure great adversity.
gm: That which does not become easier through familiarity— There is no such thing at all. Therefore, by becoming familiar with small harms, Endure great harms!

dm: Why do you not see the meaningless suffering Caused by snakes, gadflies, and the like, By sensations such as hunger and thirst, And by afflictions such as skin rashes?
gm: From snakes and gadflies, Sensations of hunger, thirst, and so forth, And conditions like rashes and so forth— Why have I not seen pointless sufferings?

dm: Against heat, cold, rain, wind, and the like, And against sickness, bondage, beatings, and so forth, I shall not be sensitive or fragile; For if I am, the harm will only increase.
gm: Towards heat, cold, rain, wind, and so forth, Sickness, bondage, beatings, and so forth, I should not be overly sensitive; If I do so, the harm increases.

dm: Some, when they see their own blood, Become even more exceptionally brave and steadfast; Others, when they see the blood of another, Become dazed and faint.
gm: When some see their own blood, They become exceptionally brave and steadfast; When some see the blood of others, They faint and fall unconscious.

dm: This arises from whether the mind is steady Or whether it has fallen into a state of cowardice; Therefore, disregard all harm, And remain unassailable by sufferings.
gm: That is due to the steadfastness of the mind, Or due to a cowardly nature. Therefore, disregarding harms, Make yourself unaffected by sufferings!

dm: Even when suffering arises, The wise should not allow their mind to be disturbed. For in the battle against the afflictions, There is much harm during the fight.
gm: Even when suffering arises, the wise Should not cloud the clarity of the mind. When waging war with the afflictions, During battle, harms are many.

dm: Disregarding all suffering, To conquer the enemies of hatred and the like— These are the victorious heroes; The rest are merely slaying corpses.
gm: Having disregarded all sufferings, Those who conquer enemies such as anger— They are the victorious heroes; The rest slay corpses.

dm: Furthermore, the qualities of suffering are: Through weariness, it dispels arrogance, Compassion arises for those in cyclic existence, One avoids misdeeds and delights in virtue.
gm: Furthermore, the quality of suffering is That through sorrow, arrogance is dispelled, Compassion arises for those in cyclic existence, Sin is shunned, and virtue is delighted in.

dm: Since one does not feel anger toward the great sources of suffering Such as bile and the like, Why be angry with sentient beings? They too are all impelled by conditions.
gm: Towards bile and so forth, which are Great sources of suffering, without being angry, Why be angry at those with minds? They too are all incited by conditions.

dm: For example, just as this illness arises Even though it is not desired, So too do the afflictions forcibly arise Even though they are not desired.
gm: For example, even without wishing it, Just as this sickness arises, Likewise, even without wishing it, Afflictions forcefully arise.

dm: Without thinking, "I shall be angry," People spontaneously become angry; Without thinking, "I shall arise," Anger likewise arises.
gm: Even without thinking, "I shall get angry," People get angry without choice; Even without thinking, "I shall produce it," Anger likewise arises.

dm: All faults, as many as there are, And various kinds of misdeeds, All arise through the power of conditions; They do not possess any independence.
gm: All however many faults there are, and Various kinds of sins— All these arise from the power of conditions; They do not possess independence.

dm: Even those assembled conditions Have no intention to produce anything; And that which is produced by them Has no intention, "I am being produced."
gm: Even those assemblages of conditions Have no intention, "We shall produce." And that which is produced by them has no Intention, "I shall be produced."

dm: That which is desired as the "Primal Substance" And that which is imputed as the "Self," Do not arise by intentionally thinking, "I shall come into being."
gm: Whatever is asserted as the "Primary Matter," and Whatever is imputed as the "Self"— Thinking, "I myself shall arise," They do not purposefully arise.

dm: If it does not exist because it has not been born, Then at that time, what could have the desire to be born? Since it is always distracted by sense objects, It is also not something that could cease.
gm: If it does not exist prior to arising, At that time, what wishes to arise? Since it would be permanently distracted by objects, It would also never cease.

dm: If that self were permanent, It would clearly be inactive, like space. Even if it were to encounter other conditions, What could they do to something that is unchanging?
gm: If that self is permanent, Like space, it is evidently inactive. Even if it meets with other conditions, What can be done to the unchanging?

dm: If it remains as it was before even at the time of acting, Then what has the action done to it? What kind of connection could there be Such that one could say, "This is its action"?
gm: If even at the time of acting it remains as before, What did the action do to it? By saying, "This is its action," What connection could there be?

dm: In this way, everything is dependent on other factors, And because of those factors, it lacks independence. Knowing this, one will not become angry At any phenomena, which are like magical illusions.
gm: Thus, everything is under the power of others, And that which has power is itself powerless. Having understood this, one will not get angry Towards all things, which are like emanations.

dm: If you ask, "Who is there to prevent what? Even the act of prevention is not reasonable," It is not unreasonable to desire the cessation Of sufferings that arise in dependence upon that.
gm: "By what is what to be reversed? Reversing too is illogical," if one says; In dependence upon that, the wish for sufferings' Continuum to be severed is not illogical.

dm: Therefore, whether it be an enemy or a friend, Should you see them acting improperly, Reflect that "This has arisen from such conditions," And in that way, remain at ease.
gm: Therefore, whether it is an enemy or a friend, If I see them doing what is improper, Thinking, "This arose from such conditions," I will remain happy, reflecting in this way.

dm: If things were accomplished by one's own independent will, Then since no one desires to suffer, Suffering would never arise For any embodied being at all.
gm: If things were accomplished by their own will, Since no one desires suffering, For all embodied beings, Suffering would not occur for anyone.

dm: Through heedlessness, people even harm themselves With thorns and the like; For the sake of obtaining women and other such objects, They are consumed by craving and engage in fasting and the like.
gm: Due to carelessness, even to themselves, They do harm with thorns and so forth; In order to obtain women and the like, They become obsessed and starve themselves and so forth.

dm: Some hang themselves or leap from cliffs, Consume poison or unwholesome food, And through non-meritorious conduct, They inflict harm upon themselves.
gm: Some hang themselves or jump from cliffs, Eat poison or unwholesome food, And through non-meritorious conduct, They bring harm upon themselves.

dm: When they are under the power of afflictions, They even kill their own beloved selves; At that time, how could they possibly Refrain from harming the bodies of others?
gm: When, overpowered by afflictions, They even kill their beloved selves, At that time, to the bodies of others, How could they not cause harm?

dm: Since they are driven by the arising of afflictions To engage in such acts as killing themselves, If compassion does not arise for them, What is the point of becoming angry?
gm: When, due to the arising of afflictions, They engage in killing themselves and so forth, If compassion does not at least arise, What point is there in becoming angry?

dm: If it is the nature of the childish To cause harm to others, It is inappropriate to be angry with them; It is like resenting fire for its nature to burn.
gm: If doing harm to others Is the nature of the childish, It is illogical to become angry at them, Like resenting fire for its nature of burning.

dm: Alternatively, if this fault is adventitious And sentient beings are gentle by nature, It is still inappropriate to be angry, Just as it is to resent the sky for being filled with smoke.
gm: But if that fault is adventitious, And the nature of sentient beings is gentle, Even then it is illogical to become angry, Like resenting space when smoke arises in it.

dm: If I am angry at the one who throws it Because they directly employed a stick or other weapon, Then since they too were incited by hatred, It is more appropriate to be angry at that hatred.
gm: Although sticks and the like are directly utilized, If I become angry at the one who wields them, Since they too are impelled by hatred, It is logical to be angry at hatred.

dm: In the past, I myself inflicted Such harm upon sentient beings; Therefore, it is only right that this harm Should befall me, who caused injury to others.
gm: In the past, to sentient beings, I have done harm such as this; Therefore, since I have harmed sentient beings, It is logical that this harm comes to me.

dm: Both his weapon and my body Are the causes of this suffering. Since he has drawn the weapon and I have provided the body, At whom should I be angry?
gm: Their weapons and my body Are both causes of suffering; They produced the weapon and I the body, At which one should I be angry?

dm: This body is like a human-shaped abscess, Painful and unable to bear being touched. Since I, blinded by craving, have grasped it, At whom should I be angry when it is harmed?
gm: Like a human-shaped ulcer, Painful and unable to bear being touched; When, blinded by craving, I have grasped it, When it is harmed, at whom should I be angry?

dm: Childish beings do not desire suffering, Yet they crave the causes of suffering. Since they are harmed by their own faults, Why should they be resentful toward others?
gm: Childish ones do not desire suffering, Yet they crave the causes of suffering; When harmed by my own faults, Why should I resent others?

dm: For example, just as the guardians of hell And the forest of sword-leaves are produced By one's own karma, At whom should I be angry?
gm: Like the guardians of hell, And the forest of sword-leaves, This is produced by my own karma, So at whom should I be angry?

dm: Impelled by my own past actions, Those who harm me have arisen; If by this they go to the hells, Have I not been the one to ruin them?
gm: Instigated by my own karma, Those who harm me appear; If because of this they go to hell, Have I not ruined them?

dm: By relying on these people, My many sins are purified through patience; Yet by relying on me, They go to the hells of long-lasting suffering.
gm: By relying upon them, Through patience my many negative actions are cleansed; But by relying upon me, they Will go to the long-lasting suffering of hell.

dm: I am the one who causes them harm, And they are the ones who benefit me; Why, then, O wicked mind, Do you perversely become angry?
gm: I am the one who harms them, While they are the ones who benefit me; Why perversely, O wicked mind, do you become angry?

dm: If I possess the virtue of a patient intention, I shall not go to the hells; If I protect myself, What harm has been done to them in this?
gm: If I possess the good qualities Of intention, I will not go to hell; If I protect myself, What will happen to them here?

dm: However, if I retaliate with harm, They will not be protected, And my own conduct will also be ruined; Thus, my ascetic practice will be destroyed.
gm: But if I cause harm in return, They will not be protected, And my conduct will also decline; Thus my ascetic practice will be destroyed.

dm: Since the mind is not a physical entity, No one can destroy it anywhere; Because of intense attachment to the body, The body is afflicted by sufferings.
gm: Because the mind is bodiless, No one can destroy it anywhere; Because of deep attachment to the body, The body is harmed by sufferings.

dm: If contempt, harsh speech, And unpleasant words Do not cause any harm to the body, Why, O mind, do you become so angry?
gm: Contempt, speaking harsh words, And those unpleasant words— Since they do not harm the body, O mind, why do you become so angry?

dm: If the dislike that others have for me Does not consume me in this life or in other lives, Why should I be averse to it?
gm: That others dislike me, Since that, in this life or another, Will not consume me, Why do I dislike it?

dm: If I am averse to this because it creates obstacles to my gain, My gains will be discarded in this world, But my sins will remain firm.
gm: Because it hinders my gain, If I do not desire this, My gain will be left behind here, But my negative actions will remain steadfast.

dm: It is better that I die this very day Than to live a long life through wrong livelihood; Even if I were to remain for a long time, The suffering of death will be exactly the same.
gm: It is better that I die this very day, Than to live long by wrong livelihood; Even if I remain for a long time, The suffering of death will be just the same.

dm: Suppose one person experiences happiness for a hundred years in a dream and then wakes up, And another experiences happiness for just a brief moment and then wakes up;
gm: Having experienced happiness in a dream for a hundred years, Whoever awakens, And having experienced happiness for just an instant, Whoever awakens—

dm: For both of those who have awakened, That happiness never returns. Whether one’s life is long or short, At the time of death, it is exactly the same.
gm: For both of those who awaken, That happiness will not return; For both a long life and a short life, At the time of death they end up just the same.

dm: Even if one acquires great wealth And enjoys happiness for a long time, Just like someone plundered by thieves, One will depart naked and empty-handed.
gm: Even if I acquire abundant gains, And enjoy happiness for a long time, Just like being robbed by a thief, I will depart naked and empty-handed.

dm: If you think, "I shall live on my gains And, while doing so, exhaust my sins and perform merit," Yet you become angry for the sake of that gain, Will your merit not be exhausted and will you not incur sin?
gm: If you say, "By living on account of gains, I will exhaust negative actions and perform merit," If I become angry for the sake of gains, Will not merit be exhausted and negative actions created?

dm: If the very purpose for which I live Is itself undermined, What is the use of a life That consists only of committing sins?
gm: That very purpose for which I live, If it is destroyed, That performs only negative actions— What is the use of such a life?

dm: If you say you are angry at those who speak unpleasantly Because they harm sentient beings, Then why are you not likewise angry When others are spoken of unpleasantly?
gm: If you say, "Because it causes sentient beings to lose faith, I become angry at those who speak unpleasant words," When unpleasant words are spoken about others, Why do you not likewise become angry?

dm: Since a lack of faith depends on others, If you can tolerate those who have no faith, Then since the arising of afflictions depends on others, Why can you not tolerate those who speak unpleasantly?
gm: Because lack of faith depends on others, If you tolerate those without faith, Because it depends on the arising of afflictions, Why do you not tolerate those who speak unpleasant words?

dm: Toward those who revile and destroy Sacred images, stupas, and the sublime Dharma, It is not appropriate for me to feel hatred, For the Buddhas and the like cannot be harmed.
gm: Towards images, stupas, and the sublime Dharma, Even if someone disparages or destroys them, It is inappropriate for me to have anger, For the Buddhas and so forth suffer no harm.

dm: Toward those who cause harm to my Gurus, relatives, and friends, I should see that these events arise from conditions, As previously explained, and thus restrain my anger.
gm: Towards gurus, relatives, and so forth, And even those who do harm to friends, Through conditions, in the previous manner, Seeing that it occurs, turn back anger.

dm: Since harm is inflicted upon embodied beings By both those with minds and those without, Why single out and bear a grudge against those with minds? Therefore, you should endure all harm.
gm: To embodied beings, animate And inanimate things both do harm; Why single out the animate and hold resentment? Therefore, be patient with harm.

dm: Some commit misdeeds out of delusion; If others, being deluded, become angry, Who among them is without fault, And who is the one who is at fault?
gm: Some commit faults through ignorance, And some, being ignorant, become angry. Among them, who is to be considered faultless? And who is to be considered at fault?

dm: Why did I previously commit those actions By which others now cause me harm? Since everything is dependent upon karma, Why should I be angry with this?
gm: That which causes others to do harm— Why did I do those actions in the past? If everything depends upon karma, Why should I hold resentment toward this?

dm: Having seen this, I shall strive in every way To gather merit, so that all beings May come to have a mind of mutual love For one another.
gm: Seeing this to be so, by all means, So that everyone will have loving thoughts towards one another, In order to bring this about, I will Exert myself in meritorious deeds.

dm: For example, when a fire that has broken out in one house Moves to another house, One should pull out and discard the straw Or whatever else causes it to spread.
gm: For example, when a fire burning a house Spreads into another house, Whatever straw and so forth it spreads to, That should be taken out and discarded.

dm: Likewise, when the mind becomes attached to something And the fire of hatred begins to spread, One should discard that immediately Out of fear that one's merit will be consumed.
gm: Likewise, whatever the mind is attached to, If the fire of hatred spreads to it, Fearing that merit will be burned, It should be discarded instantly.

dm: If a man condemned to death is freed By having a hand cut off, why is that not excellent? If, through human suffering, One is spared from hell, why is that not excellent?
gm: If a person to be killed has his hand cut off And escapes, why is that not good? If through human suffering One is freed from hell, why is that not good?

dm: If I am unable to endure even this much present suffering, Then why do I not turn away from anger, Which is the cause of the sufferings of hell?
gm: Even for this much suffering right now, If I cannot endure it, Then the cause of suffering in hell, Anger, why do I not avert it?

dm: For the sake of my desires, I have experienced Being burned and so forth in the hells thousands of times, Yet I have accomplished neither my own benefit Nor the benefit of others.
gm: For the sake of desires, burning and so forth, I have experienced in hell thousands of times, but I did not accomplish my own benefit, Nor did I accomplish the benefit of others.

dm: Since this is not harmful to that extent, And great purposes will also be accomplished, It is right to take only joy in this suffering That dispels the harm of all migratory beings.
gm: This is not so harmful, And great benefits will also be accomplished; In the suffering that dispels the harm of wandering beings, It is appropriate here only to rejoice.

dm: If others find the happiness of joy By praising those who possess good qualities, Why, O mind, do you not also praise them And likewise rejoice in that way?
gm: If others, by praising those possessing good qualities, Attain the joy of happiness, O mind, by praising them too, Why do you not rejoice in that way?

dm: This happiness of your rejoicing Is a source of bliss that is blameless; It is permitted by those endowed with excellence, And is the supreme way of attracting others.
gm: This joy of your rejoicing Produces happiness and has no blame; It is approved by those possessing good qualities, And is also supreme in gathering others.

dm: If you do not desire this happiness Thinking, "In that way, the other person would be happy," Then by ceasing to give wages and the like, You will be ruined in both this life and the next.
gm: Thinking, "Others will become happy in that way," If you do not want this happiness, Because you forsake giving wages and so forth, You will be ruined in the seen and the unseen.

dm: When your own virtues are being praised, You even wish for others to be happy; But when the virtues of others are being praised, You do not even wish for your own happiness.
gm: When your own good qualities are spoken of, You want others to be happy too. When others' good qualities are spoken of, You do not want yourself to be happy.

dm: Since you have generated the mind of enlightenment Out of a desire for all sentient beings to be happy, Why do you become angry When sentient beings find happiness for themselves?
gm: Because you desire happiness for all sentient beings, Having generated the mind of awakening, If sentient beings find happiness themselves, Why do you become angry because of that?

dm: If you desire for sentient beings to attain Buddhahood, Which is honored by the three worlds, Why are you distressed when you see them Receive even a meager amount of honor and respect?
gm: To awaken into Buddhahood worshipped by the three worlds, If you desire for sentient beings, Having seen them receive mere meager respect, Why do you become tormented by that?

dm: Those whom you should support are your own dependents, To whom you yourself should be giving; If they find a livelihood through a relative, Would you not be glad instead of becoming angry?
gm: Whoever is to be nurtured, you nurture; They are to be given to by you yourself. If they find a livelihood from a relative, Do you not rejoice, but become angry instead?

dm: If you do not wish for them to have even this, How can you wish for them to attain enlightenment? Where is the bodhicitta in one Who becomes angry at the prosperity of others?
gm: If you do not want this for wandering beings, How can you desire awakening for them? For one who is angry at another's prosperity, Where is the mind of awakening?

dm: Whether that person receives it from another, Or it remains in the benefactor's house, In either case, it is not yours; So what does it matter to you whether it is given or not?
gm: If he receives that from him, Or if it remains in the benefactor's house, In all ways, since you do not have it, What does it matter whether it is given or not given?

dm: Why do you discard your own merit, faith, and good qualities? Tell me, why are you not angry at yourself For failing to grasp the gains that have come?
gm: Merit and faith, Or your own good qualities, why do you cast them away? Not taking hold of the gains that occur, Tell me, why do you not become angry?

dm: Not only do you feel no remorse For the sins you yourself have committed, But do you actually wish to compete With others who have performed meritorious deeds? Second Fascicle.
gm: You have committed negative deeds yourself, And not only are you without sorrow, But with others who have performed meritorious deeds, Do you want to compete together? The Second Fascicle.

dm: Even if an enemy is unhappy, What reason is there for you to rejoice in that? Your mere wishful thinking Will not become a cause of harm to them.
gm: Even if an enemy is unhappy, What is there for you to rejoice in? Merely by your wishing, It does not become a cause of harm to them.

dm: Even if that suffering were to be accomplished Through your desire, what reason is there for you to rejoice? If you think you will be satisfied by this, What could be more ruinous than that?
gm: If by your desires that suffering Is accomplished, what is there for you to rejoice in? If you say, "I will be satisfied," What is more ruinous than that?

dm: This hook cast by the fisherman of the afflictions Is an unbearable barb; Having been caught by it, you will surely be boiled In the cauldrons of hell by the hell-guardians.
gm: This hook, cast by the fisherman of the afflictions, Is an unbearable barb. Caught by it, in the cauldrons of hell, The guardians of hell will boil me.

dm: The honors of praise and fame Do not become merit, nor do they become long life; They do not become strength, nor are they health, And they do not even bring physical comfort.
gm: Praise, fame, and honor Will not become merit, nor will they become long life; Will not become my strength, and are not health; Nor will they make the body comfortable.

dm: If I were one who understood my own best interests, What benefit for myself would I find in those things? If it is mere mental pleasure that I seek, I might as well devote myself to gambling, alcohol, and the like.
gm: If I recognize my own welfare, What welfare of mine is there in that? If I desire only mental happiness, I should rely on gambling, alcohol, and the like.

dm: If, for the sake of fame, I squander my wealth And even bring about my own death, What use are these mere syllables? Once dead, who is it that will experience pleasure from them?
gm: For the sake of fame, losing wealth, And even getting myself killed, What is the use of mere syllables? When dead, who will be happy from them?

dm: When their sandcastles crumble, Children weep in despair; Likewise, when praise and fame decline, My own mind is just like a child's.
gm: When a sandcastle collapses, Children howl in despair. Likewise, when praise and fame decline, My own mind is like a child.

dm: Since sound is inanimate, It cannot possibly have the intention to praise me. If it is said that my joy comes from the fact that others are pleased, Perhaps that is the cause of my joy?
gm: First of all, since sound is mindless, It cannot possibly have the intention to praise me. The renown that "Others are pleased with me"— Perhaps that is the cause of joy.

dm: Whether that pleasure is directed toward someone else or toward myself, What benefit is another's joy to me? That joy and happiness belong only to that person; I do not obtain even a fraction of it.
gm: Whether it is directed at another or myself, How does the joy of another benefit me? That joy and happiness belongs to them alone; I do not obtain a share of it.

dm: If I am made happy by their happiness, Then I should feel the same way toward everyone. If I am happy because others are pleased, Why am I not happy when they find joy in others?
gm: If I am happy through their happiness, I should do the same toward everyone. How is it that when they become happy By rejoicing in others, I am not happy?

dm: Therefore, the joy that arises From thinking, "I am being praised," Is likewise unreasonable, And is nothing but the behavior of a child.
gm: Therefore, thinking, "I am being praised," The joy that arises in me— Since that also is unjustified in this way, It is nothing but the behavior of a child.

dm: Praise and the like distract me; They also destroy my sense of disillusionment. They cause envy toward those with good qualities, And they destroy my excellence as well.
gm: Praise and the like distract me, And also destroy my disillusionment; They cause jealousy toward those with good qualities, And destroy excellence as well.

dm: Therefore, are those who are present To destroy my praise and the like Not actually engaged in protecting me From falling into the lower realms?
gm: Therefore, regarding my praise and the like, Those who stand close by to destroy them— Are they not engaged in protecting me From falling into the lower realms?

dm: For me, who seeks liberation, I do not need the shackles of gain and honor. How could I be angry with those Who act to release me from my bonds?
gm: Since I seek liberation, I do not need the bonds of gain and honor. Those who free me from being bound— How could I be angry at them?

dm: For me, who wishes to enter into suffering, They are like a blessing from the Buddha; They have become the very door that prevents my fall, So how could I be angry with them?
gm: When I wish to enter into suffering, Like the blessing of the Buddha, They become a gate that prevents me from passing. How could I be angry at them?

dm: It is also not right to be angry with them, Thinking, "This person is an obstacle to my merit." Since there is no austerity equal to patience, Shall I not abide in that?
gm: Thinking, "This one is an obstacle to my merit," It is also inappropriate to be angry at them. Since there is no austerity equal to patience, Should I not abide in it?

dm: If, due to my own faults, I do not practice patience toward this person, I am merely creating an obstacle for myself Regarding this cause of merit that has arrived.
gm: If, through my own fault, I do not practice patience here, When the cause of merit is present, I am solely the one making an obstacle to it.

dm: Since that which does not occur in the absence of something, But does occur when that thing is present, Is defined as its cause, How can it be called an obstacle?
gm: If one thing does not arise without another, And comes to be when it is present, Since that very thing is its cause, How can it be called an obstacle?

dm: A beggar who arrives at the proper time Is not an obstacle to generosity; And one who enables the taking of vows Cannot be called an obstacle to ordination.
gm: By a beggar who arrives at the right time, No obstacle to giving is created; One who grants ordination Cannot be called an obstacle to ordination.

dm: In this world, beggars are many, But those who cause harm are rare; For if I do not cause harm to others, No one will cause harm to me.
gm: Beggars in the world are indeed plentiful, But those who cause harm are rare, For if I have not harmed others, No one will cause me harm.

dm: Therefore, like a treasure appearing in one's home Without being sought through wearisome toil, Because he becomes a helper in my bodhisattva conduct, I should rejoice in my enemy.
gm: Therefore, accomplished without toil, Like a treasure appearing in the house, Since they become my helper in bodhisattva conduct, I should delight in my enemies.

dm: Since it was accomplished by both him and me, The fruit of this patience Should be offered to him first, For in this way, he is the cause of patience.
gm: Since it is accomplished by this one and myself, Therefore, the fruit of patience Should first be offered to them, For they are the cause of patience.

dm: If you say that this enemy should not be honored Because they have no intention for me to practice patience, Then why honor the sublime Dharma, Which is also a fit cause for accomplishment but lacks intention?
gm: If you say, "Because they have no intention to accomplish my patience, This enemy is not to be venerated," Then since it is a suitable cause for accomplishment, Why do you venerate the sublime Dharma?

dm: If you say that this enemy should not be honored Because they have the intention to cause harm, Then if they were to strive for my benefit like a physician, How could my patience ever be achieved?
gm: If you say, "Because they have the intention to harm, This enemy is not to be venerated," If they strove to benefit me like a doctor, How could my patience be accomplished?

dm: Therefore, since patience arises In dependence upon a mind of intense malice, That very person is the cause of patience, And is as worthy of honor as the sublime Dharma.
gm: Therefore, since patience arises In dependence on a very hateful mind, Because they are the very cause of patience, They are worthy of veneration just like the sublime Dharma.

dm: For this reason, the Sage has spoken of the "field of sentient beings" And the "field of the Victors." Many who have pleased them have, In this way, reached the perfection of excellence.
gm: Therefore, the field of sentient beings And the field of the Conquerors, the Sage has proclaimed. By pleasing them, many Have thus reached the far shore of excellence.

dm: Since the attainment of the Buddha's qualities Depends equally upon sentient beings and the Victors, Why is it that you do not show the same respect To sentient beings as you do to the Victors?
gm: From sentient beings and from the Conquerors, The accomplishment of a Buddha's qualities is alike. Just as one respects the Conquerors, Why is it not the practice to do so for sentient beings?

dm: Their excellence is not based on their intention, but on the result; In that same way, Sentient beings also possess qualities, And for that reason, they are equal.
gm: The qualities of their intentions are not by themselves equal; It is due to the fruit that they are equal. Sentient beings also have qualities, And therefore they are equal.

dm: Whatever offerings are made to one who possesses a loving mind, That is the very greatness of sentient beings. Whatever merit comes from faith in the Buddhas, That too is the very greatness of the Buddhas.
gm: Whatever offering is made to one possessing a loving mind, That is the greatness of sentient beings. Whatever merit comes from faith in the Buddha, That too is the greatness of the Buddha.

dm: Since they possess a share in accomplishing the qualities of a Buddha, They are therefore asserted to be equal. Yet no one is equal to the Buddhas, Who are infinite oceans of excellence.
gm: Because they have a share in accomplishing a Buddha's qualities, Therefore they are asserted to be equal. Yet, regarding the boundless ocean of qualities, No one is equal to the Buddhas.

dm: If even a mere fraction of the qualities belonging to that unique collection of supreme excellence Appears in someone, Then offering the entire threefold world to honor them Would still be too little.
gm: Of the unique collection of supreme qualities, If merely a fraction of those qualities Appears in someone, in order to venerate them, Even offering the three realms would be too small.

dm: Since sentient beings possess a share in the arising of the supreme Buddha-Dharma, It is reasonable, based on this mere correspondence, To consider sentient beings as objects of worship.
gm: A fraction of generating the supreme qualities of a Buddha Is possessed by sentient beings; therefore, In accordance with just this fraction, It is fitting to venerate sentient beings.

dm: Furthermore, for those who have become my unwavering friends And who perform immeasurable benefit, What other way is there to repay them Than by pleasing sentient beings?
gm: Furthermore, to those who are unwavering friends And who perform immeasurable benefit, Other than pleasing sentient beings, What else could be a repayment?

dm: Since those who sacrifice their bodies and enter the Avīci hell Are repaid by benefiting these beings, Therefore, even if they cause me great harm, I shall act toward them all with nothing but goodness.
gm: For those for whose sake they give up their bodies and enter the Avīci hell, Benefiting them becomes a repayment; Therefore, even if they cause great harm, I should act toward all with complete goodness.

dm: Since those who have become my masters do not even regard their own bodies, How could a deluded person like me Act with pride toward them, Instead of acting as their servant?
gm: Even my own lords, Because they do not consider even their own bodies, How could a fool like me Act with pride toward them and not act as a servant?

dm: Since the Sages are delighted by the happiness of beings, And are displeased when they are harmed, By making them happy, all the Sages are delighted, And by harming them, one harms the Sages.
gm: Those by whose happiness the Sages are pleased, And by harming whom displeasure arises; By bringing joy to them, all the Sages are pleased, And by harming them, harm is done to the Sages.

dm: Just as one whose body is completely ablaze Cannot find any mental pleasure through sensual gratifications, Likewise, when sentient beings are harmed, There is no way for the Great Compassionate Ones to be pleased.
gm: Just as when one's body is completely engulfed in fire, No desirable things can make the mind happy, Likewise, when harm is done to sentient beings, There is no way for the greatly compassionate ones to be pleased.

dm: Therefore, whatever harm I have done to beings, Which has caused displeasure to all the Great Compassionate Ones, I confess each and every one of those sins today; I pray the Sages will forgive whatever has displeased them.
gm: Therefore, whatever harm I have done to wandering beings, Which has caused all the greatly compassionate ones to be displeased, I individually confess that negative deed today; I pray that the Sages forgive whatever displeasure I have caused.

dm: In order to please the Tathāgatas, From this day forth I shall remain a servant to the world. Even if many beings should kick me or trample upon my head, Or even kill me, I shall not retaliate; may the Protectors of the World be pleased.
gm: In order to please the Tathāgatas, From today onward I shall be a servant to the world. Even if the multitudes of wandering beings strike my head with their feet, Or kill me, I will not retaliate; may the protectors of the world be pleased!

dm: There is no doubt that those whose very nature is compassion Have taken all these beings as their own selves. Since these very beings are seen in the nature of the Protectors, Why do I not show respect to them?
gm: Those possessing the nature of compassion Have made all these wandering beings into themselves; of this there is no doubt. These very ones seen in the form of sentient beings Are the protectors themselves; why do I not respect them?

dm: This alone is what pleases the Tathāgatas, This is also the perfect accomplishment of one's own welfare, This alone dispels the suffering of the world; Therefore, I shall always make this my practice.
gm: This alone is what pleases the Tathāgatas; This alone is also the perfect accomplishment of my own purpose; This alone is also what dispels the suffering of the world; Therefore, I should always practice this alone.

dm: For example, even if some of a king's men Should cause harm to many people, Those who are far-sighted Will not retaliate, even if they have the power to do so.
gm: For example, if one of the king's men Causes harm to many people, Farsighted people, Even if they are capable, do not harm him in return,

dm: This is because such a person is not acting alone; The king's might is his power. Likewise, one should not despise Even a weak person who causes harm.
gm: Because he is not alone, The might of the king is his power; Likewise, a weak harm-doer Should not be despised at all.

dm: For the guardians of hell and the compassionate ones are their allies. Therefore, just as subjects placate a fierce king, One should please all sentient beings.
gm: Because the wardens of hell And the compassionate ones are their forces; Therefore, just as subjects please a fierce king, I should please sentient beings.

dm: Even if a king were to become enraged, Could he inflict the torments of hell, Which are the consequences one must experience By displeasing sentient beings?
gm: Even if a king were to become angry, By displeasing sentient beings, Whatever is to be experienced— Could he inflict that harm of hell?

dm: Even if a king were to be pleased, He could not possibly bestow the state of Buddhahood, Which is what is attained By pleasing sentient beings.
gm: Even if a king were to be pleased, Through having pleased sentient beings, Whatever is to be attained, He could not possibly grant Buddhahood itself.

dm: Not to mention the future attainment of Buddhahood, Which arises from pleasing sentient beings, Why do you not see that even in this very life, Great glory, fame, and happiness are achieved?
gm: Arising from pleasing sentient beings, Let alone the future accomplishment of Buddhahood, In this very life, great glory, Fame, and happiness will come; why do you not see this?

dm: In the cycle of existence, through patience one attains beauty and the like, As well as health and renown, A very long life, And the extensive happiness of a universal monarch.
gm: While in saṃsāra, through patience, beauty and the like, Health, and fame, An extremely long life, and The vast happiness of a universal monarch are attained.

dm: This concludes the sixth chapter, entitled "The Teaching on Patience," from the *Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva*.
gm: From Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva, the sixth chapter, named "Teaching Patience."

dm: The Perfection of Diligence
gm: Chapter Seven: Teaching Joyous Effort

dm: Thus, with patience, one should initiate diligence, For enlightenment dwells in those who strive in this way. Just as there is no movement without wind, Merit does not arise without diligence.
gm: Thus, having patience, I should undertake diligence. For enlightenment abides in diligence. Just as there is no movement without wind, Merit does not arise without diligence.

dm: What is diligence? It is delighting in the virtuous. Its opposing factors should be explained: Laziness, attachment to what is base, And the despondency of self-contempt.
gm: What is diligence? It is delight in virtue. Its opposing factors shall be explained: Laziness, clinging to what is bad, and Despondency, which is self-contempt.

dm: Through savoring the taste of idle pleasure, And the craving that relies on sleep, One does not feel weariness for the suffering of cyclic existence; From these, laziness fully arises.
gm: Tasting the pleasure of idleness, and Craving that relies on sleep; From feeling no weariness toward the sufferings of saṃsāra, Laziness comes to arise.

dm: Having been caught by the hunters of the afflictions, And having entered the snare of rebirth, You have walked into the jaws of the Lord of Death; How can you still not realize this?
gm: Having been snared by the fowler of afflictions, Having entered the net of birth, And having gone into the mouth of the Lord of Death, How is it that you still do not know?

dm: Have you not seen your own kind Being killed one by one? Yet you still rely on sleep, Like a buffalo in the hands of a butcher.
gm: That your own group is gradually being killed, Have you not seen it? Yet whoever relies on sleep, Is like an outcast and a buffalo.

dm: With all paths of escape completely blocked, And while the Lord of Death is watching you, How can you take pleasure in eating, And how can you find such joy in sleeping?
gm: When all paths are blocked, And the Lord of Death is watching, How can you enjoy eating, And how can you enjoy sleeping like this?

dm: Since death will come very quickly, For as long as you can, gather the accumulations. Even if you abandon laziness at that time, What can you do when it is no longer the right time?
gm: Because death will come very quickly, Until then, the accumulations should be gathered. Even if laziness is abandoned at that time, Being out of time, what can be done?

dm: While thinking, "This is not yet done," And "This is only half-finished," The Lord of Death suddenly arrives; "Alas! I am destroyed!" you will think.
gm: "This is undone, this is just begun, And this remains only half-done"— When the Lord of Death suddenly arrives, One will think, "Alas, I am ruined!"

dm: With eyes red and swollen from the force of grief, Tears will stream down your face; As your relatives lose all hope, You will gaze upon the faces of the messengers of the Lord of Death.
gm: Swollen by the force of sorrow, Red eyes shedding tears upon their faces, Relatives having lost hope, And looking at the faces of Yama's messengers.

dm: Tormented by the memory of your own sins, And hearing the sounds of the hells, You will soil your body in terror; When you have become thus delirious, what will you do?
gm: Tormented by the memory of one's own evils, And hearing the sounds of hell, Clothed in excrement out of terror, When one becomes delirious, what can be done?

dm: If you are possessed by such fear in this life, Like a live fish writhing on the ground, What need is there to mention the unbearable Sufferings of hell resulting from your sinful deeds?
gm: If you are fearful in this life, Like a live fish rolling about, Having committed evils, what need is there to mention The unbearable sufferings of hell?

dm: When touched by even warm water, Your tender flesh is intensely scalded; Having committed the actions that lead to hell, How can you remain so at ease?
gm: When touched by hot water, The tender-fleshed find it extremely hot. Having committed the deeds of hell, Why do you remain comfortably like this?

dm: Desiring results without exertion, And being thin-skinned, you are beset by many harms; Though seized by death, you act like an immortal; Alas, you are destroyed by your own sufferings!
gm: Desiring the result without exerting effort, Being fragile and experiencing many harms, Yet acting like a god while seized by death— Alas, you will be destroyed by sufferings!

dm: Relying upon this boat of a human form, Cross over the great river of suffering; Since this boat will be difficult to find again later, O foolish one, do not sleep at such a time!
gm: Relying on the boat of a human body, Free yourself from the great river of suffering. Since this boat will be hard to find later, Fool, do not sleep at this time!

dm: Having abandoned the supreme joy of the sublime Dharma, Which is a boundless cause of delight, Why do you delight in distractions, Frivolity, and the like, which are the causes of suffering?
gm: Which is a boundless cause of joy, Having abandoned the supreme joy of the holy Dharma, In distraction by the causes of suffering, And in frivolity and the like, why do you delight?

dm: Without despondency, with an army of forces, With earnest application and self-mastery, Practice the equality of self and others, And practice the exchange of self and others.
gm: Without despondency, and with the forces, Applying oneself earnestly, and mastering oneself, Equalizing self and other, And exchanging self and other, you should practice!

dm: One should not be discouraged, thinking, "How could I ever attain enlightenment?" For the Tathāgata, the Speaker of Truth, Has spoken this truth.
gm: Thinking, "How could I attain enlightenment?" I should not be despondent, For in this way the Tathāgata, Who speaks the truth, has spoken this truth:

dm: Even those who have become flies, gadflies, bees, Or likewise those who have become insects, If they develop the power of diligence, Will attain the supreme enlightenment so difficult to find.
gm: "Flies, mosquitoes, and bees, And likewise whatever is born as a worm, Even they, if they generate the power of effort, Will attain unsurpassable enlightenment, which is hard to find."

dm: Since I have been born as a human with the right potential, And recognize what is beneficial and what is harmful, If I do not abandon the conduct of a Bodhisattva, Why should I not attain enlightenment?
gm: Since someone like me is born as a human by birth, And recognizes what is beneficial and harmful, If I do not forsake the enlightenment conduct, Why should I not attain enlightenment?

dm: If you are afraid, thinking that you must give away Your limbs and so forth, It is merely the fear of a confused person Who has failed to analyze what is heavy and what is light.
gm: "But my arms, legs, and so forth, Must be given away, so I am afraid," if I think— Without examining what is heavy and what is light, Due to foolishness I am merely afraid.

dm: For countless tens of millions of eons, You have been cut, pierced, burned, and split apart many times over, Yet you have not attained enlightenment; And this will not lead to the attainment of enlightenment.
gm: For countless tens of millions of eons, I have been cut many times, Pierced, burned, and split apart, But did not attain enlightenment.

dm: The suffering I endure to achieve enlightenment is finite; It is like the pain of an incision made in the body To remove and destroy the harm of a deeply embedded splinter.
gm: The suffering of my accomplishing enlightenment Has a limit; To remove the harm of an internal thorn, It is like the suffering of making a cut in the body.

dm: All physicians use medical treatments To eliminate the discomfort of disease; Therefore, to destroy a multitude of sufferings, One should endure a minor discomfort.
gm: Even all doctors, through medical treatments, Cure illness with discomfort. Therefore, to destroy many sufferings, I should endure a minor discomfort.

dm: The Supreme Physician does not employ Common medical treatments such as these; Through extremely gentle procedures, He heals immeasurable and grievous illnesses.
gm: Such ordinary medical treatments Are not performed by the supreme physician; With an extremely gentle method, He cures immeasurable great diseases.

dm: The Guide first engages one in the giving of things such as vegetables; Once accustomed to that, one later gradually gives even one's own flesh.
gm: Even in the giving of vegetables and so forth, The Guide initially engages one. Having become accustomed to that, later on, One will gradually give away even one's own flesh.

dm: When one has developed an attitude toward one's own body As being like vegetables and the like, Then what difficulty could there be In giving away one's flesh and so forth?
gm: When toward one's own body A mind arises that views it like vegetables and so forth, At that time, in giving away flesh and so forth, What difficulty is there in that?

dm: Because non-virtue is abandoned, there is no suffering; Because of wisdom, there is no unhappiness. In this way, it is through distorted conceptions And non-virtue that the mind and body are harmed.
gm: By abandoning misdeeds, there is no suffering; By being wise, there is no displeasure. Thus, wrong conceptualizations And misdeeds harm the mind and body.

dm: If the body is at ease through merit, And the mind is at ease through wisdom, Then even while remaining in samsara for the sake of others, Why would those with compassion ever be weary?
gm: Through merit, the body is at ease, And through wisdom, the mind is at ease. Even while remaining in cyclic existence for the sake of others, Why would the compassionate ones become weary?

dm: Because this, through the power of the awakening mind, Exhausts previous misdeeds And gathers an ocean of merit, It is explained as superior to the Hearers.
gm: Because through the power of this awakening mind Former misdeeds are exhausted, And because it gathers an ocean of merit, It is explained to be supreme over the Hearers.

dm: Therefore, having mounted the horse of the awakening mind, Which dispels all weariness and fatigue, As one proceeds from joy to joy, What person of intelligence would ever succumb to despondency?
gm: Therefore, riding the horse of the awakening mind, Which dispels all weariness and fatigue, Proceeding from happiness to happiness, Who with a knowing mind would fall into despair?

dm: To accomplish the welfare of sentient beings, one's forces are aspiration, steadfastness, joy, and relinquishment. Aspiration is generated by fearing suffering and contemplating its benefits.
gm: The forces to accomplish the benefit of sentient beings Are aspiration, firmness, joy, and relinquishment. Aspiration is generated through the fear of suffering And contemplating its benefits.

dm: Thus, having abandoned the opposing factors, One should strive to increase diligence through the powers of aspiration, pride, joy, relinquishment, Earnest application, and mastery.
gm: Thus, having abandoned the discordant factors, Through aspiration, pride, joy, and relinquishment, And the powers of earnest application and mastery, I should strive to increase joyful endeavor.

dm: I must eliminate the immeasurable faults of both myself and others; Since for each and every one of these faults, It would take an ocean of eons to exhaust them.
gm: The faults of myself and others, Being immeasurable, I must destroy; Wherein for even each single fault, An ocean of eons will be exhausted.

dm: If I do not perceive in myself even a fraction of the effort Needed to begin exhausting these faults, Then as a vessel of immeasurable suffering, Why does my heart not burst?
