gm: Of that initiation of exhausting faults, If I do not see even a fraction in myself, Being an abode of immeasurable suffering, Why does my heart not burst?

dm: I must accomplish many virtues for both myself and others; Yet if even for a single virtue, One must train for an ocean of eons,
gm: The good qualities of myself and others, Being many, I must accomplish; Wherein if for even each single quality One must familiarize for an ocean of eons,

dm: I have never developed the habit of practicing even a fraction of such virtues. It is astonishing that I have rendered this birth, Which was somehow obtained, so meaningless.
gm: I, for even a fraction of a good quality, Have never generated familiarization; Having somehow found this birth, It is astonishing that I have made it meaningless.

dm: I have not made offerings to the Blessed One, Nor have I provided the joy of great festivals; I have not performed service for the Teachings, Nor have I fulfilled the hopes of the poor.
gm: I have not made offerings to the Blessed Ones, I have not provided the happiness of great festivals, I have not performed deeds for the teaching, I have not fulfilled the wishes of the poor.

dm: I have not granted fearlessness to the frightened, Nor have I given comfort to the distressed; I have merely produced the pain and suffering Of the womb of my mother.
gm: Not having given fearlessness to the fearful, And not having given happiness to the afflicted, I have merely produced the pangs And suffering of my mother's womb.

dm: Because I lacked devotion to the Dharma In the past and even now, I have come to such a state of destitution; Who would ever abandon devotion to the Dharma?
gm: Because previously and even now, I have been devoid of aspiration for the Dharma, Such destitution has come about; Who would forsake aspiration for the Dharma?

dm: The Sage has taught that aspiration is the root of all virtuous qualities; Its own root, in turn, is constant meditation upon the results of karmic ripening.
gm: Of all wholesome factors, The Sage has stated that the root is aspiration, And its root constantly is Meditating on the ripened results.

dm: Physical suffering, mental unhappiness, Various kinds of fear, And separation from what is desired— All these arise from the practice of misdeeds.
gm: Suffering and mental unhappiness, Various kinds of fears, And separation from what is desired Will arise from engaging in misdeeds.

dm: By performing the virtues intended by the mind, Wherever one may go, In that very place one will be honored By the rewards that are the fruits of that merit.
gm: By performing wholesome deeds intended in the mind, Wherever one may go, There, through that merit, One will be manifestly honored with the offerings of its results.

dm: Although those who commit sins desire happiness, Wherever they may go, Those very sins will, in that place, Utterly crush them with the weapons of suffering.
gm: Although those who commit misdeeds desire happiness, Wherever they may go, There, through those misdeeds, They are completely destroyed by the weapons of suffering.

dm: Abiding within the heart of a vast, fragrant, and cool lotus, Their splendor nourished by the food of the Victorious One's melodious speech, Possessing a supreme body born from a lotus blossomed by the Sage's light, Through their virtue they become a Son of the Sugata dwelling in the presence of the Victorious One.
gm: Dwelling in the core of a vast, fragrant, and cooling lotus, Whose splendor is produced by the food of the Victor's sweet speech, With a supreme body born from a lotus blossomed by the Sage's light, Through wholesome deeds one becomes a son of the Sugata dwelling before the Victor.

dm: With their skin entirely flayed by the henchmen of Yama, they are utterly tormented, And molten copper, melted by a searing fire, is poured over their bodies; Pierced by flaming swords and spears until their flesh is torn into hundreds of pieces, They fall upon the intensely blazing iron ground as a result of their many non-virtues.
gm: Utterly tormented by the henchmen of Yama stripping away one's skin entirely, Molten copper melted by intensely hot fire poured onto one's body, Pierced by blazing swords and short spears, one's flesh scattered in a hundred pieces, Through many unwholesome deeds, one falls onto a ground of intensely blazing iron.

dm: Therefore, one should aspire to virtue, And cultivate it with genuine respect. Having undertaken the rite of the Vajradhvaja, One should cultivate the pride of self-confidence.
gm: Therefore, one should aspire to the wholesome, And meditate upon it with reverence; According to the method of the Vajradhvaja, Having begun, one should meditate on self-confidence.

dm: First, examine your resources, And then decide whether to begin or not. It is best not to begin at all, But once begun, one should not turn back.
gm: First, having examined one's capacity, One should either begin or not begin; Not beginning is best, But having begun, one should not turn back.

dm: By becoming habituated to this in other lives, Sin and suffering will increase. Furthermore, the time for the result will be inferior, And even that goal will not be achieved.
gm: Becoming accustomed to that in other lives, Misdeeds and suffering will increase; Other deeds and the time of results as well Will become inferior, and that will not be accomplished either.

dm: One should apply pride to these three: Actions, afflictions, and ability. Thinking, "I alone shall do it," This is the pride of action.
gm: Actions, afflictions, and capacity: One should generate self-confidence regarding these three. Thinking, "I shall do this alone," This is the self-confidence of action.

dm: Since this world, under the power of afflictions, Is unable to accomplish its own welfare, Migratory beings are not capable like me; Therefore, I shall do this.
gm: Since this world, powerless through afflictions, Is unable to accomplish its own benefit, Wandering beings are not capable like me; Therefore, I shall do this.

dm: If others perform inferior tasks, How can I remain idle? I do not act out of pride; For me, to be without pride is supreme.
gm: If others are performing inferior actions, How can I myself remain idle? I do not do this out of pride, For me, having no pride is supreme.

dm: When encountering a dying snake, Even a crow acts like a Garuda. If I am weak and feeble, Even a minor downfall will cause me harm.
gm: When encountering a dead snake, Even a crow acts like a garuda. If I myself am weak, Even a minor downfall will cause harm.

dm: For one who is despondent and has abandoned effort, How could there be liberation from misfortune? By generating the pride of exertion, Even the great will find it difficult to overcome you.
gm: For one who is despondent and casts aside effort, Is there liberation from destitution? But by generating self-confidence and effort, One is difficult to defeat even by the great.

dm: Therefore, with a steadfast mind, I shall overcome all downfalls; For if I am defeated by a downfall, My wish to conquer the three realms will become a mockery.
gm: Therefore, with a steadfast mind, I shall conquer the downfalls; If I am defeated by downfalls, My desire to conquer the three realms becomes a laughingstock.

dm: I shall triumph over everything; None shall triumph over me. As a son of the Lion-like Conqueror, I shall abide in this pride.
gm: I shall conquer all, And no one shall conquer me. I, a son of the Victorious Lion, Should abide in this self-confidence.

dm: Those beings who are overcome by pride are afflicted; They do not possess the pride of which I speak. The truly proud do not fall under the power of the enemy, Whereas those others are under the power of the enemy of pride.
gm: Any being who is overcome by pride Is afflicted, not self-confident; The self-confident do not fall under the power of the enemy, They fall under the power of the enemy of pride.

dm: Inflated by the pride of the afflictions, They are led by that pride to the lower realms; Their human joy is destroyed, and They become slaves eating the food of others,
gm: Those inflated by the affliction of pride Are led to the lower realms by pride, Destroying their human joys, And becoming slaves who eat others' food,

dm: The foolish, the ugly, and the weak, Are held in contempt everywhere; If even those ascetics who are puffed up with pride Are counted among the conceited, Then tell me, how much more pathetic are the lowly?
gm: Stupid, ugly, and weak, They will be despised everywhere. If ascetics puffed up with pride Are also included among the proud, Tell me, what kind of wretched beings are they?

dm: Whoever maintains pride in order to conquer the enemy of pride Is the truly proud one, the victorious hero; For they have certainly vanquished the burgeoning enemy of pride, And as they wish, they bring the fruit of the Conquerors to perfection for all beings.
gm: Whoever holds self-confidence to conquer the enemy of pride, He is the truly self-confident one and the victorious hero. Whoever definitively destroys the thriving enemy of pride, Perfects the fruit of victory according to the desires of beings.

dm: If I must dwell in the midst of the faction of afflictions, I shall endure in a thousand ways; Like a lion among foxes and the like, I shall not be overcome by the host of afflictions.
gm: When dwelling in the midst of a host of afflictions, One should endure in a thousand ways; Like a lion among foxes and the like, One should not be harmed by the host of afflictions.

dm: Even if great danger should arise, Just as a person protects their eyes, Likewise, even when peril occurs, I shall not fall under the power of the afflictions.
gm: Even if great peril arises, Just as a person protects his eyes, Likewise, even if peril arises, One should not fall under the power of afflictions.

dm: Just as one desires the joyful results of play, One should be attached to whatever task is at hand; One should find delight in that work, And never be satiated by it.
gm: Just as one desires the joyful fruit of a game, Whatever task is to be done, One should be attached to that action, And finding no satiety, rejoice in that action.

dm: Although actions are performed for the sake of happiness, It is uncertain whether happiness will actually result; But for one whose very work is happiness, How could they be happy without doing that work?
gm: Even if one acts for the sake of happiness, It is uncertain whether happiness will result; But for one whose very action brings happiness, How can there be happiness without doing that action?

dm: If one is never sated by sensual desires, Which are like honey on the edge of a razor, Then how could one ever be sated by merit, Which ripens into peace and happiness?
gm: Like honey smeared on a razor's edge, If one is not satiated by sensual desires, Having a ripening of happiness and peace, How could one ever be satiated with merit?

dm: Therefore, in order to bring the task to completion, One should engage in that work Just as an elephant, tormented by the midday sun, Plunges into a lake upon encountering it.
gm: Therefore, in order to complete the task, Just as an elephant tormented by the midday sun Plunges into a lake upon encountering it, One should also engage in that action.

dm: If one's strength declines, One should set it aside in order to resume it later; When a task is well-accomplished, one should leave it behind, Desiring the next and the next.
gm: If one's strength declines, One should set it aside in order to resume it later. If it is well completed, desiring the next And the next, one should abandon it.

dm: Just as a veteran warrior in the heat of battle Faces the clash of an enemy's sword, One should dodge the weapons of the afflictions And rise up to defeat the enemy afflictions.
gm: Together with veteran enemies, Like clashing swords on a battlefield, One should dodge the weapons of afflictions, And strike to destroy the enemies of afflictions.

dm: Just as one would swiftly pick up a sword Dropped in battle out of fear, So too, if the weapon of mindfulness is lost, One should quickly retrieve it by remembering the terrors of hell.
gm: If one drops one's sword in battle, One quickly picks it up out of fear; Likewise, if the weapon of mindfulness is lost, Remembering the fear of hell, one should quickly take it up.

dm: Just as poison spreads through the body By depending on the blood, So too will a fault pervade the mind If it finds an opportunity.
gm: Just as poison, by relying on the blood, Spreads throughout the body, Likewise, if an opportunity is found, Faults will spread through the mind.

dm: Just as one carrying a vessel filled with mustard oil, Followed by a man with a drawn sword threatening to kill him, Is terrified of spilling it, so should the practitioner be focused.
gm: Just as one carrying a vessel filled with mustard oil, With a sword-bearer standing nearby, Fearing the threat of death if it spills, An ascetic should likewise exert himself.

dm: Therefore, just as one would swiftly spring up If a snake crawled into one's lap, So too, when sleep and lethargy approach, One should quickly repel them.
gm: Therefore, if a snake comes into one's lap, Just as one would quickly jump up, Likewise, if sleep and lethargy come, One should quickly repel them.

dm: For every fault that occurs, I shall reproach myself and reflect for a long time, "By whatever means necessary, I must ensure that this does not happen to me again."
gm: For each and every fault that arises, Reproaching oneself, by all means, 'This will not happen to me again, I will act in this way'—so should one ponder for a long time.

dm: Thinking, "How can I become habituated to mindfulness In these various circumstances?" Through this cause, I shall desire to meet with teachers Or to perform the appropriate tasks.
gm: With the thought, 'How in these situations Will mindfulness become a habit?' For this reason, one should seek encounters Or appropriate actions.

dm: In order to have the capacity for all activities Before starting any work, I should recall the discourse on heedfulness And make myself rise with alacrity.
gm: So that before undertaking any task, One will have the capability for everything, Thus, recalling the teachings on heedfulness, One should make oneself rise lightly.

dm: Just as a tuft of cotton is moved to and fro By the coming and going of the wind, So should I be governed by enthusiasm; In that way, success will be achieved.
gm: Just as the going and Coming of the wind control the cotton fluff, Likewise, being controlled by joy, In that way, success will be achieved.

dm: From the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, this concludes the seventh chapter, titled "The Explanation of Diligence."
gm: From Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva, this is the seventh chapter, entitled The Teaching on Joyous Effort.

dm: Chapter Eight: The Exposition of Meditative Concentration
gm: Chapter Eight: Teaching Meditation

dm: Having thus generated diligence, One should place the mind in meditative concentration. A person whose mind is distracted Dwells between the fangs of the mental afflictions.
gm: Having thus generated joyous effort, One should place the mind in meditative concentration. A person whose mind is distracted Dwells between the fangs of the afflictions.

dm: Through solitude of body and mind, Distractions will not arise. Therefore, one should renounce the world And completely cast aside discursive thoughts.
gm: Through the isolation of body and mind, Distraction does not arise. Therefore, one should abandon the worldly life And completely discard discursive thoughts.

dm: Because of attachment and craving for gain and the like, One does not renounce the world. Therefore, completely abandon these things, And the wise should analyze in this way.
gm: Because of attachment and for the sake of gain and so forth, Through craving, one does not abandon the world. Therefore, having completely abandoned these, The wise should analyze in this way.

dm: Through special insight thoroughly conjoined with calm abiding, One should understand that the mental afflictions are completely destroyed. Therefore, one should first seek calm abiding; This is achieved by those who find genuine delight in detachment from the world.
gm: By special insight completely endowed with calm abiding, Knowing that the afflictions are destroyed, One should first seek calm abiding; and that too Is accomplished by joyful detachment from the world.

dm: Since all is impermanent, who that is impermanent Would feel a true attachment to another? Because of that, for thousands of lifetimes, One will never again see the beloved.
gm: What impermanent being Would be truly attached to the impermanent? Through that, for thousands of lifetimes, They will not see their loved ones.

dm: If they are not seen, there is no joy, And the mind will not remain in meditative equipoise; Even if they are seen, there is no satisfaction, And one is tormented by craving just as before.
gm: Not seeing them, one will not be joyful, And the mind will not rest in equipoise. Even seeing them, one will not be satisfied, And will be tormented by craving as before.

dm: If one is attached to sentient beings, The perfect reality is completely obscured. It destroys even a mind of disillusionment, And in the end, one will be tormented by grief.
gm: If one forms attachments to sentient beings, Ultimate reality is completely obscured, The mind of disillusionment is also destroyed, And in the end, one will be tormented by sorrow.

dm: By thinking only of them, This life will pass away in vain. Through impermanent friendships, Even the eternal Dharma is destroyed.
gm: By merely thinking about them, This life will pass away meaninglessly. Because of impermanent friends and relatives, Even the eternal Dharma will be destroyed.

dm: If one shares the same conduct as the foolish, One will certainly go to the lower realms. If they lead one to what is unwholesome, What is the use of relying on the childish?
gm: If one acts with equal fortune to the childish, One will certainly go to the lower realms. If they lead one to what is unequal, What is the use of relying on the childish?

dm: In a single instant they become friends, And in a mere moment they turn into enemies. Because they react with anger toward things that should bring joy, Ordinary beings are difficult to please.
gm: In a single instant they become friends, And in a brief moment they even become enemies. Since they become angry at causes for joy, Ordinary people are difficult to please.

dm: If one speaks for their benefit, they become angry, And they even turn one away from what is helpful. If their own words are not heeded, They become enraged and will fall into the lower realms.
gm: If one speaks beneficially, they get angry, And they turn me away from what is beneficial. If one does not listen to their words, They become angry and go to the lower realms.

dm: They are jealous of superiors and competitive with equals; They are arrogant toward inferiors and conceited when praised. If something unpleasant is said, they become angry; When could one ever receive benefit from a fool?
gm: Envious of superiors, competitive with equals, Arrogant toward inferiors, conceited when praised, And prone to anger when spoken to unpleasantly— When is benefit ever obtained from the childish?

dm: If one associates with the childish, then from such childishness, Self-praise, the disparagement of others, And talk that delights in cyclic existence and the like, All manner of non-virtue will certainly arise.
gm: If one associates with the childish, Praising oneself and disparaging others, And talking about the joys of cyclic existence and so forth, Non-virtue will certainly arise in every way.

dm: Thus, relying on one another in such a way Will result in nothing but ruin; Since they do not accomplish my purpose, And I will not be of benefit to them either.
gm: Thus, associating oneself with others Will merely lead to ruin. They will not accomplish my benefit, And I will not accomplish their benefit.

dm: I shall flee far away from the childish. If I encounter them, I shall please them with a joyful manner, Yet without becoming overly intimate, I shall maintain a polite and ordinary relationship.
gm: One should flee far away from the childish. When meeting them, one should please them with joy, Without becoming very close, Interacting well as mere acquaintances.

dm: Like a bee taking nectar from a flower, Take only that which is meaningful for the Dharma; And remain without intimacy toward anyone, As if you had never seen them before.
gm: Like a bee taking nectar from a flower, Having taken only the meaning of Dharma, As if never having seen them before, One should remain without familiarity toward everyone.

dm: If I harbor such pride, thinking, "I have many gains and honors, And many people are fond of me," Then fear will arise after death.
gm: "I have much gain and respect," "Many are fond of me"— If one harbors such conceit, Fear will arise after death.

dm: Therefore, whatever it is that your deluded mind Becomes attached to, Those very things will combine to arise As suffering, multiplied a thousandfold.
gm: Therefore, whatever the thoroughly deluded mind Becomes attached to, Along with that, a thousandfold Suffering will manifest and arise.

dm: Therefore, the wise should not form attachments, For from attachment, fear is born. Since these things are by nature subject to loss, Remain steadfast and understand this well.
gm: Therefore, the wise should not be attached; From attachment, fear arises. Since these will naturally be left behind, Remain steadfast and fully understand this.

dm: Though one may acquire many gains, And though fame and renown may arise, Even with a collection of gain and fame, There is no knowing where one will go.
gm: Even if many gains are acquired, And fame and a good reputation arise, Together with the collection of gains and fame, There is no knowing where one will go.

dm: If there are others who disparage me, What reason is there for me to be pleased by praise? If there are others who praise me, What reason is there for me to be displeased by disparagement?
gm: If there are others who disparage me, What joy is there for me in praise? If there are others who praise me, What displeasure is there in disparagement?

dm: Since sentient beings have such diverse inclinations, Even the Victors cannot satisfy them all; What need is there to mention a wretched person like me? Therefore, I shall abandon concern for the world's opinions.
gm: Sentient beings have diverse inclinations; If even the Victors cannot please them, What need to mention an inferior one like me? Therefore, I should abandon worldly thoughts.

dm: Sentient beings disparage those who have no possessions, And speak ill of those who have them. Since they are by nature so difficult to get along with, How can any joy arise from associating with them?
gm: Sentient beings disparage those without gains, And speak unpleasantly of those with gains. With those who are naturally difficult to associate with, How can joy ever arise?

dm: Because the childish find no pleasure Unless their own interests are served, The Tathāgatas have said that no childish person is a friend; Thus have the Tathāgatas spoken.
gm: Because the childish do not experience joy Unless it is for their own benefit, "None of the childish are true friends," Thus the Tathāgatas have spoken.

dm: In the forest, the wild animals, the birds, and the trees Do not speak unpleasant words. When shall I come to dwell together With those whose company is a delight?
gm: In the forest, deer and birds, And trees do not speak unpleasantly; With those whose company is joyful, When will I dwell together?

dm: Having made my home in a cave, an empty temple, or at the foot of a tree, When shall I come to be without attachment, Never looking back, And become free from all clinging?
gm: In a cave or an empty shrine, Or dwelling at the foot of a tree, When will I never look back, And become free from attachment?

dm: When shall I dwell in vast, naturally spacious regions That are not claimed as "mine," Acting with total freedom And without attachment?
gm: In places not held as "mine", Which are naturally vast, Acting freely and without attachment, When will I abide?

dm: Possessing only a few items such as an alms bowl, And wearing clothes that no one else desires, When shall I come to dwell without fear, Even without attempting to conceal this body?
gm: With merely a begging bowl and the like, Wearing garments unwanted by anyone, And not even concealing this body, When will I dwell fearlessly?

dm: Having gone to a charnel ground, When shall I come to treat as equal My own body and the skeletal remains of others, Seeing them both as having the nature of decay?
gm: Having gone to the charnel ground, The bones of others and my own body, As having the nature of perishing, When will I view them equally?

dm: This very body of mine Will eventually become such that Even jackals will not approach it Because of its stench.
gm: Even this very body of mine, By whose stench even foxes Will not approach near, Will become exactly like that.

dm: Although this body arose as a single entity, The flesh and bones that were born with it Will disintegrate and separate; What need is there to mention other loved ones?
gm: Although this body arose as one, The flesh and bones that were born together Will perish and separate from one another; What need to mention other friends?

dm: One is born alone, And likewise, one dies alone; Since others do not take a share of one's suffering, What use are friends who only create obstacles?
gm: When born, one is born alone, And when dying, one dies alone; Since no other takes a share of the suffering, What is the use of friends who are hindrances?

dm: Just as travelers on a road Take up a temporary lodging, So too do those on the path of existence Take up a place of birth.
gm: Just as those who enter upon a journey Take up a place to stay, In the same way, those entered on the path of existence Fully take up a place of birth.

dm: While the world is grieving all around, As long as this body has not yet Been carried away by four men, In the meantime, I shall go to the forest.
gm: While the whole world mourns, As long as four men Have not carried this away from there, Until then, go to the forest.

dm: Having made myself free of friends and free of enemies, This body shall dwell alone in a secluded place; Regarding myself as already dead, There will be no mourning even when I actually die.
gm: Having made no friends and no enemies, This body dwelling alone in solitude, Having considered it as already dead, Even when dying, there is no mourning.

dm: Since there is no one nearby To cause the harm of mourning, No one at all will distract me From such practices as the recollection of the Buddha.
gm: Since there is no one staying nearby To cause grief or harm, By this, the recollection of the Buddha and so forth Will not be distracted by anyone.

dm: Therefore, in a forest that is exceedingly delightful, Free of hardship, blissful, and the pacifier Of all distractions, I shall dwell entirely alone.
gm: Therefore, in exceptionally delightful Forests, with little trouble and happy, Pacifying all distractions, I shall dwell completely alone.

dm: Abandoning all other thoughts, With a mind focused only on myself, I shall strive to settle the mind in meditative equipoise And to bring it under discipline.
gm: Having abandoned all other thoughts, With a single-pointed intention, In order to settle the mind in equipoise And to subdue it, I shall strive.

dm: In this world and in the next, Desires produce ruin; Here, they lead to being killed, bound, and mutilated, And in the next, they bring about the hells and so forth.
gm: In this world and in the next, Desires produce ruin: Here, killing, bondage, and amputation, And in the next, establishing hells and so forth.

dm: For whose sake you previously employed male and female messengers, And for whose sake you did not shrink from even sin or infamy, And for whose sake you disregarded everything,
gm: Previously through male and female messengers, For whose sake I made many requests, And regarding sins or ill repute, For whose sake I did not hesitate;

dm: Entering into dangers and exhausting your wealth— Those very things that you embrace with such supreme delight Are nothing other than skeletons;
gm: I also entered into danger, And exhausted my wealth; By fully embracing whom I was supremely delighted—those very ones

dm: If they are nothing but skeletons and nothing else, And are neither independent nor a self, Why, after desiring them intensely and becoming thoroughly attached, Do you not go to the state beyond sorrow?
gm: Are nothing but skeletons, nothing else. Being neither independent nor a self, Strongly desiring and fully clinging to them, Why do you not proceed to nirvāṇa?

dm: That which you first exerted yourself to lift, And which looked down bashfully even when drawn up— Whether it was seen before or not, That face was covered by a cloth.
gm: Which at first was lifted up with effort, And though drawn near, looked down out of modesty; Whether seen before or unseen, Whose face was covered by a cloth;

dm: That face of your affliction, Is now revealed just as it is; Now that you see it being uncovered by the vultures, Why do you flee from it?
gm: That face which tormented you, Just as it has now become manifest, Having seen it unveiled by vultures, Why do you flee from it now?

dm: Even when others merely looked with their eyes, You kept it thoroughly guarded; While it is being devoured by them, Why, O miser, do you not protect it?
gm: Even when others looked at it with their eyes, It was completely guarded; Now that it is being eaten by them, Miser, why do you not guard it?

dm: Seeing this heap of flesh being eaten by vultures and others, Why do you honor the food of others with flower garlands, Sandalwood, and ornaments?
gm: Seeing this heap of flesh, When vultures and others eat it, Why do you offer to the food of others Garlands of flowers, sandalwood, and ornaments?

dm: Seeing it as nothing but a heap of bones, If you are terrified even when it is motionless, Why are you not afraid when it is moved by someone, Like a reanimated corpse?
gm: Having seen it as merely a heap of bones, If you are terrified even when it does not move, When it was moved by something, like a zombie, Why were you not afraid?

dm: Since both excrement and saliva arise from the very same food, Why do you dislike the excrement, And yet, why do you delight in the saliva?
gm: From a single food alone, If feces and saliva are produced, Out of these, you dislike the feces, So why do you delight in the saliva?

dm: Instead of taking delight in a pillow, Which is soft to the touch like cotton, The lustful are deluded regarding the impure, Claiming, "It does not leak a foul odor."
gm: Of cotton, which is soft to the touch, You do not delight in a pillow, Saying it does not emit a foul odor; The lustful are deluded by filth.

dm: Since you are attached to this when it is covered, Why do you not desire it when it is uncovered? If you have no need for it then, Why do you embrace it when it is covered?
gm: If you are attached to it even when covered, Why do you not desire it when uncovered? If you have no need for it uncovered, Why do you embrace it when covered?

dm: If you have no attachment to what is impure, Why do you embrace in your lap another, A cage of bones bound together by sinews, And plastered over with the mud of flesh?
gm: If you have no attachment to filth, To a cage of bones tied together with sinews And plastered with the mud of flesh, Why do you embrace another in your lap?

dm: You yourself contain plenty of filth, And you constantly wallow in that; Yet, out of a craving for the impure, You also desire other bags of filth.
gm: You yourself contain much filth, Which you continually make use of, Yet for other bags of filth as well, Out of a craving for filth, you desire them.

dm: If you say, "I am fond of this flesh," And desire to touch and look at it, Then why do you not desire flesh In its natural, insentient state?
gm: Saying, "I delight in this flesh," If you desire to touch and look at it, Which is of a mindless nature, How can you desire the flesh?

dm: That mind which you desire Cannot be touched or seen, And that which can be touched is not consciousness; What is the use of such a meaningless embrace?
gm: That mind which you desire Cannot be touched or seen, And whatever can be is not conscious; What is the point of a meaningless embrace?

dm: It is not so wonderful that you do not realize The foul nature of another's body; But that you do not realize your own very self To be foul is truly a great wonder.
gm: That another's body is of an unclean nature, Not realizing this is not so amazing; That you yourself are filth itself, Not realizing this is truly amazing!

dm: Having abandoned the young lotus Opened by the rays of a cloudless sun, Why does your mind, with its attachment to the impure, Take delight in a cage of filth?
gm: Opened by the rays of a cloudless sun, Abandoning a fresh lotus, With a mind attached to filth, Why do you delight in a cage of filth?

dm: If you do not wish to touch a patch of ground Because it is soiled with filth, How can you wish to touch the body From which that very filth arose?
gm: A place smeared with filth, If you do not wish to touch, From which that filth arose, How can you wish to touch the body?

dm: If you have no attachment to what is impure, Then why do you embrace in your lap another Who was produced by that seed And arose from an impure field?
gm: If you have no attachment to filth, Arisen from a field of filth, And generated by its seed, Why do you embrace another in your lap?

dm: You do not desire even a tiny worm That arises from filth, Yet you desire a body that is a mass of many impurities And was likewise born from filth.
gm: A filth-worm arisen from filth, Even a tiny one, you do not desire, Yet a body whose nature is much filth, And born of filth, you desire.

dm: Not only do you not feel revulsion For your own impurity, But out of a craving for filth, You also desire other bags of impurity.
gm: Towards your own filth, Not only do you not disparage it, But out of craving for filth, You desire another bag of filth.

dm: Even pleasant things like camphor, Or boiled rice and vegetables, Once taken into the mouth and spat out, Make even the ground foul and unclean.
gm: Even pleasing things like camphor, Or cooked rice and vegetables, If put into the mouth and spat out, Make even the ground foul and filthy.

dm: If you still have doubts about such impurity, Even though it is plainly evident, Then observe other impure bodies Abandoned in the charnel grounds.
gm: If such filth as this Is obvious, yet you doubt it, The bodies discarded in the charnel grounds, Look at that other filth as well.

dm: If you know that great terror would arise If the skin were peeled back, Then how could you ever again Find pleasure in that very same thing?
gm: If the skin is peeled away from it, Great fear will arise; Knowing this, how can you Feel joy in that very thing again?

dm: Even the fragrance applied to the body Is that of sandalwood and the like, not of anything else. Why then do you become attached to one thing Because of the fragrance of another?
gm: That scent smeared on the body Is sandalwood and so forth, nothing else; Because of that scent of another thing, Why are you attached to another?

dm: If it is naturally foul-smelling, Is it not better to be unattached to it? Why do those with meaningless worldly cravings Anoint it with sweet scents?
gm: If its nature is foul-smelling, Is it not better to not be attached to it? Those who pointlessly burn with craving in the world, Why do they smear it with sweet scents?

dm: If the fragrance is that of sandalwood, What part of it comes from the body? Why then do you become attached to one thing Because of the fragrance of another?
gm: If the sweet scent belongs to sandalwood, What does that have to do with the body here? Because of the scent of another thing, Why are you attached to another?

dm: If the body’s natural state—with its long hair and nails, Yellowish teeth, and the stench of mud— Is a terrifying sight when left naked, Why do you take such pains to polish it?
gm: If long hair and nails, Yellowish teeth, and a foul, muddy smell, Imbue the nature of the body, And make it terrifying indeed when naked,

dm: Why do you groom it so zealously, As if it were a weapon that will only harm you? Through the efforts of those deluded regarding the self, The entire earth is thrown into turmoil by the mad.
gm: Like a weapon that harms oneself, Why make efforts to clean and polish it? Through efforts driven by self-delusion, This earth is thoroughly agitated by madmen.

dm: If you feel revulsion in a charnel ground Upon seeing nothing but a heap of bones, Why do you delight in the "city charnel ground," Which is filled with moving skeletons?
gm: Having seen just a skeleton, If you feel disgust in the charnel ground, Pervaded by moving skeletons, Are you delighted by the charnel ground of the city?

dm: That which has become so impure Cannot be obtained for free; By striving for its sake, one suffers exhaustion And is harmed by the torments of hell and the like.
gm: That which has thus become filthy, Cannot be obtained without a price; Exhaustion from accomplishing that goal, And harm in hells and so forth will follow.

dm: Since a child is unable to increase wealth, What happiness is there when one reaches one's prime? If one's life is exhausted by the accumulation of wealth, Once old, what is the use of sensual desires?
gm: Since as a child one cannot amass wealth, When coming of age, what happiness is there in this? If life is exhausted by amassing wealth, What can be done with desires in old age?

dm: Some wretched, lustful people, Utterly exhausted by a long day's work, Return home and lay their weary bodies Down to sleep like corpses.
gm: Some miserable people with desires, Utterly exhausted by the day's work, Come home with worn-out bodies, And sleep exactly like corpses.

dm: Some are afflicted by the hardships of travel And the suffering of going far away; Though they long for their wives and children, They do not see them for years on end.
gm: Some suffer the afflictions of traveling abroad, And the misery of going far away; Although longing for their wives and children, They do not see them for years on end.

dm: Deluded by the desire for their own benefit, They sell themselves for the sake of profit; Yet without attaining it, they are meaningless, Driven by the winds of others' labor.
gm: Utterly deluded about what benefits themselves, Even selling themselves for that very purpose, They do not obtain it, and uselessly Are driven by the wind of others' work.

dm: Some sell their own bodies And, powerless, are put to work by others; Even when their wives give birth, It happens in the wilderness or at the foot of a tree.
gm: Some sell their own bodies, And powerlessly become employed by others; Even when their wives give birth to children, They are simply born at the foot of trees in the wilderness.

dm: Fools deceived by desire, Thinking, "I must make a living," Enter into battle fearing the loss of life, And for the sake of profit, they go into servitude.
gm: Fools deceived by desires, Wishing for a livelihood and thinking, "I will make a living," Enter into battle despite fearing the loss of their lives, And go into slavery for the sake of profit.

dm: Some who are full of desire even have their bodies mutilated; Some are impaled on the points of stakes; Some are pierced by short spears; And some are even seen being burned.
gm: Some with desires even have their bodies mutilated, Some are impaled on the points of stakes, Some are stabbed with short spears, And some are seen being burned.

dm: Through the torments of accumulating, guarding, and losing, One should understand that wealth is an endless source of ruin. Those who are distracted by their attachment to wealth Have no opportunity to be liberated from the suffering of cyclic existence.
gm: Through the torments of amassing, protecting, and losing it, Wealth should be known as endless ruin. Those who are distracted by attachment to wealth Have no opportunity for liberation from the miseries of existence.

dm: For those possessed by desire, such faults are many and the benefits are few; It is like a beast of burden pulling a cart, That eats only a few mouthfuls of grass.
gm: For those with desires, these and so forth Are the many disadvantages and little benefit, Just like beasts of burden drawing a chariot Eating a few mouthfuls of grass.

dm: For the sake of such a small benefit, which is not even rare for a beast to achieve, Those tormented by their karma destroy This precious human life of leisure and endowment, so difficult to find.
gm: Which is not rare even when accomplished by beasts; For the sake of whatever is that small benefit, This hard-to-find, perfect freedom and endowment Is destroyed by those tormented by karma.

dm: Desires will certainly perish and cause one to fall into the hells and other lower realms; Because it is not for a great purpose, one undergoes constant wearisome toil.
gm: Desires will certainly perish, And they cause one to fall into hell and so forth; For the sake of what is not great, at all times, Whatever fatigue and hardship has occurred,

dm: If Buddhahood could be accomplished with even a millionth part of such hardship, Then for those possessed by desire, compared to the conduct of enlightenment, There is great suffering but no enlightenment.
gm: If by just a ten-millionth fraction of that Hardship, Buddhahood is accomplished, Those with desires have greater suffering than in the Bodhisattva's conduct, And yet they have no awakening.

dm: If one considers the sufferings of the hells and so forth, Even weapons, poison, fire, precipices, And enemies cannot be compared to the objects of desire.
gm: If one considers the sufferings of hell and so forth, For desires, weapons, Poison, fire, precipices, And enemies cannot even serve as examples.

dm: Thus, having become weary of desires, One should generate a delight in solitude, Within peaceful forests That are empty of strife and afflictions.
gm: Having thus generated revulsion for desires, Generate joy for solitude. Empty of disputes and afflictions, In the peaceful forests,

dm: On delightful, expansive stone slabs like palaces, Cooled by the sandalwood-scented moonlight, Fanned by the silent, peaceful forest breeze, One walks about, contemplating the welfare of others.
gm: The fortunate ones, cooled by moonlight and sandalwood, On broad flat stones, delightful mansions, Fanned by the silent, peaceful forest breeze, Pace while contemplating what benefits others.

dm: In empty houses, at the foot of trees, or in caves, Staying wherever and for as long as one desires, Having abandoned the suffering of guarding and possessing, One lives in spacious relaxation, free from attachment.
gm: In empty houses, at the foot of trees, and in caves, Staying wherever and for however long they desire, Having abandoned the suffering of guarding possessions, They live carefree without dependence.

dm: Acting with independence and without attachment, Having no connection with anyone at all, That joy of contentment, whatever it may be, Is difficult even for Indra to find.
gm: Acting independently and without attachment, Unconnected to anyone at all, Whatever is the joyful conduct of contentment, Even Indra has difficulty finding it.

dm: By means of these and other such aspects, Having reflected upon the virtues of solitude, One should completely pacify discursive thoughts, And meditate upon the awakening mind.
gm: Through these and other ways, Having considered the qualities of solitude, With discursive thoughts fully pacified, One should cultivate the awakening mind.

dm: One should first strive to meditate On the equality of oneself and others; Since all are equal in happiness and suffering, One should protect everyone just as one does oneself.
gm: The equality of self and other One should first strive to meditate upon. Since happiness and suffering are equal, All should be protected like oneself.

dm: Just as the body, despite its many different parts like the hands and so forth, Is protected as a single entity, So too are all diverse beings, with their various joys and sorrows, One in their equal desire for happiness, just as I am.
gm: Although the divisions of hands and so forth are many, Just as they are one as a body to be fully protected, Likewise, the different migrating beings, with their happiness and suffering, Are all one in equally desiring happiness, like oneself.

dm: If my own suffering Does not cause harm to the bodies of others, Nevertheless, because I cling to it as "mine," That suffering is unbearable to me.
gm: If my suffering Does not harm the bodies of others, Even so, that suffering is mine, Unbearable due to clinging to self.

dm: Likewise, although the suffering of others Does not fall upon me, Nevertheless, because of attachment to a self, That suffering is difficult to bear.
gm: Likewise, although the sufferings of others Do not fall upon me, Even so, that suffering is mine, Difficult to bear due to clinging to self.

dm: I should dispel the suffering of others Because it is suffering, just like my own; I should benefit others Because they are sentient beings, just like my own body.
gm: I should dispel the suffering of others Because it is suffering, like my own suffering. I should benefit others Because they are sentient beings, like my own body.

dm: Since both myself and others Are equal in desiring happiness, What is so special about me That I strive for my own happiness alone?
gm: When both myself and others Are equal in desiring happiness, What difference is there with myself, That I strive for the happiness of myself alone?

dm: Since both myself and others Are equal in not desiring suffering, What is so special about me That I protect myself and not others?
gm: When both myself and others Are equal in not desiring suffering, What difference is there with myself, That I protect myself and not others?

dm: If I do not protect them Because their suffering does not harm me, Then why protect against future suffering, Since it does not harm me now?
gm: If, because their suffering Does not harm me, I do not protect them, Future suffering also If it does not harm, why protect against it?

dm: The conceptual thought that "I" will experience that Is a mistaken conception, For the one who dies is one, And the one who is born is another.
gm: The thought that "I will experience it" Is a false conception; Thus, the one who dies is another, And the one who is born is another.

dm: If the suffering of any particular person Must be protected against by that person alone, Then since the suffering of the foot is not that of the hand, Why should the hand protect it?
gm: If whenever the suffering of anyone Is to be protected by that one himself, The suffering of the foot is not the hand's, Why should it be protected by it?

dm: If you argue that even if it is illogical, One acts in this way because of grasping at a self, Then whatever is illogical regarding self and others Is precisely what should be abandoned as much as possible.
gm: If you say, "Though it is illogical, here One engages through grasping at self," That which is illogical regarding self and others Is to be abandoned to the best of one's ability.

dm: What are called "continua" and "assemblies" Are false, like garlands, armies, and the like. Since there is no one who possesses suffering, Who could be the owner of this?
gm: What are called a continuum and a collection Are false, like a rosary, an army, and so forth. Since there is no one who possesses suffering, Therefore, who will have control over this?

dm: Because suffering has no owner, All instances of it are without distinction. Since it is suffering, it must be dispelled; What is the use of making restrictions here?
gm: Since suffering has no owner, All are entirely without distinction. Because it is suffering, it is to be dispelled. What is the use of restriction there?

dm: "Why should the suffering of all be averted?" Is not a point of contention. If it is to be averted, then all of it must be averted; If not, then I am just like other sentient beings.
gm: "Why should the suffering of all Be prevented?" There is no room for debate: If prevented, all should be prevented. If not, I too am like sentient beings.

dm: If you ask, "Since compassion brings about so much suffering, Why should one strive to generate it?" If one contemplates the suffering of the world, How can the suffering of compassion be considered great?
gm: "Since compassion has much suffering, Why forcibly generate it?" If one asks: When one contemplates the suffering of beings, How is the suffering of compassion great?

dm: If by means of a single suffering, A multitude of sufferings can be eliminated, Then those endowed with compassion should certainly Bring about that suffering for themselves and others.
gm: If by a single suffering Many sufferings will be eliminated, The compassionate one should generate that suffering For oneself and others.

dm: Therefore, although Supuṣpacandra Knew of the harm the king would inflict, He did not avert his own suffering, So that the suffering of many might be exhausted.
gm: Therefore, Supuṣpacandra, Even while knowing the king's harm, Did not dispel his own suffering, So that the suffering of many would be exhausted.

dm: Thus, those whose mind-streams are habituated, Finding joy in the pacification of others' suffering, Will plunge even into the Avīci hell Like swans into a lotus pond.
gm: Thus, those whose continuums are accustomed, Because they delight in pacifying others' suffering, Like a swan into a lotus pool, Will plunge even into the Avīci hell.

dm: When sentient beings are liberated, What ocean of joy could be greater? Is that not sufficient in itself? What is the use of desiring liberation for oneself?
gm: When sentient beings are liberated, The ocean of joy that exists— Is that itself not sufficient? What is the use of desiring liberation?

dm: Therefore, even when acting for the benefit of others, There is no conceit or sense of wonder; Because one is single-mindedly devoted to the welfare of others, There is no hope for a ripening result.
gm: Therefore, even when acting for the benefit of others, There is no conceit or amazement. Delighting solely in the benefit of others, There is no hope for a ripened result.

dm: Therefore, just as I protect myself From even the slightest unpleasantness, I should likewise cultivate a protective mind And a heart of compassion toward others.
gm: Therefore, just as to a small degree I protect myself even from unpleasant words, Likewise, a mind of protecting others and A mind of compassion should be cultivated in this way.

dm: Through the power of habituation, One comes to perceive the drops Of another's semen and blood as "I," Even though they are not inherently one's own.
gm: Through habituation, regarding others' Drops of semen and blood, Even though they lack any entity, Just as one apprehends them as "I,"

dm: In the same way, why should the bodies of others Not also be held as "I"? It is not difficult to establish My own body as being other.
gm: Likewise, regarding the bodies of others as well, Why not apprehend them as "I"? Positing my own body as others Is not difficult in that way.

dm: Having recognized oneself as being full of faults And others as an ocean of virtues, One should practice completely discarding self-grasping And adopting others.
gm: Knowing oneself to be flawed, and others To be an ocean of qualities, Completely discarding grasping at self And taking up others should be meditated upon.

dm: Just as the hands and other parts Are accepted as limbs of the body, Why are all embodied beings Not accepted as limbs of the world?
gm: Just as hands and so forth Are accepted as being limbs of the body, Likewise, as limbs of transmigratory beings, Why are embodied beings not accepted?

dm: Just as the thought of "I" has arisen Toward this selfless body through habituation, Why should the thought of "I" not likewise Arise toward other sentient beings through habituation?
gm: Just as towards this selfless body The mind of "I" has arisen through habituation, Likewise, towards other sentient beings as well, Why would the mind of "I" not arise through habituation?

dm: Therefore, when acting for the benefit of others, No sense of conceit or wonderment will arise, Just as when one has eaten food oneself, No expectation of a reward arises.
gm: If it is like that, the benefit of others, Even when done, amazement and conceit do not arise, Just as when one has eaten food oneself, There arises no hope for a reward.

dm: Therefore, just as I protect myself From even the slightest unpleasantness, I should likewise cultivate a protective mind And a mind of compassion toward the world.
gm: Therefore, just as to a small degree I protect myself even from unpleasant words, Likewise, a mind of protecting transmigratory beings and A mind of compassion should be habituated.

dm: Therefore, the Protector Avalokiteśvara, Out of great compassion, In order to dispel the fears of beings in cyclic existence, Blessed even his own name.
gm: Therefore, the protector Avalokiteśvara, Out of great compassion, for transmigratory beings, In order to dispel the fears of the assembly, Blessed even his own name.

dm: One should not turn back from hardships; For through the power of such habituation, Even that whose very name once caused fear, Becomes something one is unhappy to be without.
gm: One should not turn back from difficulties, For by the power of habituation in this way, Even someone whose name one feared to hear, Without them, one becomes joyless.

dm: Whoever wishes to quickly provide protection For both themselves and others, Should practice the supreme secret: The exchanging of oneself and others.
gm: Whoever, regarding oneself and others, Wishes to quickly protect them, The exchange of self and others, Which is the supreme secret, should be practiced.

dm: Because of attachment to this body of mine, Fear arises even toward small things that cause alarm; Who would not detest as an enemy This body that gives rise to such fear?
gm: Through attachment to this body of mine, Fear arises at even small sources of fear; Towards that body which gives rise to fear, Who would not be hostile as if towards an enemy?

dm: Desiring to perform the rituals to heal The body’s ailments, such as hunger and thirst, People kill birds, fish, and deer, Or lie in wait along the paths.
gm: For whichever body's illnesses like hunger and thirst, Wishing to perform the treatment to cure them, Birds, fish, and wild animals Are killed and ambushed on the road.

dm: If those who, for the sake of profit and honor, Kill even their own fathers and mothers, And steal the property of the Three Jewels, Will be burned in the Incessant Hell,
gm: Whoever, for the sake of profit and respect, Kills even their father and mother, and, Having stolen the wealth of the Three Jewels, Will therefore burn in the Incessant Hell;

dm: What wise person would desire, Protect, and make offerings to such a body? Who would not view it as an enemy, And treat it with contempt?
gm: What wise person, towards that body, Would desire, protect, and venerate it? Towards this, who, as if towards an enemy, Would not look and not despise it?

dm: Thinking, "If I give this away, what will I have to enjoy?" Is the way of a demon, thinking only of one's own benefit. Thinking, "If I use this myself, what will I have to give?" Is the Dharma of the gods, thinking of the welfare of others.
gm: "If I give, what will I consume?"— Thinking of one's own purpose is the way of a demon. "If I consume, what will I give?"— Thinking of others' purpose is the quality of a deity.

dm: If one harms others for the sake of oneself, One will be tormented in the hells and other lower realms. If one harms oneself for the sake of others, One will attain all forms of excellence.
gm: If, for one's own sake, one harms others, One will be tormented in hell and so forth. If, for others' sake, one harms oneself, One will obtain all excellences.

dm: One who desires high status for oneself Will be reborn in the lower realms, in wretchedness, and as a fool. If that very desire is transferred to others, One will attain good migrations and be honored.
gm: Through wishing for oneself to be exalted, One will fall to bad migrations and become base and foolish. If that very thing is shifted to others, One will obtain happy migrations and respect.

dm: If one employs others for one's own benefit, One will experience servitude and the like. If one employs oneself for the benefit of others, One will experience lordship and the like.
gm: If one employs others for one's own purpose, One will experience servitude and so forth. If one uses oneself for the purpose of others, One will experience lordship and so forth.

dm: Whatever happiness there is in the world, It all arises from desiring the happiness of others. Whatever suffering there is in the world, It all arises from desiring one's own happiness.
gm: Whatever happiness there is in the world, All of that arises from wishing for others' happiness. Whatever suffering there is in the world, All of that arises from wishing for one's own happiness.

dm: What need is there to say more? Observe the difference between these two: The childish who work for their own sake, And the Sages who work for the sake of others.
gm: What need is there to say much? Childish beings act for their own purpose, and The Sage acts for the purpose of others. Look at the difference between these two!

dm: If one does not truly exchange One's own happiness for the suffering of others, Buddhahood will not be attained, And there will be no happiness even in cyclic existence.
gm: One's own happiness and the sufferings of others, If one does not perfectly exchange them, One will not achieve Buddhahood, and Even in cyclic existence there will be no happiness.

dm: Setting aside the next life, Even the goals of this life will not be achieved, Just as a servant will not do his work And a master will not pay his wages.
gm: Let alone the next world, With servants not doing their work and Masters not paying wages, Even the purpose of this life will not be accomplished.

dm: Having abandoned the perfect happiness That achieves well-being in both the seen and the unseen, Through the cause of inflicting suffering on others, The deluded take up unbearable misery.
gm: Of that which accomplishes seen and unseen happiness, Entirely abandoning the excellent joy, Through the cause of inflicting suffering on others, The foolish take on unbearable suffering.

dm: Whatever harm exists in the world, And however many fears and sufferings there may be, If they all arise from grasping at a self, Then what use is that great demon to me?
gm: Whatever harm there is in the world, and However much fear and suffering there is, If all of that arises from grasping at a self, What use is that great demon to me?

dm: If I do not completely let go of the self, I will be unable to abandon suffering, Just as one who does not let go of fire Is unable to avoid being burned.
gm: If one does not completely let go of oneself, One cannot abandon suffering, Just as if one does not let go of fire, One cannot avoid being burned.

dm: Therefore, in order to pacify harm to myself And to pacify the suffering of others, I shall give myself away to others And cherish others as I do myself.
gm: Therefore, to pacify harm to myself and To pacify the suffering of others, I should give myself to others and Hold others as myself.

dm: O mind, you must understand with certainty: "I am now under the power of others." Except for the welfare of all sentient beings, You must now think of nothing else.
gm: "I am under the control of others"— O mind, you should definitely know this, and Apart from the purpose of all sentient beings, Now you should not think of anything else.

dm: It is not right to achieve your own ends With eyes and so forth that belong to others; It is not right to act for your own sake With those eyes and so forth that are for their sake.
gm: With eyes and so forth that are under the control of others, It is not appropriate to accomplish one's own purpose. With eyes and so forth that are for their purpose, It is not appropriate to act wrongly toward them.

dm: Therefore, make sentient beings your primary concern; Whatever you see upon my body, Snatch it away and use it To act for the benefit of others.
gm: Therefore, sentient beings should be made principal, and Whatever I see on my body, Having taken it away, I will use it to benefit others.

dm: Having identified oneself with those who are inferior and so forth, And having identified others as oneself, With a mind free of conceptual doubt, Meditate on envy, rivalry, and pride.
gm: Having made the lower and so forth into oneself, and Having made oneself into the other, With a mind free of conceptualization, I should meditate on jealousy, rivalry, and pride.

dm: "This one is honored, but I am not; I have not obtained such things as this. This one is praised, while I am reviled; This one is happy, while I am suffering."
gm: This one is respected, but I am not. I have not found wealth like this one, and This one is praised, while I am disparaged. This one is happy, but I am suffering.

dm: "I am the one who does the work, While this one remains in a state of ease. This one is renowned as great in the world, While I am known as lowly and without merit."
gm: I do all the work, and This one abides in happiness itself. This one is great in the world, and I am known as inferior and without good qualities.

dm: What is the use of one who lacks good qualities? I myself am fully endowed with good qualities. There are those compared to whom this person is inferior, And there are those compared to whom I am superior.
gm: What can be done about being without good qualities? All of us are indeed endowed with good qualities. There are those compared to whom this one is inferior, and There are those compared to whom I am supreme.

dm: The decline of my ethical discipline, views, and so forth, Is due to the power of the afflictions and is not under my control. I must be healed as much as possible, And I shall even accept the hardship involved.
gm: The decline of discipline, view, and so forth Is due to the power of afflictions; it is not under my control. I should be healed as much as possible, and I will willingly accept even harm.

dm: If, however, I am not the one to be healed by him, Why does he treat me with contempt? What use are his good qualities to me? I am the one who possesses good qualities.
gm: However, if I am not to be healed by this one, Why does he despise me? What use are his good qualities to me? This one himself possesses good qualities.

dm: Lacking compassion for beings who dwell in the jaws of the miserable realms, He is outwardly conceited about his qualities, And wishes to challenge the wise.
gm: Abiding in the jaws of the vicious lower realms, This one is without compassion for beings. Outwardly conceited about his good qualities, He wishes to contend with the wise.

dm: Looking at one who is equal to himself, In order to make himself superior, He will certainly secure his own gain and honor, Even through contention.
gm: Having looked at those equal to me, In order to make myself superior, My wealth and respect Will definitely be established even through dispute.

dm: I shall ensure that my own good qualities Are made known to the entire world, While ensuring that no one ever hears Of any good qualities he may possess.
gm: By all means, my good qualities Will be clear to the whole world, and Furthermore, whatever good qualities this one has, I will ensure that no one hears of them.

dm: I shall conceal my own faults, And I shall be the one who is honored, not he. I shall secure great gain today, And I shall be the one who is respected, not he.
gm: My faults will also be hidden, and I will be venerated, but not this one. Today I have well found wealth, and I will be respected, but not this one.

dm: I shall watch with long-lasting delight As this person is brought to ruin. I shall make him the laughingstock of all beings, And the object of their mutual derision.
gm: Upon this one being made miserable, I will look with joy for a long time. He will be the laughingstock of all beings, and Mutual disparagement will be brought about.

dm: It is said that this miserable one is even competing with me. But is he my equal in learning, wisdom, Physical appearance, lineage, or wealth?
gm: This miserable one is even renowned To be contending together with me. Are his learning and wisdom, or Form, caste, and wealth equal to mine?

dm: Having heard of my own virtues Being proclaimed to all in this way, I shall experience the thrill of joy that makes my hair stand on end, And I shall fully enjoy that happiness.
gm: Thus proclaimed to all, Having heard of my good qualities, Thrilled with the arising of joy, I will fully enjoy happiness and well-being.

dm: Even if he should acquire some gain, If he is working for me, I shall give him only enough for his livelihood, And I shall take the rest by my own power.
gm: Even if this one has wealth, If he does my work, Having given him just enough to live on, I will take it by my power.

dm: I shall cause his happiness to decline, And I shall constantly subject him to harm; For throughout hundreds of lifetimes, He has caused me harm within saṃsāra.
gm: This one shall be made to fall from happiness, and Be constantly subjected to my harm. In all hundreds of ways, This one has harmed me in saṃsāra.

dm: O mind, though countless eons have passed while you desired to pursue your own interests, Through such great hardship, You have achieved nothing but suffering.
gm: O mind, because you desired to accomplish your own purpose, Even though countless eons have passed, With such great weariness, You have accomplished only suffering.

dm: Therefore, you must certainly and thoroughly apply yourself to the welfare of others; Since the Buddha's word is unerring, You will later see the benefits of this.
gm: Thus, you must certainly Fully engage in the purpose of others. Since the words of the Muni are infallible, You will see its good qualities later.

dm: If you had performed this work in the past, It would be impossible for you to be in this present state, Lacking the perfect bliss of a Buddha.
gm: If in former times You had performed this action, A state other than the perfect happiness of a Buddha, Such a situation as this could not possibly occur.

dm: Therefore, just as you have grasped as "I" these drops of others' semen and blood, You should likewise habituate yourself to regarding others in the same way.
gm: Therefore, just as Upon the drops of semen and blood of others, You have grasped as "I", Likewise make it a habit with others too.

dm: Having formed the great conception of "other," Seize whatever appears as your own body, And take that very thing away, To use it for the benefit of others.
gm: Having become a great spy for others, Whatever appears on my body, Having stolen those very things, You should practice what is beneficial for others.

dm: "I am happy, but others are not; I am high, but others are low; I am the benefactor, but others are not"— Why do you not feel envy toward yourself in this way?
gm: "I am happy, others are unhappy, I am high, others are low, I do what is beneficial, others do not." Why do you not feel jealous of yourself?

dm: Separate yourself from your own happiness, And take the sufferings of others upon yourself. At all times, examine your own faults, Asking, "What is this [self] doing?"
gm: Separate yourself from happiness, and Apply the suffering of others to yourself. Thinking, "What is this one doing at any time?" Examine your own faults.

dm: Even when others commit a wrong, Transform it into your own fault; And though your own mistake be small, Confess it openly to many people.
gm: Even when faults have been committed by others, Transform them into your own faults; And even if a fault committed by yourself is small, Confess it fully to many people.

dm: By speaking highly of the renown of others, Let your own reputation be eclipsed. Like the lowliest of servants, Employ yourself in all matters of benefit.
gm: By exalting the reputation of others, Suppress your own reputation. Like the lowest of servants, Employ yourself for all purposes.

dm: This [self] is faulty by nature, So do not praise it for any fleeting qualities. Act in such a way that no one at all Will ever know of its virtues.
gm: This one is of a faulty nature, Do not praise it for its adventitious good qualities. By all means, regarding its good qualities, Act so that no one at all will know them.

dm: In short, whatever harm you have done To others for your own sake, Let that harm fall upon yourself For the sake of sentient beings.
gm: In short, for the sake of your own purpose, Whatever harm you have done to others, For the sake of the purpose of sentient beings, Let that harm descend upon yourself.

dm: Do not allow it to grow strong In an overbearing and arrogant manner; Like a new bride, Remain bashful, fearful, and restrained.
gm: Lest it become domineering, Do not foster its strength. Just like a new bride, Keep it bound by modesty and fear.

dm: That should be done, and one should remain so; You must not act in that way. In this manner, you must be brought under control; If you transgress this, you shall be suppressed.
gm: "Do that! Remain like that! You must not do like that!" In this way, subjugate it, And if it transgresses that, it must be punished.

dm: However, if you, my mind, do not act accordingly Even when you have been so instructed, Then, since all faults reside in you, You shall simply be suppressed.
gm: However, even if instructed like that, O mind, if you do not do so, Since all faults rely upon you, You yourself will just have to be punished.

dm: The former time when you could ruin me Was another matter; Now that I see you, where can you go? I shall crush all of your pride.
gm: The former times when you ruined me Were a different time; Now I see you, where will you go? I shall destroy all your arrogance.

dm: Furthermore, abandon the thought that you still have your own interests; I have sold you to others. Do not be distressed, but offer up your service.
gm: "I still have my own purpose"— Cast away that thought which thinks it exists! Since I have sold you to others, Do not feel sorrow, offer your services.

dm: If, through heedlessness, you do not give yourself to sentient beings, You will certainly hand me over to the guardians of hell.
gm: If, becoming careless, I do not give you to sentient beings, You will surely hand me over To the guards of hell.

dm: By handing me over in that way, you have caused me to suffer for a long time; Now, remembering those grudges, I shall destroy your self-interested thoughts.
gm: In that way, you have indeed Handed me over, and I have suffered for a long time; Remembering those grudges, I shall destroy your thinking of your own purpose.

dm: Therefore, if I desire to be happy, I should not seek my own pleasure. Therefore, if I desire to protect myself, I should constantly protect others.
gm: Therefore, if I wish to be happy, I must not make myself happy. Therefore, if I wish to protect myself, I must always protect others.

dm: To whatever extent this body is pampered and cared for, To that same extent it falls into a state of extreme fragility.
gm: To whatever extent this body Is thoroughly cared for, To that very extent, it falls into Becoming extremely fragile.

dm: For one who has fallen into such a state, Even this entire earth is unable to satisfy their desires; Who then can fulfill such cravings?
gm: And even for that which has fallen in that way, Its desires, even by this entire earth, Cannot be fulfilled; So who is able to fulfill its desires?

dm: When one desires the impossible, afflictions and a shattered peace of mind will arise; However, for one who is independent of all such things, their excellence is inexhaustible.
gm: Desiring the impossible brings afflictions, And disappointed hopes will also arise. But for one who does not depend on anything, Their excellence knows no exhaustion.

dm: Therefore, one should not provide any opportunity for the desires of the body to increase; Whatever one does not grasp as attractive is the finest of things.
gm: Therefore, for the desires of the body, One should not give the opportunity to increase. Not grasping at whatever is pleasant— That is an excellent thing.

dm: Ultimately ending in ashes, it is inert and moved by others; Why do I grasp this unbearable, impure form as a self?
gm: Ultimately ending in ashes, Motionless, to be moved by others, An unbearable, impure form— Why do I grasp at this as 'I'?

dm: Whether it is alive or even if it is dead, What use is this machine to me? If it is no different from a clod of earth or the like, Alas, why do I not dispel my pride?
gm: Whether it is alive or whether it is dead, What use is this machine to me? If there is no difference between this and a clod of earth, Alas, why do I not dispel my pride?

dm: By following the dictates of the body, I have accumulated meaningless suffering; What is the use of attachment or anger Toward this thing that is just like a piece of wood?
gm: By taking care of the body, Having accumulated meaningless suffering, Attachment and anger— What use are they for this thing similar to wood?

dm: Whether I nurture it in this way, Or it is eaten by vultures and the like, Since it has neither attachment nor hatred, Why then do I feel attachment for it?
gm: Whether it is cared for by me in this way, Or whether it is eaten by vultures and the like, Since it has no attachment and no anger, Why do I become attached to it?

dm: If that which is angered by insults And that which is pleased by praise Is itself without consciousness, For whose sake do I exert myself?
gm: That which is angered by blame, And that which is delighted by praise— If it itself lacks any knowing, For whose sake have I toiled?

dm: If you say that those who desire this body Are my friends, Since everyone desires their own body, Why do I not take pleasure in them as well?
gm: Whoever desires this body, If I think, 'They and I are friends,' Since everyone desires their own body, Why do I not rejoice in them?

dm: Therefore, without attachment, I shall give up this body for the benefit of all beings; Thus, although it has many faults, I shall maintain it as a tool for my actions.
gm: Therefore, without attachment, I shall give up my body to benefit beings. Thus, even though it has many faults, It should be retained as an instrument for action.

dm: Therefore, enough of childish behavior! Following in the footsteps of the wise, And recalling the instructions on conscientiousness, I shall dispel sleep and mental dullness.
gm: Therefore, enough with childish behavior! I shall follow in the footsteps of the wise, And, remembering the teachings on conscientiousness, I shall turn away from sleep and lethargy.

dm: Therefore, in order to clear away obscurations, I shall withdraw my mind from mistaken paths, And always rest it in meditative equipoise Upon the perfect object of focus.
gm: Therefore, in order to clear away obscurations, Having withdrawn the mind from wrong paths, Constantly upon the perfect object, I shall rest in meditative equipoise.

dm: This concludes the eighth chapter, titled "The Explanation of Meditative Concentration," from the *Entering the Conduct of a Bodhisattva*.
gm: From Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva, the eighth chapter, called The Teaching on Meditative Concentration.

dm: Chapter Nine: The Perfection of Wisdom
gm: Chapter Nine: The Perfection of Wisdom

dm: All of these various branches Were taught by the Sage for the sake of wisdom. Therefore, those who wish to pacify suffering Should generate wisdom.
gm: All these branches The Sage taught for the sake of wisdom. Therefore, those who wish to pacify Suffering should generate wisdom.

dm: The conventional and the ultimate: These are held to be the two truths. The ultimate is not an object of the intellect; The intellect is said to be the conventional.
gm: The relative and the ultimate— These are asserted to be the two truths. The ultimate is not the domain of the intellect; The intellect is said to be the relative.

dm: In this regard, two kinds of worlds are seen: The yogic and the ordinary. In that regard, the ordinary world Is invalidated by the yogic world;
gm: In this regard, two kinds of world are seen: Yogis and ordinary people. In this regard, the ordinary world Is invalidated by the world of yogis.

dm: Even yogis are superseded by those at higher and higher levels Due to differences in their intellect. Both are accepted through examples they agree upon, Because they do not analyze for the sake of the result.
gm: Even yogis, due to differences in intellect, Are invalidated by successively higher ones. Through examples accepted by both, Because they are unanalyzed, for the sake of the result.

dm: The worldly perceive things and conceptualize them As being truly real, rather than like an illusion; It is on this point that The yogis and the worldly dispute.
gm: People of the world see entities, And conceptualize them as truly real, Not as being like illusions; therefore, here, Yogis and the world dispute.

dm: Even the direct perception of forms and so forth Exists by worldly renown, not by valid cognition. This is as false as the common renown Of purity in things that are actually impure.
gm: Even the direct perception of forms and so forth Is through convention, not through valid cognition. That is false, just like the convention Of being clean and so forth regarding what is unclean and so forth.

dm: For the sake of engaging the world, The Protector taught these things as if they were real; If you object that they are not even momentary, And that this is contradictory even in conventional truth,
gm: "For the sake of guiding the world, The Protector taught entities. In reality, They are not momentary." If one says, "This contradicts even the relative,"

dm: There is no fault in the conventional truth of the yogis, For they see reality in relation to the world; Otherwise, the world's perception would invalidate The realization that a woman's body is impure.
gm: There is no fault in the yogi's relative; In relation to the world, they see reality. Otherwise, the apprehension of women as unclean Would be invalidated by the world.

dm: How can merit from an illusory Conqueror Be the same as if he were truly existent? If sentient beings are like illusions, Then how are they reborn after death?
gm: Merit from a Victorious One who is like an illusion Is just as it is for one who truly exists. "If sentient beings are like illusions, How are they born after dying?"

dm: As long as the conditions are assembled, For that long even an illusion will arise. How can a sentient being be truly existent Merely because their continuity lasts a long time?
