gm: As long as conditions are assembled, For that long, even illusions will occur. How, merely through a long continuum, Does a sentient being truly exist?

dm: In killing an illusory person and the like, There is no sin because they lack a mind; But in the case of one who possesses an illusory mind, Merit and sin do arise.
gm: In killing an illusory person and so forth, Because there is no mind, there is no sin; But regarding that which possesses an illusory mind, Merit and sin arise.

dm: Because mantras and such lack the capacity, An illusory mind does not arise from them. Arising from various conditions, That illusion is itself of various kinds.
gm: Because mantras and so forth lack the capacity, Illusory minds do not arise. Arising from various conditions, Illusions themselves are also various.

dm: Nowhere is there any single condition That has the power to produce everything. If ultimate reality is nirvana And cyclic existence is the conventional, then
gm: That a single condition has the capacity for everything Nowhere exists. "If the ultimate is nirvāṇa, And saṃsāra is the relative, in that case,

dm: Since even a Buddha would be in cyclic existence, What would be the use of the conduct of enlightenment? As long as the continuity of conditions is not severed, Even an illusion will not cease;
gm: Even a Buddha would cycle in saṃsāra, so What is the point of bodhisattva conduct?" If the continuum of conditions is not severed, Even an illusion is not reversed;

dm: But since the continuity of conditions is severed, It does not arise even conventionally. When even the confusion itself does not exist, By what means can an illusion be perceived?
gm: But because the continuum of conditions is severed, It does not arise even relatively. "When even the deceptive mind does not exist, By what is the illusion perceived?"

dm: When, for you, the illusion itself Does not exist, then what is perceived? If it were something else in reality, That aspect would be the mind itself.
gm: When, for you, even the illusion itself Does not exist, then what is perceived? "If it exists as another in reality, That aspect is the mind itself."

dm: When the mind itself is an illusion, Then what is seen, and by what is it seen? The Protector of the World has also said That the mind does not see the mind.
gm: If the mind itself is an illusion, Then what is seen by what? Even the Protector of the World Stated that the mind does not see the mind.

dm: Just as the edge of a sword cannot Cut itself, so it is with the mind. Just as a lamp’s own nature Perfectly illuminates itself,
gm: Just as the blade of a sword Does not cut itself, so too the mind. If [you say], "Just as a lamp Perfectly illuminates its own entity,"

dm: A lamp is not something to be illuminated, Because it is not obscured by darkness. Just as the blueness of a blue crystal Does not depend upon anything else,
gm: A lamp is not something to be illuminated, Because it is not obscured by darkness. "Unlike a crystal, a blue thing Does not depend on another for its blueness;

dm: So too, some things are seen to depend On others, while some are seen not to depend. That which is not blue cannot make itself blue; It is not made so by itself.
gm: So also some are seen to depend On another, and some not to depend." When it is not blue itself, It does not make itself blue.

dm: If you say, "The lamp illuminates," Having known this through cognition, Then by what is it known that the mind is luminous, Such that you can say so?
gm: That a lamp illuminates Is known by cognition and thus expressed; That the intellect itself is luminous, Having been known by what, is so expressed?

dm: Since it is never seen by anyone at all, Whether it is clear or not clear, Is like the graceful posturing of a barren woman's daughter; It is meaningless even to speak of it.
gm: If it is not seen by anyone at all, Whether it is luminous or not luminous, Like the alluring pose of a barren woman's daughter, Expressing it is meaningless.

dm: If self-awareness does not exist, How can consciousness be remembered? Memory arises through a connection to the experience of something else, Just like the venom of a rat.
gm: "If self-awareness does not exist, How is consciousness remembered?" It is remembered from its connection to experiencing another, Like the poison of a rat.

dm: If it were self-luminous because it is seen When endowed with other conditions, Then, just as a vase is seen through the application of a perfected eye-salve, The eye-salve itself would not be the vase that is seen.
gm: "Endowed with other conditions, Because it sees, it illuminates itself." Through the application of accomplished eye-ointment, A vase is seen, but not the eye-ointment itself.

dm: Whatever is seen, heard, or known, Is not what is to be negated here; What is to be overturned here is the conceptualization of them as true, Which is the cause of suffering.
gm: How things are seen, heard, and known Is not to be refuted here; Here, what becomes the cause of suffering, The conceptualization of true existence, is to be reversed.

dm: If an illusion is not other than the mind, And yet you do not consider it to be the same, If it were a real entity, how could it not be other? If you say it is not other, then it cannot exist as a real entity.
gm: "Illusion is not other than the mind, And if it is not conceived as being not other," If it is a real entity, how is it not other? If it is not other, it does not exist as an entity.

dm: Just as an illusion is not true, So too is the mind that sees it; If cyclic existence were based on a real entity, It would otherwise be like empty space.
gm: Just as an illusion, although not true, Is an object of sight, so is the perceiving mind. "If saṃsāra has a real basis, it functions; Otherwise, it would be like space."

dm: Since a non-entity depends upon an entity, How could it possess the capacity for action? Your mind would then be without any companion, It would become entirely solitary.
gm: "Since a non-entity depends on a real entity, How could it be endowed with a function?" Your mind, being without a companion, Would become entirely alone.

dm: When the mind is free from a perceived object, At that time, all are Tathāgatas. That being the case, what excellence is there In the conceptual construction of "Mind Only"?
gm: When the mind is free of an apprehended object, At that time, all are Tathāgatas. Even in that case, in Mind Only, What merit is there in conceptualizing it?

dm: Even if one knows things are like an illusion, How will the afflictions be averted? For even the creator of an illusory woman May feel desire for her.
gm: Even if one knows things to be like an illusion, How are the afflictions repelled? Since, toward an illusory woman, Even her creator generates attachment.

dm: The creator of such things is an object of knowledge, For the latencies of the afflictions have not been abandoned. Therefore, when one sees that object, The latency for emptiness is very weak.
gm: Her creator has not abandoned The latent tendencies of the afflictions toward objects of knowledge; Therefore, when he sees her, His latent tendencies for emptiness are weak.

dm: By habituating the latency for emptiness, The latency for substantial things will be abandoned; And by habituating the thought that "nothing exists," Even that will later be abandoned.
gm: By familiarizing with the latent tendencies of emptiness, The latent tendencies of entities will be abandoned; By familiarizing with "there is nothing at all," That too will later be abandoned.

dm: When one thinks that "nothing exists," And the substantial thing to be analyzed is not perceived, At that time, how can a non-entity, lacking any basis, Remain before the mind?
gm: When one asserts, "Such and such does not exist," And the entity to be examined is not observed, At that time, how can a non-entity without a basis Remain before the mind?

dm: When neither entities nor non-entities Remain before the mind, Then, since there is no other aspect, It is thoroughly pacified in non-apprehension.
gm: When both entities and non-entities Do not remain before the mind, At that time, since there is no other aspect, It is completely pacified, without an object of focus.

dm: Just as a wish-fulfilling jewel or a wish-granting tree Completely fulfills all hopes, Likewise, through the power of the aspirations of those to be trained, The form of the Victorious One appears.
gm: Just as a wish-fulfilling jewel and a wish-granting tree Completely fulfill hopes, Likewise, due to those to be tamed and prayers of aspiration, The form of the Victorious One appears.

dm: For example, just as a Garuḍa shrine, Once established, remains even after the practitioner has passed away, And continues to pacify poisons and the like Even though a long time has elapsed since his passing.
gm: For example, when a garuḍa shrine Has been accomplished and its creator has passed away, Even though a long time has passed since his death, It pacifies poison and so forth.

dm: Constructing a shrine to the Victorious One In accordance with the conduct of enlightenment Accomplishes all purposes, even though The Bodhisattva has passed into nirvana.
gm: In accordance with the bodhisattva's conduct, The shrine of the Victorious One is also accomplished; Even when the Bodhisattva has passed Into nirvāṇa, he accomplishes all aims.

dm: If one makes offerings to that which lacks a mind, How can it be possessed of a result? Because it is explained that whether they remain or have passed into nirvana, It is exactly the same.
gm: "Since offerings are made to one without a mind, How can there be a result?" Because whether he remains or has passed into nirvāṇa, It is taught that it is exactly the same.

dm: Whether from the perspective of conventional or ultimate truth, The scriptures state that there is a result, Just as there is a result From offerings made to the actual Buddha.
gm: Whether conventionally or in reality, It is suitable, for scriptures state that there is a result; For example, toward a true Buddha, Just as it is endowed with a result.

dm: Liberation comes from seeing the truths; What is the use of seeing emptiness? Because the scriptures state that without this path, There is no enlightenment.
gm: "One is liberated by seeing the truths; What is the use of seeing emptiness?" Because scriptures state that without this path, There is no awakening.

dm: If the Mahāyāna were not established, How would your own scriptures be established? Because this is established for both of us, Initially, this was not established for you.
gm: "If the Mahāyāna is not established, How is your scripture established?" "Because this is established for both of us." "Initially, this was not established for you."

dm: Whatever conditions make you believe in that, They are the same for the Mahāyāna as well. If it were true because two others accept it, Then the Vedas and so forth would also be true.
gm: By whatever conditions you believe in that, That is the same for the Mahāyāna too. If it is true because two others accept it, The Vedas and so forth would also become true.

dm: If you say it is because the Mahāyāna is contested, Since your own scriptures are contested by non-Buddhists, And other scriptures are contested by your own and other schools, They would also have to be rejected because they are contested.
gm: If you say the Mahāyāna is subject to dispute, The scriptures are disputed by non-Buddhists, And other scriptures are disputed by ourselves and others; Since they are subject to dispute, they would have to be discarded.

dm: If the root of the teaching is the monkhood itself, Then even being a monk is a difficult state to maintain. For those whose minds are still directed toward objects, Even nirvana is a difficult state to maintain.
gm: If being a monk is the root of the teaching, Even being a monk is difficult to establish. For those whose minds have apprehension, Even nirvāṇa is difficult to establish.

dm: If one is liberated through the abandonment of afflictions, Then one should become so immediately thereafter. Even if they are free from afflictions, The potency of karma is still seen within them.
gm: If one is liberated by abandoning afflictions, It would occur immediately upon that. Even though there are no afflictions, in them The power of karma is seen.

dm: If you argue that for the time being it is certain that there is no craving that constitutes grasping, Then why should this craving not exist—just like their confusion—even if it is not of an afflicted nature?
gm: As for the craving for appropriation, If you say it is certain that it does not exist; Even if that craving is not an affliction, Why would it not exist, like ignorance?

dm: Craving is conditioned by feeling, and they also possess those feelings. A mind that possesses an object of observation will remain fixed upon something.
gm: Craving occurs due to the condition of feeling; Those ones also have feelings. A mind that is endowed with apprehension Will rest upon something.

dm: A mind that is devoid of emptiness, even if it has ceased, will arise once again, Just like the meditative absorption of non-perception; Therefore, one should meditate on emptiness.
gm: A mind separated from emptiness, Though ceased, will arise again, Like the meditative absorption without discrimination; Therefore, one should meditate on emptiness.

dm: If you accept that any speech which accords with the sutras is the word of the Buddha, Then why do you not accept the majority of the Mahayana, Which is similar to your own sutras?
gm: If any speech that enters into the sūtras Is asserted to be spoken by the Buddha, Is it not asserted that the majority of the Mahāyāna Is equal to your sūtras?

dm: If, because of a single exception, everything were to be considered faulty, Then why would the whole not be the word of the Victorious One, Because a single point is similar to the sutras?
gm: If, due to a single one that is not included, All become faulty, Then due to a single one that is equal to the sūtras, Why are they not all spoken by the Victorious One?

dm: Regarding those words whose depth could not be fathomed By the likes of the great Mahākāśyapa, Because you have not understood them, Who are you to say they should not be accepted?
gm: Any speech whose depth was unfathomed By Mahākāśyapa and the rest, Just because you do not understand it, Who would make it unacceptable?

dm: To remain in cyclic existence for the sake of those suffering through delusion, Liberated from the extremes of attachment and fear, And having accomplished the state of abiding in cyclic existence— This is the fruit of emptiness.
gm: For the sake of those who suffer due to ignorance, Being freed from the extremes of attachment and fear, Remaining in saṃsāra becomes established; This is the result of emptiness.

dm: Thus, it is not reasonable To direct refutations toward the position of emptiness. Therefore, without harboring any doubt, One should meditate upon emptiness.
gm: Thus, toward the side of emptiness, Refutation is not appropriate. Therefore, without hesitation, One should meditate on emptiness.

dm: Emptiness is the antidote To the darkness of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations. Why, then, would those who desire to swiftly attain omniscience Not meditate upon it?
gm: Of the obscurations of afflictions and knowables, Emptiness is the antidote to the darkness. By one who wishes to quickly become omniscient, How could one not meditate on it?

dm: If fear arises toward something that produces suffering, Then fear should arise toward that; But emptiness is what pacifies suffering, So how could fear arise toward it?
gm: Whatever entity produces suffering, From that, fear will arise. Since emptiness pacifies suffering, How can fear arise toward it?

dm: If there were some "self," Then one might be afraid of anything; But since there is no self at all, Who is there to be afraid?
gm: If any self existed, Fear would arise from anything. Since no self exists at all, Who is there to be afraid?

dm: Teeth, hair, and nails are not the self; The self is not the bones or blood; It is not the mucus or the phlegm, Nor is it the lymph or the pus.
gm: Teeth, hair, and nails are not the self; The self is not bone or blood. It is not snot, nor is it phlegm, And it is neither serum nor pus.

dm: The self is not fat or sweat; The lungs and liver, too, are not the self. Other internal organs are not the self; The self is not the excrement or the urine.
gm: The self is not fat or sweat, And lungs and liver are not the self. The other internal organs are also not the self, And the self is not feces or urine.

dm: Flesh and skin are not the self; Heat and wind are also not the self. The orifices are not the self in any way; The six consciousnesses are also not the self.
gm: Flesh and skin are not the self, And warmth and wind are not the self. The cavities are not the self, and in all ways The six consciousnesses are not the self either.

dm: If the consciousness of sound were permanent, Then sound would be apprehended at all times. If there is no object of knowledge, what does it perceive? On what basis could it be called "consciousness"?
gm: If the consciousness of sound is permanent, It would apprehend sound at all times. If there is no object of knowledge, what does it cognize, And due to what is it called a consciousness?

dm: If that which lacks cognition were consciousness, Then it would follow that even a piece of wood is consciousness. Therefore, it is certain that without the presence of an object of knowledge, There is no consciousness.
gm: If there is consciousness without cognizing, It would logically follow that wood is also consciousness. Therefore, it is certain that without a nearby Object of knowledge, there is no consciousness.

dm: If it is that very same consciousness that knows a form, Why at that time does it not also hear? If you say it is because the sound is not present, Then the consciousness of that sound is also absent.
gm: If that very same consciousness cognizes form, Why is there no hearing at that time? If it is because sound is not nearby, Then the consciousness of it is also non-existent.

dm: How could that which has the nature of apprehending sound Become that which apprehends form? One person being designated as both father and son Is not the ultimate reality.
gm: How could that which has the nature of apprehending sound Become the apprehender of form? One being both father and son Is designated, but it is not ultimate reality.

dm: In this way, sattva, rajas, and tamas Are neither son nor father. They are not observed to have a nature That possesses the apprehension of sound.
gm: Thus, sattva, rajas, and Tamas are neither son nor father; And it is not seen to have a nature Possessing the apprehension of sound.

dm: If it is seen in another mode, like an actor, Then it is not permanent. If that other mode is the reality itself, Then that oneness is a oneness never seen before.
gm: If, like an actor, it takes on a different guise, And if that very same thing is seen, it is not permanent. If that different guise is that very same thing, That unity is an unprecedented one.

dm: If that other mode is not real, Then describe its own inherent nature. If you say it is consciousness itself, then in that case, It would follow that all beings are one.
gm: If the different guise is not true, Then explain its own nature. If you say it is consciousness itself, then in that case, It would logically follow that all people are one.

dm: Those with mind and those without mind would also Become one, because they are the same in their mere existence. When their specific differences are mistaken, What could then be the basis for their similarity?
gm: Conscious and unconscious things, too, Would become one, because their existence is the same. When differences are false, What then is the basis for similarity?

dm: That which is without mind is also not the self, Because it lacks consciousness, just like a vase and so forth. However, if it were the self because it is endowed with consciousness, It would follow that when it is not conscious, the self would perish.
gm: The unconscious is not the self either, Because it is unconscious, like a vase and so forth. However, if you say it cognizes because it possesses consciousness, When it cognizes, it logically follows that the unconscious perishes.

dm: If the self is immutable, What could consciousness possibly do to it? Thus, being unconscious and inactive, It would be as if space were made into the self.
gm: But if the self has no change, What is done to it by consciousness? Thus, unconscious and devoid of activity, Space might as well be made into the self.

dm: If the self does not exist, The connection between action and result is illogical; Since the action perishes after being performed, Whose action would it be?
gm: If the self does not exist, The connection between actions and results is not logical, Because if one perishes after performing an action, Whose action will it be?

dm: Since it is established for both of us That the action and the basis of the result are distinct, And that there is no self acting therein, Is this dispute not pointless?
gm: That the bases of the action and the result are different, and That there is no self operating there, Is established for both of us, so Is it not pointless to debate here?

dm: To see a cause existing simultaneously with its result Is not possible; It is by relying on a single continuum That the "agent" and "experiencer" are taught.
gm: That the one possessing the cause also possesses the result— To see this is impossible. It is in dependence upon a single continuum That an agent and an experiencer are taught.

dm: The minds of the past and future Are not the self, because they do not exist; If, however, the presently arising mind were the self, Then when that mind perishes, the self would also cease to exist.
gm: The mind of the past and the future Is not the self, because it does not exist. But if the arisen mind is the self, When that perishes, there is no self either.

dm: For example, when the trunk of a plantain tree Is dissected into its parts, nothing is found; Likewise, when sought through analytical investigation, The self is not found to be real.
gm: For example, the trunk of a banana tree, When divided into parts, is nothing at all; Likewise, when analytically Searched for, the self is also not real.

dm: If sentient beings do not exist, Then for whom should one feel compassion? It is directed toward those imputed by delusion, Which are accepted for the sake of the result.
gm: If sentient beings do not exist, Toward whom does one practice compassion? Toward whatever is imputed by the delusion That is accepted for the sake of the result.

dm: If there are no sentient beings, whose is the fruit? That is true, yet such an aspiration is made from the perspective of delusion. For the sake of pacifying suffering, One should not dispel the delusion regarding the result.
gm: If sentient beings do not exist, whose is the result? That is true, but it is asserted due to delusion. For the sake of entirely pacifying suffering, The delusion regarding the result should not be reversed.

dm: The pride that is the cause of suffering Increases through the delusion of a self. If you say that this cannot be averted, Then meditating on selflessness is the supreme remedy.
gm: Pride, which is the cause of suffering, Increases because of the delusion of a self. If you say, "Even that cannot be reversed," Meditating on selflessness is the best.

dm: The body is not the feet or the calves; The thighs and the waist are not the body either. The belly and the back are not the body; The chest and the shoulders are not the body either.
gm: The body is not the feet or the calves, The thighs and the waist are also not the body. The belly and the back are not the body, And the chest and the arms are not the body.

dm: The ribs and the hands are not the body, Nor are the armpits and the shoulders the body. The internal organs are not it either, And if the head and the neck are also not the body, Then what in this is the body?
gm: The ribs and the hands are not the body, The armpits and the shoulders are not the body. The inner organs are also not it, And the head and the neck are not the body; What is the body in all this?

dm: If this body were to abide in all these parts By way of its individual portions, Then while the parts would indeed abide in the parts, Where would the body itself abide?
gm: If this body were to abide in all of these In a partial manner, The parts would indeed abide in the parts, But where does it itself abide?

dm: If the body in its entirety Were to abide in the hands and so forth, Then as many as there are such parts as hands, There would be that many bodies.
gm: If the entirety of the body itself Were to abide in the hands and so forth, However many hands and so forth there are, There would be that many bodies.

dm: If the body is not found outside or within its parts, How could the body exist in the hands and so forth? If it is not something other than the hands and so forth, How could it possibly exist?
gm: If the body does not exist outside or inside, How does the body exist in the hands and so forth? If it does not exist other than the hands and so forth, How does it exist?

dm: Therefore, the body does not exist; it is only due to delusion That the notion of a body arises with respect to the hands and so forth, Just as the mind perceives a person in a scarecrow Due to a particular arrangement of shape.
gm: Therefore, there is no body; with regard to the hands and so forth, Due to delusion, there is the concept of a body, Because of a specific configuration of shapes, Just like the concept of a person with regard to a cairn.

dm: As long as the collection of conditions remains, The body appears like a person; Likewise, as long as the hands and so forth are present, The body will appear to exist therein.
gm: As long as the collection of conditions lasts, The body appears like a person. Likewise, as long as it is present in the hands and so forth, For that long, the body appears there.

dm: Similarly, since it is a collection of fingers, What indeed is the "hand"? Since that too is a collection of joints, And the joints themselves can be divided into their own parts,
gm: Likewise, because it is a collection of fingers, What would the hand be? And since that too is a collection of joints, The joint, too, by its division into its own parts,

dm: Even the parts are reduced to atoms, And those atoms are divided into directional facets. Since the directional facets are also devoid of parts, They are like space; therefore, even atoms do not exist.
gm: And the part also by its division into particles, And that particle also by its division into directional parts, And since the division of directions is devoid of parts, It is like space; therefore, even particles do not exist.

dm: Such being the case, what discerning person Would be attached to forms that are like a dream? When the body is thus non-existent, Then who is a man and who is a woman?
gm: Thus, what intelligent person would be attached To form, which is like a dream? When the body does not exist in that way, Then what is a man and what is a woman?

dm: If suffering exists in its own right, Why does it not afflict those who are joyful? If happiness is real, why do those tormented by grief and the like Not find joy in delicious food and such?
gm: If suffering truly existed, Why does it not harm the very joyful? If happiness [truly existed], for those overcome with grief and so forth, Why do delicious foods and so forth not cause joy?

dm: If it is argued that it is not experienced because it is overwhelmed by something more powerful, How can that which is not of the nature of experience Be a sensation?
gm: If it is because it is overshadowed by something stronger That it is not experienced, How can that which is not of the nature of experience Be a feeling?

dm: If you say that suffering exists in a subtle state And its gross form has merely been removed, Then that is simply a state of joy other than that; If you say it is subtle, then that too is of the same nature.
gm: "Suffering exists in a subtle state; Has its gross state not been removed?" If you say, "That is merely a joy distinct from that," Then that subtle state too is [a state] of that [joy].

dm: If, because an opposing condition has arisen, Suffering is not produced, Then is it not established that what is considered "feeling" Is merely a stubborn conceptual attachment?
gm: If, because a contrary condition has arisen, Suffering does not arise, Is it not established that the conception of feeling Is merely conceptual clinging?

dm: For that very reason, one should meditate On this analytical investigation as its antidote; The meditative concentration arising from the field of such analysis Is the food of the yogi.
gm: For this very reason, the antidote to this Is to meditate on this analytical discernment; That which arises from the field of analysis Is the food of the yogi's concentration.

dm: If there is a gap between the sense faculty and the object, Where would those two meet? If there is no gap, they are but one; What, then, could meet with what?
gm: If there is a gap between the sense faculties and objects, Where would they meet? Even if there is no gap, they are a single entity, So what would meet with what?

dm: An atom cannot enter another atom, For it has no space and they are equal in size. Without entering, there is no mingling, And without mingling, there is no contact.
gm: An atom does not enter an atom, For they have no empty space and are of equal size. Without entering, there is no mixing, And without mixing, there is no meeting.

dm: How could it be logical to speak of "contact" Between things that have no parts? If you have ever seen contact occurring without parts, Then please demonstrate it.
gm: How could it be reasonable to say That what is partless can meet? If meeting and being partless Have been seen together, show it!

dm: For a consciousness that is formless, Contact is not at all logical. A collection also lacks substantial reality, Just as was previously analyzed.
gm: For consciousness, which has no body, Meeting is not reasonable at all. Neither is it for an aggregation, because it does not exist as a real entity, Just as was analytically examined before.

dm: If, in this way, there is no contact, From what could feeling arise? For what purpose is all this toil? What could cause harm to what?
gm: Thus, if contact does not exist, From what would feeling arise? What is the purpose of this weariness? What would harm what?

dm: When there is no experiencer at all, And feeling itself does not exist, Then, having seen this situation, Why does craving not turn away?
gm: When there is no feeler at all, And feeling also does not exist, At that time, having seen this situation, Why would craving not be turned away?

dm: Since seeing and even touching Are of the nature of dreams and illusions, And arise simultaneously with the mind, That feeling is not seen by it.
gm: Seeing or even touching, Have a nature like a dream or an illusion. Because it arises simultaneously with the mind, Feeling is not perceived by it.

dm: Even if born previously or later, They would be remembered but not experienced. The self does not experience itself, Nor is it experienced by others.
gm: Even by what arises before or after, It is remembered, but not experienced. It does not experience itself, And it is not experienced by others either.

dm: There is no experiencer at all, And therefore, feeling itself does not exist. Thus, how can this collection, Which is devoid of a self, be harmed by this?
gm: There is no feeler at all, Therefore, feeling itself is not real. Thus, for this selfless aggregate, How could it be harmed by this?

dm: The mind does not abide in the sense faculties, Nor in forms and so forth, nor in between them. It is not the mind within, nor is it without, Nor is it to be found anywhere else.
gm: The mind does not abide in the sense faculties, Nor in forms and so forth, nor in between them. The mind is not inside, nor is it outside, And it is not found anywhere else.

dm: That which is not the body, nor something other than it, Neither mixed with it nor separate in any way, Is not even the slightest thing; therefore, Sentient beings are by nature in the state of nirvana.
gm: That which is not in the body, nor anywhere else, Not mixed, nor apart from it anywhere, Is nothing whatsoever; therefore, Sentient beings are by nature in nirvāṇa.

dm: If consciousness existed prior to the object of knowledge, Then directed toward what would it arise? If consciousness and the object of knowledge are simultaneous, Then directed toward what would it arise?
gm: If consciousness exists before the object of knowledge, Directed towards what would it arise? If consciousness and the object of knowledge are simultaneous, Directed towards what would it arise?

dm: If, however, it exists after the object of knowledge, Then from what would consciousness arise? In this way, the arising of all phenomena Cannot be understood.
gm: Or if it exists after the object of knowledge, Then from what does consciousness arise? In this way, of all phenomena, Arising cannot be realized.

dm: If in that way the conventional does not exist, How could there be the two truths? Furthermore, if that conventional exists through another, How could sentient beings pass into nirvana?
gm: If, in this way, conventional reality does not exist, How could the two truths exist in that? And if that is due to another conventional reality, How could sentient beings pass into nirvāṇa?

dm: This is the conceptualization of another's mind; It is not one's own conventional reality. If that is later ascertained, then it exists; Otherwise, the conventional simply does not exist.
gm: This is the conception of another mind; It is not one's own conventional reality. If it is ascertained later, it exists; If not, conventional reality itself does not exist.

dm: Conceptual thought and the object to be analyzed Are both mutually dependent. Based upon what is renowned in the world, All analytical investigations are expressed.
gm: Conception and the object to be conceived, The two are mutually dependent. Relying on what is conventionally known, All analyses are expressed.

dm: When one analyzes with an analysis That is itself being analyzed, Then because that analysis is also to be analyzed, There is no end to it.
gm: When analysis Is analyzed by analysis, Then that analysis too, Because it is analyzed, has no end.

dm: When the object of analysis is thoroughly analyzed, There is no basis remaining for the analysis. Because there is no basis, it does not arise, And that is described as nirvana.
gm: If the object of analysis has been analyzed, There is no basis for analysis. Because there is no basis, it does not arise, And that too is expressed as nirvāṇa.

dm: For those who hold that these two are real, Their position is extremely difficult to maintain. If the object is established through the power of consciousness, What basis is there for the existence of consciousness itself?
gm: According to those who hold these two to be true, That very position rests in great difficulty. If the object is established by the power of consciousness, What is the basis for the existence of consciousness itself?

dm: If, however, consciousness is established through the object of knowledge, What basis is there for the existence of the object of knowledge? If they exist through mutual dependence, Then both of them will be non-existent.
gm: Or if consciousness is established from the object of knowledge, What is the basis for the existence of the object of knowledge? If they exist by the power of one another, Both also would not exist.

dm: If there is no father without a son, From what could the son himself have arisen? Without a son, there is no father; Likewise, both of them are non-existent.
gm: If without a son there is no father, From what does the son himself arise? In the absence of a son, there is no father; Likewise, those two themselves do not exist.

dm: Just as a sprout is produced from a seed, And the seed itself is known by that very sprout, Why is the existence of the object of knowledge not realized By the consciousness that arises from it?
gm: A sprout arises from a seed, and Just as that very seed is known by it, By consciousness, which arises from the object of knowledge, Why is the existence of that [object] not known?

dm: If a consciousness other than the sprout Realizes that the seed exists, Then by what means is the existence of that consciousness, Which realizes that object of knowledge, itself realized?
gm: By a consciousness that is other than the sprout, If the existence of the seed is known, By which that object of knowledge is known, From what is the existence of the consciousness itself known?

dm: For the time being, through worldly direct perception, All causes are seen. The distinctions in the lotus stalk and so forth Are produced by the distinctions among their causes.
gm: For now, by worldly direct perception, All causes are seen. The variations such as the stalk of the lotus Are produced by the variations of causes.

dm: If you ask what created the variety of causes, It is from the very variety of preceding causes. Why is a cause able to produce an effect? It is from the very power of the preceding cause.
gm: If one asks, what made the variations of causes? From the variations of prior causes themselves. Why are causes able to produce effects? From the power of prior causes themselves.

dm: If Īśvara is the cause of the world, Then for a start, explain who Īśvara is. If you say he is the elements, that may be so; But why weary yourself over a mere name?
gm: If Īśvara is the cause of beings, Tell me, for now, what is Īśvara? If one says it is the elements, so be it; But what is the use of exhausting oneself over a mere name?

dm: However, because earth and the others are multiple, Impermanent, inert, and not divine, And because they are things to be trodden upon and are impure, They are not Īśvara himself.
gm: However, earth and so forth are multiple, Impermanent, devoid of movement, not divine, Objects to be stepped upon, and impure; They are not Īśvara himself.

dm: Īśvara is not space, because space is inert; He is not the self, as that has already been refuted. And if the creator is also inconceivable, What is the point of speaking of him as "inconceivable"?
gm: Īśvara is not space, because it is devoid of movement; He is not the self, because it was already refuted before; And as for a creator who is inconceivable, What is the use of speaking of the inconceivable?

dm: Furthermore, what is it that he is asserted to produce? Are not the self, the earth, and so forth, And the nature of Īśvara himself, also eternal? Since consciousness arises from objects of knowledge,
gm: And what is it that he wishes to produce? Are not the self, those such as earth, And the essence of Īśvara permanent? Consciousness arises from the object of knowledge, and

dm: Pleasure and pain have arisen from karma since beginningless time. Tell me, what is it that is created by him? If there is no beginning to the cause, How could there be a beginning to the effect?
gm: Happiness and suffering are from beginningless karma; Tell me, what was produced by him? If the cause has no beginning, How can the effect have a beginning?

dm: Why does he not create constantly? For he is not dependent on anything else. If there is nothing that was not created by him, Upon what would he depend?
gm: Why does he not create continuously? He does not depend on another. If there is nothing else that was not made by him, Upon what would he depend?

dm: If he depends on something, then the collection of conditions Is the cause, and not Īśvara. When the collection is present, he has no power not to produce, And without it, he has no power to produce.
gm: If he depends, then the collection itself Would be the cause, and not Īśvara. When assembled, there is no power not to produce, And without them, there is no power to produce.

dm: If he acts without desiring to do so, It follows that he is under the power of another. If he does desire to act, he is dependent upon that desire; If he is thus dependent, how can he be Īśvara?
gm: If Īśvara creates without desiring it, It follows that he is under the control of another. Even if he desires, he is dependent upon desire. If he creates, how is he Īśvara?

dm: Those who claim that atoms are eternal Have already been refuted previously. The Sāṃkhyas assert that a permanent Primal Substance Is the cause of the world.
gm: As for those who assert permanent atoms, They have also already been refuted earlier. The permanent Pradhāna is the cause of beings; This is what the Sāṃkhyas assert.

dm: The equilibrium of the qualities known as Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas Is proclaimed to be the Primal Substance; Their disequilibrium is said to be the world.
gm: The qualities known as Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas, Abiding in equilibrium, Are termed Pradhāna; In disequilibrium, they are said to be beings.

dm: It is illogical for a single entity to have three natures; Therefore, it does not exist. Likewise, the qualities themselves do not exist, Because they too each have a threefold nature.
gm: For one thing to have three natures Is illogical, therefore it does not exist. Likewise, the qualities do not exist, Because they too would each have three aspects.

dm: If the qualities do not exist, then even the existence Of sound and so forth becomes extremely remote. It is also impossible for pleasure and the like To exist in insentient things such as clothing.
gm: If the qualities do not exist, sound and so forth Would be very far from existing. In insentient objects like cloth and so forth, It is impossible for pleasure and so forth to exist.

dm: If things possess the nature of their cause, Has the analysis of things not already been completed? For you, the cause is pleasure and so forth, But from that, clothing and the like do not arise.
gm: If things are the nature of their cause, Have things not already been analyzed? Your cause is also pleasure and so forth, And from that, cloth and so forth do not arise.

dm: Pleasure and the like arise from clothing and such; Since those do not exist, pleasure and the like do not exist. Furthermore, a state in which pleasure and the rest are permanent Is never observed at any time.
gm: Pleasure and so forth are from cloth and so forth; Since they do not exist, pleasure and so forth do not exist. Moreover, permanent pleasure and so forth Are never observed.

dm: If pleasure and the rest were manifest as existing entities, Why is their experience not perceived? If that itself becomes subtle, How can it be both coarse and subtle?
gm: If the manifestation of pleasure and so forth exists, Why is the experience not apprehended? If that itself becomes subtle, How can it be both coarse and subtle?

dm: By abandoning the coarse and becoming subtle, Those coarse and subtle states are themselves impermanent. Why, then, do you not accept that All things are likewise impermanent?
gm: Since it becomes subtle after abandoning coarseness, That coarseness and subtlety are impermanent. Likewise, why do you not assert That all things are impermanent?

dm: If the coarse state is not other than the pleasure, Then the manifest pleasure is itself impermanent. If you claim that nothing non-existent can ever arise Because it lacks being,
gm: If coarseness is not other than pleasure, Manifest pleasure is impermanent. If you assert that nothing nonexistent Arises, because it does not exist,

dm: Then even if you do not wish it, The arising of a manifest state from what was non-existent remains a fact. If the effect exists within the cause, Then one who eats food would be eating filth.
gm: The arising of what is unmanifest Remains, even though you do not assert it. If the result abides in the cause, One who eats food would eat excrement.

dm: With the price of a garment, buy cotton seeds And wear them instead. If the world does not see this due to ignorance, Then those who know the truth have established this very fact.
gm: With the price of a cotton cloth, Buy a cotton seed and wear it. If the ignorant world does not see it, It is established by the knowers of reality.

dm: If that knowledge exists even in the world, Why is it not seen? If the world is not a valid authority, Then even seeing what is manifest is not true.
gm: That knowledge is also in the world; Since it exists, why is it not seen? If the world is not a valid cognition, Seeing the manifest is also not true.

dm: If a valid authority is not valid, Would that which is measured by it not be false? In that case, the meditation On emptiness would be untenable.
gm: If valid cognition is not valid, Is what is measured by it not false? In reality, emptiness; Meditating on it therefore becomes untenable.

dm: Without contacting the imagined entity, Its non-existence cannot be apprehended. Therefore, whatever entity is false, Its non-existence is clearly false as well.
gm: Without contacting the imputed entity, Its nonentity is not apprehended. Therefore, whatever entity is false, Its nonentity is clearly false.

dm: Thus, when a son dies in a dream, The conceptual thought that he does not exist Is an obstacle to the conceptual thought that he exists, And yet that [thought] is also false.
gm: Thus, when a child dies in a dream, The conceptualization thinking, "He does not exist," For the conceptualization of his existence Is the block, and that is also false.

dm: Therefore, when analyzed in such a manner, Nothing at all exists without a cause, Nor does it abide within conditions, Whether they be individual or assembled.
gm: Therefore, by analyzing in this way, Nothing whatever exists without a cause. In individual or assembled Conditions, it also does not abide.

dm: It does not come from elsewhere, It does not remain, and it does not depart. What difference is there between a magical illusion And this which the deluded take to be real?
gm: Neither does it come from elsewhere, Nor does it abide, nor does it go. This which the ignorant take as true, What difference does it have from an illusion?

dm: Whatever is conjured by illusion, And whatever is produced by causes— Examine where it has come from, And examine also where it goes.
gm: Whatever is emanated by an illusion, And whatever is emanated by causes, Where does it come from, And where does it go? Examine this!

dm: Whatever is seen through the proximity of something else, And does not exist without it, Is like a fabricated reflection; How could there be any true reality in that?
gm: Whatever, through the proximity of something, Is seen, and is not when that is absent, Is artificial and similar to a reflection; How can there be true existence in that?

dm: If a thing already exists, What need is there for a cause? If, on the other hand, it does not exist, What need is there for a cause?
gm: For an entity that exists, What need is there for a cause? Yet even if it does not exist, What need is there for a cause?

dm: Even by means of hundreds of millions of causes, A non-existent thing cannot be transformed. How could that state ever be an entity? And what else could possibly become an entity?
gm: Even by a hundred million causes, A nonentity cannot be transformed. How could that state be an entity? And what else could become an entity?

dm: If an entity cannot exist while it is non-existent, When will it ever become an entity? As long as an entity has not been produced, It will not be separated from non-existence.
gm: If existence is impossible at the time of nonexistence, When will it become an existing entity? Without the entity being produced, It will not separate from that nonentity.

dm: If it is not separated from non-existence, The opportunity for existence is impossible. Nor can an entity become non-existent, For that would entail having a dual nature.
gm: If it does not separate from nonentity, There is no opportunity for an entity to exist. An entity also does not become nonexistent, Because it would follow that it has two natures.

dm: Thus, there is no cessation, And likewise, there is no existence. Therefore, all these wandering beings Are eternally unborn and unceasing.
gm: Thus, there is no cessation, And there is no entity; therefore, All these migrating beings Are always unproduced and unceased.

dm: Wandering beings are like a dream; When analyzed, they are like a plantain tree. Between nirvāṇa and the state not passed beyond sorrow, In reality, there is no distinction.
gm: Migrating beings are like a dream; When analyzed, they are like a plantain tree. Even passing into nirvana or not passing into nirvana, In reality, have no difference.

dm: Thus, when things are empty, What is there to gain and what is there to lose? Who is there to show respect, And what is there to be held in utter contempt?
gm: Thus, with entities being empty, What is there to be gained, what is there to be lost? Who is there to do honor, Or what is there to completely despise?

dm: From what do happiness and suffering arise? What is there to be displeased with, and what is there to be pleased with? When searched for in that very reality, Who is it that craves, and for what do they crave?
gm: From what are happiness and suffering? What is there to displease, what is there to please? If searched for in reality, Who is craving and for what do they crave?

dm: When analyzed, in this world of the living, Who is it that will die here? What is it that will come to be, and what has already occurred? And who is a relative, and who is a friend?
gm: When analyzed, this world of living beings, Who is it that will die here? Who is it that will come to be, and who has been? Who are relatives and friends?

dm: Everything should be embraced by those like me As being just like space. Those who desire their own happiness Are, through the causes of conflict and excitement,
gm: That all things are like space, May those like me completely grasp. Those who desire happiness for themselves, Through causes of conflict and excitement,

dm: Greatly agitated or delighted. Through grief, exertion, and dispute, And by mutually cutting and piercing one another, They live with great hardship due to their sins.
gm: Become intensely agitated and elated. With sorrow, exertion, and disputes, Cutting and piercing one another, And through negative deeds, they live in great difficulty.

dm: Having come again and again to the higher realms And having enjoyed many pleasures, After death they fall into the long-lasting And unbearable sufferings of the lower realms.
gm: Having come again and again to the happy realms, And having experienced much happiness, After dying, into the sufferings of the lower realms, Which are long-lasting and unbearable, they fall.

dm: Within existence there are many precipices, And there, things are not as they truly are. Because there is mutual contradiction there as well, In existence, such a true reality does not exist.
gm: In existence, there are many abysses, And there, reality is not like this. And because they mutually contradict each other there, In existence, there is no such reality.

dm: Furthermore, that ocean of unbearable suffering Is beyond compare and without end. In that state, one's strength is likewise feeble, And there, one's lifespan is also very short.
gm: Furthermore, there is the incomparable and unbearable Boundless ocean of suffering. There, one thus has little strength, And there, life is also short.

dm: Even during that time, while living and free from illness, Through the hardships of activities, hunger, and fatigue, Through sleep and injury, and likewise Through meaningless association with the childish,
gm: Even there, for livelihood and health, Through activities, the weariness of hunger and sickness, Sleep, harm, and likewise Meaningless association with fools,

dm: Life passes by quickly and meaninglessly, And analytical discernment is extremely difficult to find. Moreover, when one is habituated to such distractions, Where is there any means to turn them back?
gm: Life passes quickly and meaninglessly; Discernment is extremely hard to find. And there, as for habituation to distraction, Where is the method to reverse it?

dm: Furthermore, in that state, Māra exerts himself To make one fall into the great miserable realms. There, the wrong paths are numerous, And it is difficult to transcend even doubt.
gm: Even there, into the great lower realms, Māra exerts himself to make them fall. There, wrong paths are many, and It is hard to overcome even doubt.

dm: Again, leisure is difficult to find, And the appearance of a Buddha is extremely rare. The river of afflictions is hard to abandon; Alas, suffering will continue in succession!
gm: Once again, leisure is hard to find, and The appearance of a Buddha is extremely hard to encounter. The river of afflictions is hard to abandon, so Alas, suffering will continue in succession.

dm: Even though they are in such extreme misery, Those who do not see their own suffering While remaining in this river of pain— Alas, they are worthy of compassion!
gm: Although suffering so extremely like this, Those who do not see their own suffering, These beings dwelling in the river of suffering, Alas, are worthy of sorrow.

dm: For example, just as some might bathe again and again Only to cast themselves repeatedly into fire, So too do these beings imagine themselves happy While remaining in a state of intense suffering.
gm: For example, like some who bathe again and again, And having done so, enter the fire again and again, Thus, in extreme suffering, Even while dwelling, they pride themselves on being happy.

dm: Thus, by behaving as if they will never grow old or die, They are first of all killed in these very places, And then the unbearable fall into the lower realms occurs.
gm: Thus, as if there were no aging and death, To those who live behaving in such a way, First of all, having been killed, The unbearable fall into the lower realms will come.

dm: When shall I be able to pacify those tormented by the fires of suffering With a cooling rain of my own bliss, Which has arisen from the clouds of merit, And thus become a source of peace?
gm: Thus, for those tormented by the fire of suffering, Well-arisen from the clouds of merit, With the rain of my own accumulation of happiness, When will I pacify them?

dm: When, by respectfully accumulating the collection of merit In a manner free from conceptual reference, Shall I teach emptiness to those Who are ruined by their conceptual grasping?
gm: When, in a non-apprehending manner, Having respectfully gathered the accumulation of merit, To those who are ruined by apprehension, Will I teach emptiness?

dm: The ninth chapter of the Engaging in the Bodhisattva Deeds, the Perfection of Wisdom.
gm: From Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva, this is the ninth chapter, on the Perfection of Wisdom.

dm: Chapter Ten: Dedication
gm: Chapter Ten: Dedication

dm: Through whatever virtue I have gained By composing this "Engaging in the Bodhisattva Deeds," May all wandering beings Enter into the conduct of enlightenment.
gm: To the Conduct of a Bodhisattva, By my having composed the Entering, Through whatever virtue that is, may all wandering beings Enter the bodhisattva conduct.

dm: May all those in every direction Who are suffering from diseases of body and mind Obtain an ocean of happiness and joy Through the power of my merit.
gm: In all directions, those with body and mind, However many are sick with suffering, May they, by my merit, Attain an ocean of happiness and joy.

dm: For as long as they remain in cyclic existence, May their happiness never decline; May wandering beings attain The uninterrupted bliss of the Bodhisattvas.
gm: For as long as they remain in saṃsāra, May they never decline from happiness. May wandering beings, of a bodhisattva, Attain uninterrupted happiness.

dm: In all the world systems, However many hells there may be, May the embodied beings within them Rejoice in the happiness of Sukhavati.
gm: In the realms of the world, the hells, However many there are, In them, may embodied beings Rejoice with the happiness of Sukhāvatī.

dm: May those tormented by cold find warmth; May those tormented by heat Be cooled by the infinite rivers Flowing from the great clouds of the Bodhisattvas.
gm: May those tormented by cold attain warmth. From the great clouds of the bodhisattvas, By the boundless rivers that have arisen, May those tormented by heat be cooled.

dm: May the forest of sword-leaves Become for them a dense sandalwood grove; May the Shalmali trees likewise Grow into wish-fulfilling trees.
gm: May the forest of sword-leaves also Become a dense sandalwood forest for them. May the trunks of the śālmali trees also Grow as wish-fulfilling trees.

dm: May they be beautified by the melodious calls of mallards, ruddy geese, swans, and cranes; May the regions of hell become delightful With lakes of great fragrant lotuses, And may they be made beautiful by such sweet sounds.
gm: Waterfowl, ducks, and geese, Swans and so forth—may they be beautified by their sweet calls. With lakes possessing greatly fragrant lotuses, May the regions of hell become delightful.

dm: May those heaps of glowing coals become heaps of jewels; May the scorched earth be spread as a crystal floor; May the mountains of the Crushing Hell also become Celestial palaces of offerings, filled with Sugatas.
gm: May those heaps of coal become heaps of jewels. May the burning ground be paved as a crystal ground. May the mountains of the Crushing Hell also, of offerings Become immeasurable palaces, filled with Sugatas.

dm: May the rain of embers, burning stones, and weapons From this moment on become a rain of flowers; And may those who strike one another with weapons Henceforth toss flowers in play.
gm: May the rain of embers, burning stones, and weapons From now on become a rain of flowers. And may that striking of one another with weapons From now on become the tossing of flowers for the sake of play.

dm: May those submerged in the fordless river, which is like a pit of fire, Their flesh all decayed and their skeletons the color of white kunda flowers, Attain celestial bodies through the power of my merit, And dwell with goddesses by the gently flowing waters.
gm: May those sinking in the unfordable river that is like a fire pit, Their flesh all destroyed, with bones the color of jasmine flowers, By the power of my virtue attain the bodies of gods, And abide together with goddesses in the Mandākinī.

dm: Why are the terrifying minions of Yama, the crows, and the vultures afraid here? Thinking, "Whose excellent power is this that dispels darkness everywhere and generates blissful joy?" They look upward and behold the blazing Vajrapāṇi dwelling in the midst of the sky; Through the force of their intense joy, may they be freed from sin and dwell in his company.
gm: "Why are the men of Yama, and the unbearable crows and vultures terrified here? Whose noble power is this, that entirely dispels darkness and generates joy and happiness?" Thinking thus, Looking upward and seeing the blazing Vajrapāṇi residing in the center of the sky, Freed from negativity through the force of intense joy, may they depart together with him.

dm: When a rain of flowers falls, mingled with scented water, And they see the glowing embers of hell extinguished with a hiss, They wonder, "What is this that has suddenly satiated us with bliss?" And thus may the denizens of hell behold Padmapāṇi.
gm: Through the falling of a rain of flowers mixed with scented water, Seeing the burning embers of hell sizzling and being extinguished, And thinking, "What is this sudden satisfaction of happiness?" May the hell beings see Padmapāṇi.

dm: Friends, cast away your fear and come here quickly to our side! Who is this radiant youth with five knots of hair who has arrived to grant us fearlessness— The compassionate Bodhisattva who thoroughly protects all beings, And through whose power we are freed from all suffering and reach the heights of joy?
gm: "Friends, cast away your fear and come quickly here to us! By whose power we are freed from all suffering and the force of joy has arrived, The one who entirely protects all wandering beings, who has given rise to bodhicitta and compassion, The blazing youth with a topknot who makes us fearless, has arrived!

dm: The crowns of a hundred gods offer worship to his lotus feet, His eyes are moist with compassion, and a rain of various flowers falls upon his head; Look at him, accompanied by the songs of praise from thousands of goddesses in lovely celestial palaces! Having seen such a Mañjughoṣa, may the denizens of hell now break into cries of joy.
gm: See how the crowns of hundreds of gods make offerings to his lotus feet, His eyes moistened with compassion, and a rain of multitudes of flowers falling upon his head, In delightful tiered palaces containing thousands of goddesses proclaiming songs of praise!" Seeing Mañjughoṣa like this, may the hell beings now cry out in joy.

dm: Thus, through my roots of virtue, may they see clouds of unobstructed Bodhisattvas such as Samantabhadra, Like clouds of bliss, raining down cool and fragrant showers; Upon seeing this, May those denizens of hell be filled with manifest joy.
gm: Likewise, by my roots of virtue, seeing Samantabhadra and other Bodhisattvas' unobstructed pleasant clouds, Letting fall a cool and fragrant rain, May those sentient beings in hell become truly joyful.

dm: May animals be free from the fear Of preying upon one another; And just like the people of the Northern Continent, May the hungry ghosts become happy.
gm: May animals be freed From the fear of eating one another. Just like the humans of Uttarakuru, May the hungry ghosts become happy.

dm: By the stream of milk flowing From the hand of the noble Avalokiteśvara, May the hungry ghosts be satisfied, And by bathing in it, may they be forever cooled.
gm: Of noble Avalokiteśvara, By the stream of milk flowing from his hands, May the hungry ghosts be satisfied, And having bathed, may they always be cooled.

dm: May the blind see forms, And may the deaf always hear sounds; Just like the goddess Māyādevī, May pregnant women also give birth without harm.
gm: May the blind see with their eyes, And the deaf always hear sounds. Just as with the goddess Māyā, May pregnant women give birth without harm.

dm: May those who are naked obtain clothing, And those who are hungry find food; May those who are thirsty obtain water, And delicious drinks as well.
gm: May the naked obtain clothing, And the hungry obtain food, May the thirsty obtain water And delicious drinks.

dm: May the destitute obtain wealth, May those afflicted by grief find joy; May the despondent be refreshed, And attain perfect steadfastness.
gm: May the destitute obtain wealth, May those tormented by sorrow obtain joy, May the despondent be restored in mind, And may their fortitude be perfect.

dm: May all sentient beings who are sick Be swiftly freed from their illnesses; May every disease of living beings, Without exception, never occur again.
gm: However many sick sentient beings there are, May they quickly be freed from illness. May the diseases of wandering beings, without exception, Never arise again.

dm: May those who are terrified be fearless; May those who are bound be liberated; May the powerless be endowed with power, And may their hearts be kind toward one another.
gm: May the frightened be fearless, May the bound be freed, May the powerless become endowed with power, And may their minds be tender toward one another.

dm: For all travelers, May every direction be auspicious; May whatever purpose they travel for Be accomplished without effort.
gm: For all travelers, May all directions be safe. Whatever purpose they are traveling for, May it be accomplished without effort.

dm: May those who have boarded boats and great ships Have the desires of their hearts fulfilled, And having safely reached the water's shore, May they rejoice together with their kinsmen.
gm: May those who embark on boats and large ships Have the wishes in their minds fulfilled, And having safely reached the shore of the water, May they rejoice together with their relatives.

dm: May those who have strayed onto desolate paths Encounter fellow travelers, And without fear of robbers, tigers, and the like, May they proceed easily without fatigue.
gm: May those wandering on astray and dreary paths Meet with fellow travelers, And without fear of bandits, tigers, and the like, May they proceed easily without fatigue.

dm: In fearful, pathless wildernesses and the like, May the gods protect children, the elderly, the helpless, And those who are asleep, intoxicated, or utterly deranged.
gm: In fearful, trackless places such as wildernesses, May children, the elderly, and the unprotected, And those who are asleep, intoxicated, or insane, Be protected by deities.

dm: May they be freed from all states of non-leisure, Endowed with faith, wisdom, and compassion, And possessing excellent food and conduct, May they always remember their past lives.
gm: Freed from all unfree states, Endowed with faith, wisdom, and compassion, And perfect in sustenance and conduct, May they always remember their past lives.

dm: May all have inexhaustible enjoyments, Just like the treasury of space. Without dispute and without harm, May they act with complete freedom.
gm: Like the treasury of space, May their enjoyments be inexhaustible, And without dispute and without harm, May they enjoy them independently.

dm: May those sentient beings who have little splendor Come to possess great splendor. May those ascetics who are physically unattractive Become endowed with perfect, beautiful forms.
gm: Whatever sentient beings have little splendor, May they become endowed with great splendor. Whatever ascetics have poor forms, May they become endowed with perfect, beautiful forms.

dm: May all the women in the world Become men. May those of lowly status attain high positions, And may their pride be utterly subdued.
gm: However many women there are in the world, May they become men. May the lowly obtain high status, And may their pride be subdued.

dm: By this merit of mine, May all sentient beings without exception, Having abandoned all misdeeds, Always engage in virtue.
gm: By this merit of mine, May all sentient beings without exception Abandon all harmful deeds And always perform virtuous ones.

dm: May they never be separated from the mind of enlightenment, May they be devoted to the conduct of awakening, May they be cared for by the Buddhas, And may they abandon the activities of Māra.
gm: Never separating from the awakening mind, And dedicating themselves to the bodhisattva conduct, May they be fully embraced by the buddhas, And abandon the actions of Māra.

dm: May all those sentient beings Have lives of immeasurable length; May they always live in happiness, And may even the sound of death never be heard.
gm: May all those sentient beings Have immeasurably long lives. May they always live happily, And may even the word "death" not be heard.

dm: May all directions be filled with groves of wish-fulfilling trees, Resounding with the sweet Dharma proclaimed By the Buddhas and the sons of the Buddhas, And may they be filled with these.
gm: With gardens of wish-fulfilling trees, Buddhas, and the children of buddhas Proclaiming the sweet sound of the Dharma, May all directions be filled.

dm: May the ground everywhere Be free from pebbles and the like, And remain naturally smooth, As level as the palm of a hand and of the nature of lapis lazuli.
gm: Everywhere, may the ground Be free of gravel and the like, As even as the palm of a hand, and of lapis lazuli, May its nature remain soft.

dm: In all the various circles of retinues, May many Bodhisattvas Dwell, having adorned the surface of the earth With their own excellence.
gm: In all the circles of retinues that exist, May many bodhisattvas Adorn the surface of the earth with their excellence, And remain dwelling there.

dm: May all embodied beings continuously hear The sound of the Dharma from birds, From trees, from all rays of light, And even from the sky itself.
gm: By all embodied beings, from birds, Trees, and all rays of light, And even from space, may the sound of the Dharma Be heard unceasingly.

dm: May they always meet with the Buddhas And the sons of the Buddhas. With infinite clouds of offerings, May they worship the teachers of the world.
gm: May they always encounter buddhas And the children of buddhas. With boundless clouds of offerings, May they make offerings to the gurus of the world.

dm: May the gods also send rain at the proper time, And may the harvests be bountiful. May kings act in accordance with the Dharma, And may the world also flourish.
gm: May the gods send rain on time, And may the harvests be perfect. May kings act in accordance with the Dharma, And may the world also prosper.

dm: May medicines be potent, And may the recitation of secret mantras be successful. May ḍākinīs, rākṣasas, and the like Be endowed with a mind of compassion.
gm: May medicines be endowed with potency, And may the recitation of secret mantras be accomplished. May ḍākinīs, rākṣasas, and the like Be endowed with minds of compassion.

dm: May no sentient being ever suffer, May they not be afraid or held in contempt, And may no one ever be unhappy.
gm: May no sentient being ever suffer, Or be afraid, or be belittled, And may none ever be unhappy.

dm: May temples be well-established, Adorned with study and recitation. May the Saṅgha always be in harmony, And may the purposes of the Saṅgha be accomplished.
gm: May monasteries, with reading and Recitation, remain well adorned. May the Saṅgha always be in harmony, And may the goals of the Saṅgha be accomplished.

dm: May those monks who desire to train Also obtain the state of solitude. Having abandoned all distractions, May they meditate with a workable mind.
gm: May monks who desire to train Attain solitary places. Having abandoned all distractions, May they meditate with pliable minds.

dm: May the nuns be endowed with requisites, And may they abandon quarreling and harm. Likewise, may all those who have gone forth Never let their ethical discipline decline.
gm: May nuns be endowed with provisions, And may they abandon quarrels and harm. Likewise, may all who are ordained Remain with unblemished discipline.

dm: Having become disillusioned by lapses in discipline, May they always exhaust their misdeeds. Having attained a higher rebirth, May their spiritual conduct not decline even there.
gm: May those with broken discipline feel remorse, And may they always exhaust their negative deeds. Having also attained higher realms, May their vows remain uncompromised even there.

dm: May the wise be honored, And may they also receive alms. May their mental continuums be completely purified, And may they be renowned in all directions.
gm: May the learned be honored And also receive alms. May their mindstreams be completely pure, And may they be renowned in all directions.

dm: May they not experience the suffering of the lower realms, And even without undergoing hardships, With bodies superior even to the gods, May they swiftly achieve Buddhahood.
gm: Without experiencing the sufferings of the lower realms, And without engaging in hardships, With bodies superior to those of the gods, May they swiftly attain buddhahood.

dm: May all sentient beings repeatedly Make offerings to all the Buddhas, And through the inconceivable bliss of the Buddhas, May they always be endowed with happiness.
gm: May all sentient beings repeatedly Make offerings to all the buddhas. With the inconceivable bliss of the buddhas, May they always be endowed with happiness.

dm: May the Bodhisattvas Fulfill their intentions to benefit wandering beings. Whatever the Protectors have intended, May that be attained by all sentient beings.
gm: May the bodhisattvas Accomplish their intentions for the welfare of beings. Whatever the protectors intend, May that be accomplished for sentient beings.

dm: Likewise, may the Pratyekabuddhas And the Śrāvakas also be happy.
gm: Likewise, may the pratyekabuddhas And the śrāvakas also be happy.

dm: Through the kindness of Mañjuśrī, Until I attain the Ground of Supreme Joy, May I always remember my past lives, And may I obtain the state of a renunciate.
gm: And through the kindness of Mañjuśrī, Until I attain the ground of Perfect Joy, May I always remember my past lives And attain ordination.

dm: May I be sustained and live, Even on a diet of the simplest food. In all my lives, may I obtain Perfect circumstances for living in solitude.
gm: May I, even with simple food, Live endowed with vitality. In all my lifetimes, May I attain the perfection of solitary places.

dm: Whenever I wish to see him, Or even wish to ask the slightest question, May I behold the Protector Mañjuśrī himself Without any hindrance.
gm: Whenever I wish to look, Or even wish to ask a slight question, May I behold the protector Mañjuśrī himself, Without any hindrance.

dm: For the sake of accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings, Reaching to the very limits of space in the ten directions, Just as Mañjuśrī acts, May my conduct also be like that.
gm: As far as the limits of space in the ten directions, In order to accomplish the aims of all sentient beings, Just as Mañjuśrī acts, May my conduct also be like that.

dm: For as long as space remains, And for as long as sentient beings remain, Until then, may I too remain, To dispel the sufferings of the world.
gm: As long as space abides, And as long as beings remain, So long may I also remain, To dispel the suffering of beings.

dm: Whatever sufferings sentient beings have, May they all ripen upon me. Through the assembly of Bodhisattvas, May all beings enjoy happiness.
gm: Whatever suffering there is for beings, May it all ripen upon me. Through the sangha of bodhisattvas, May beings experience happiness.

dm: May the teaching—the sole medicine for the suffering of beings And the source of all happiness— Endure for a long time, Together with support and honor.
gm: The sole medicine for the suffering of beings, The source of all happiness, May the teaching, along with gain and honor, Remain for a long time.

dm: I prostrate to Mañjughoṣa, Through whose kindness a virtuous mind arises. I also prostrate to my spiritual friend, Through whose kindness I have flourished.
gm: Through whose kindness a virtuous mind arises, I prostrate to Mañjuśrī. Through whose kindness I have grown, I also prostrate to the spiritual friend.

dm: This concludes the tenth chapter, entitled "Dedication," from the *Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva*.
gm: The tenth chapter, called Dedication, from Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva.

dm: Colophon
gm: Author's Colophon

dm: The *Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva*, composed by the master Śāntideva, is hereby completed.
gm: Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva, composed by the master Śāntideva, is complete.

dm: Colophon
gm: Translator's Colophon

gm: Revised and finalized by the Indian preceptor Sarvajñādeva and the chief editor-translator, the monk Paltsek, based on a Kashmiri manuscript;

dm: Later, the Indian scholar Dharmaśrībhadra and the chief editors and translators, the monks Rinchen Zangpo and Śākya Lodrö, revised, translated, and finalized it in accordance with a Central Indian manuscript and commentary.
gm: Later, it was corrected, translated, and finalized by the Indian preceptor Dharmaśrībhadra and the chief editor-translators, the monk Rinchen Zangpo and Śākya Lodrö, in accordance with manuscripts and commentaries from the central region.

dm: Furthermore, at a later time, the Indian scholar Sumatikīrti and the chief editor and translator, the monk Loden Sherab, accurately revised, translated, and thoroughly finalized it.
gm: Still later, it was correctly revised, translated, and excellently finalized by the Indian preceptor Sumatikīrti and the chief editor-translator, the fully ordained monk Loden Sherab.
